Chapter 1: Introduction, Oracle & How the Labs Work

Database and SQL concepts. Exam topic: 1 (Relational Database Concepts).

Topics in this chapter

  • 1.1 What Oracle Database Is
  • 1.2 The Five Categories of SQL Statements
  • 1.3 The 1Z0-071 (Oracle SQL) Exam
  • 1.4 The Enterprise Insight Project
  • 1.5 How the Labs Work

1.1 What Oracle Database Is

Oracle Database is a Relational DBMS built by Oracle Corporation. It main functionality is to store and manage ever growing data.

Data is a raw fact (e.g. 24000 is a ‘number’ data, while California is a ‘character’ data)

Information is a meaningful data (employee 100 earns $24000 per month in California,).

Information could be related to Business Transactions, Financial, Research, Medical, Marketing etc.

Latest Oracle version support several traditional and modern Types of data, including Numeric, Character, Timestamps, Images, Videos, Documentations, Maps, Logistics, Networks, graph and more.

Latest Oracle Database is RDBMS with many traditional and advanced features.

It stores data in structured tables (Columns and Rows)

It uses SQL as primary language to define structures, change data, query data, control access and manage transactions. It is declarative: you describe the result you want, and the optimizer decides how to get it.

Oracle’s dialect of SQL follows the ANSI/ISO standard and adds its own extensions (for example NVL, DECODE, CONNECT BY, the (+) outer-join operator). The exam tests both the standard and the Oracle-specific forms.

It provides data concurrency and consistency: Lets many users read and change data at same time without corrupting it.

It also provides indexing, concurrency control, security, backup, and highavailability features so applications can reliably store and retrieve information at scale.

Latest versions also converged for more data types, means, the same engine can manage multiple data models: traditional relational rows, JSON documents, XML, spatial/geolocation data, graph relationships, and (in Oracle 23ai and later) vector embedding used for AI search and machinelearning workloads.

SoftwareRoleDescription
Oracle DatabaseDatabase Server SoftwareDB Engine which stores and serves your data.
sqlplus Client CLIFree Built-in; Traditional Interface to write SQL and See output result.
sqlcl Client CLI (free)Free Separate download and Install; Modern Interface to write SQL and See output result.
SQL Developer Client GUI (free)Productive worksheet, schema browser, execution plans, data import/export utility support.
Sample schemasSample Data for practiceOracle’s official demo data sets: HR, CO and SH. The only data used in the labs.

Note: The labs were written against Oracle AI Database 26ai Free and the HR, CO and SH sample-schema scripts published by Oracle on GitHub. Every exam topic works identically on 19c.

1.2 The Five Categories of SQL Statements

Every SQL statement belongs to exactly one category.

Recognizing the category tells you whether the statement can be rolled back, whether it commits for you, and which privileges it needs.

CategoryNameStatementsTransaction behaviour
DQLData Query LanguageSELECTReads only; never changes data.
DMLData Manipulation LanguageINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGEChanges rows; part of a transaction; can be rolled back until you COMMIT.
DDLData Definition LanguageCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENTChanges structure; implicitly commits before and after; cannot be rolled back.
DCLData Control LanguageGRANT, REVOKEControls privileges; implicitly commits.
TCLTransaction Control LanguageCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, SET TRANSACTIONEnds or divides a transaction.

Exam focus

  • DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) and DCL statements issue an implicit COMMIT. This is a favourite exam trap.
  • TRUNCATE is DDL (fast, cannot be rolled back);
  • DELETE is DML (logged, can be rolled back).
  • MERGE is DML, it can insert and update in one statement.

Exercises, RESET and REPLAY

Each topic has numbered Exercises. Exercises that change something are followed by two boxes:

  • ↩ RESET — the exact commands that return the lab to the state it was in before the exercise. Use it when something went wrong or when you want to repeat the exercise from a clean state.
  • ↪ REPLAY — the quickest way to re-apply the exercise (usually by running the script you saved), so later chapters that depend on it keep working.

Note: Oracle also uses the words undo and redo internally (UNDO tablespace, redo log). Those are storage structures, explained in Chapter 2. The RESET and REPLAY boxes are only a study aid and have nothing to do with them.

Four Oracle techniques make RESET and REPLAY dependable. You will meet them again and again.

-- 1) Lab scripts: save each exercise as a .sql file and replay it with @HR> @labs/ch06/06_03.sql -- 2) Transaction sandbox: try DML safely, then throw it awayHR> UPDATE lab_emp SET salary = 0;       -- changes are private to your sessionHR> ROLLBACK;                            -- nothing was changed -- 3) Scratch objects: every object YOU create is prefixed LAB_ so one query finds them allHR> CREATE TABLE lab_emp AS SELECT * FROM employees;HR> DROP TABLE lab_emp PURGE;            -- RESET: remove it completely (no recycle bin) -- 4) Schema reinstall: the official installer drops and rebuilds the schema (Chapter 4)SYSTEM> @hr_install.sql                  -- answer YES to "overwrite the schema"

Caution: Rule of the lab: never run committed DML or DDL against the original sample tables. Work on LAB_ copies (created with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT). If you ever damage an original table, technique 4 restores the whole schema in about a minute.

2.1 The Relational Model in One Page

The relational model, proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970, represents all data as relations. A relation is a set of tuples that share the same attributes. In SQL those three words become table, row and column. Because a relation is a set, a table has no inherent order: the “first row” does not exist until an ORDER BY creates one.

Formal termSQL / Oracle termHR example
RelationTableEMPLOYEES
TupleRow (record)The row for employee 100
AttributeColumn (field)SALARY, HIRE_DATE
DomainData type + constraintsSALARY NUMBER(8,2)
Degree / CardinalityNumber of columns / number of rows11 columns, 107 rows
SchemaThe objects owned by one userEverything owned by HR

2.2 Keys and Referential Integrity

KeyDefinitionExample
Primary key (PK)Column(s) that uniquely identify a row. Never NULL, never duplicated. A table has at most one.EMPLOYEES.EMPLOYEE_ID
Unique keyColumn(s) that must be unique but may contain NULL. A table can have several.EMPLOYEES.EMAIL
Candidate keyAny column set that could serve as the primary key.EMPLOYEE_ID or EMAIL
Composite keyA key made of more than one column.JOB_HISTORY (EMPLOYEE_ID, START_DATE)
Foreign key (FK)Column(s) whose values must exist in the primary/unique key of a parent table (or be NULL). Enforces referential integrity.EMPLOYEES.DEPARTMENT_ID → DEPARTMENTS
Surrogate keyA meaningless generated number used as the key.CO.ORDERS.ORDER_ID
Natural keyA key that has business meaning.HR.JOBS.JOB_ID (‘IT_PROG’)

A self-referencing foreign key points back to the same table. In HR, EMPLOYEES.MANAGER_ID refers to EMPLOYEES.EMPLOYEE_ID: a manager is simply another employee. Chapters 12 and 26 exploit this.

NULL — the absence of a value

NULL is not zero and not an empty string. It means unknown or not applicable. Comparing anything to NULL gives neither true nor false but unknown, so SQL uses three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN). A WHERE clause keeps a row only when its condition is TRUE.

Exam focus

  • Any arithmetic with NULL yields NULL; NULL = NULL is not TRUE. Test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
  • Oracle treats the empty string '' as NULL in VARCHAR2 columns — a well-known difference from other databases.
  • Group functions ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)); NOT IN against a list that contains NULL returns no rows (Chapter 13).

2.3 Relationships and Cardinality

RelationshipHow it is implementedExample in the sample schemas
One-to-many (1:N)Foreign key on the “N” sideOne department has many employees (EMPLOYEES.DEPARTMENT_ID)
One-to-one (1:1)Foreign key with a unique constraintRare; for example a customer profile table
Many-to-many (M:N)An association table holding two foreign keysCO.ORDER_ITEMS links ORDERS and PRODUCTS; HR.JOB_HISTORY links EMPLOYEES and JOBS
Optional relationshipNullable foreign keyEMPLOYEES.DEPARTMENT_ID is NULL for one employee
Mandatory relationshipNOT NULL foreign keyCO.ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID
Normalisation in three sentences
  • 1NF — every column holds one atomic value (no repeating groups such as “phone1, phone2, phone3”).
  • 2NF — every non-key column depends on the whole key (no partial dependency on part of a composite key).
  • 3NF — non-key columns depend only on the key, not on each other. This is why DEPARTMENT_NAME lives in DEPARTMENTS, not in every employee row.

2.4 Relating SQL Clauses to an Entity-Relationship Diagram

An entity-relationship diagram (ERD) models the business: entities become tables, attributes become columns, relationships become foreign keys. Every part of a SELECT statement maps back to the diagram, which is the key to writing correct queries.

ERD componentSQL equivalentWhere it appears
EntityTableFROM employees
AttributeColumnSELECT last_name, salary
Instance of an entityRowRows filtered by WHERE salary > 10000
RelationshipForeign key = join conditionJOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
Cardinality (1:N)One parent row matches many child rows in a joinA department row repeats once per employee
Unique identifierPrimary keyWHERE employee_id = 100 returns at most one row
Business ruleConstraint (CHECK, NOT NULL, FK)Enforced by the table, not by SELECT
A group of instancesGroup of rowsGROUP BY department_id
The relationship between a database and SQL

The database is the stored data and its structures; SQL is the only language through which every user, tool and application talks to it. An application’s “Add employee” button, a report, an ETL job and SQL Developer all end up sending SQL text to the server. Without SQL the data is unreachable; without data SQL has nothing to operate on.

2.5 Logical and Physical Structures

Oracle separates what you see (logical) from where bytes live (physical). SQL developers work only with the logical side; DBAs manage the physical side. This separation lets a DBA move a table to faster storage without changing a single SQL statement.

LevelStructureMeaning
LogicalSchema objectTable, view, index, sequence, synonym ... owned by a user
Logical storageTablespaceA named container for segments. Defaults: SYSTEM, SYSAUX, UNDOTBS1, TEMP, USERS
Logical storageSegmentAll the storage of one object (for example the EMPLOYEES table segment)
Logical storageExtentA set of contiguous data blocks allocated to a segment
Logical storageData blockSmallest unit of I/O (default 8 KB) holding rows
PhysicalDatafileAn operating-system file that stores tablespace data
PhysicalControl fileRecords the database structure and checkpoints
PhysicalOnline redo log fileRecords every change for crash recovery

2.6 The Oracle Instance

A running Oracle Database is an instance (memory structures plus background processes) that opens a database (the files on disk). Clients never read datafiles directly; every request passes through the instance.

ComponentWhat it does for your SQL
SGA (System Global Area)Shared memory for the whole instance.
Database buffer cacheKeeps recently used data blocks so repeated queries avoid disk reads.
Shared poolLibrary cache (parsed SQL and plans) and data dictionary cache. Reusing identical SQL text avoids expensive re-parsing.
Redo log bufferHolds change records until the log writer saves them.
PGA (Program Global Area)Private memory of one server process: sort and hash work areas, session variables.
Server processExecutes the SQL of one session (dedicated server model).
DBWn (Database Writer)Writes changed (“dirty”) blocks from the buffer cache to datafiles.
LGWR (Log Writer)Writes the redo log buffer to the online redo logs. A COMMIT is durable once LGWR has written it.
CKPT (Checkpoint)Signals checkpoints so recovery after a crash is short.
SMON / PMONSystem monitor (instance recovery) and process monitor (cleans up failed sessions).
LREG (Listener Registration)Registers the database services with the listener.
ListenerA separate process on the server (default port 1521) that accepts client connections and hands them to a server process.
How a client reaches your data
Client (SQLcl, SQL Developer, application)   |  connect string:  host:port/service_name        e.g.  localhost:1521/FREEPDB1   vOracle Net  ->  Listener (port 1521)  ->  Server process  ->  Instance (SGA)  ->  Datafiles
TermDefinition
Service nameThe name a client asks for when connecting (for example FREEPDB1). The recommended way to connect.
SIDThe system identifier of one instance (for example FREE). Older style; avoid for new work.
Easy ConnectThe connect-string format host:port/service_name used throughout the labs.
SessionOne connection of one user to the instance, with its own settings and transaction.

2.7 Multitenant: CDB and PDB

Since 12c Oracle can run many pluggable databases (PDBs) inside one container database (CDB). In 21c and later, including 23ai and 26ai, multitenant is the only supported architecture for new databases. Oracle AI Database Free creates one CDB named FREE and one PDB named FREEPDB1. You always work inside FREEPDB1, which behaves like a complete database of its own. The container root CDB$ROOT is for DBAs.

NameWhat it isWhen you connect to it
FREEThe container database (CDB) serviceOnly for administrative tasks; not used in the labs
FREEPDB1The pluggable database (PDB) serviceAlways: every exercise runs here

2.8 How Oracle Processes a SQL Statement

  1. Parse — Oracle checks the syntax and the semantics (do the objects exist? do you have privileges?). It then looks in the shared pool. If an identical statement is cached it is a soft parse (cheap). Otherwise it is a hard parse: the optimizer chooses an execution plan.
  2. Bind — values for bind variables (:name) are supplied.
  3. Execute — for DML, Oracle changes the data blocks (and writes undo and redo); for a query it starts the plan.
  4. Fetch — rows of a query are returned to the client in batches.

Two ideas explain most of Oracle’s behaviour that you will meet in Chapter 16:

  • Undo stores the before-image of changed data. It makes ROLLBACK possible and gives every query a read-consistent view: a query sees the data as it was when the statement started, even while others commit changes. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
  • Redo records every change so committed work survives a crash. The SCN (system change number) is Oracle’s internal clock that orders all changes.

Exam focus

  • A transaction begins with the first DML statement and ends with COMMIT, ROLLBACK, a DDL statement, or disconnection.
  • Oracle’s default isolation level is READ COMMITTED (statement-level read consistency).

2.9 Schemas, Users and Names

A schema is the collection of objects owned by one user; in Oracle the two words are used almost interchangeably (HR is both a user and a schema). To use another schema’s object you qualify it: hr.employees.

Naming rules for objects
  • 1 to 128 bytes in 12.2 and later (30 bytes in older releases); must begin with a letter.
  • May contain letters, digits and the characters _, $ and #.
  • Must not be a reserved word (SELECT, TABLE, DATE ...) unless double-quoted.
  • Unquoted names are case-insensitive and stored in uppercase (employees = EMPLOYEES). A quoted name such as "Employees" is case-sensitive and must always be quoted. Avoid quoted names.
  • Names must be unique within a namespace: a table and a view in the same schema cannot share a name, but a table and an index can.

TypeStoresNotes

CHAR(n)Fixed-length text, blank-paddedUp to 2000 bytes. Used for codes such as COUNTRY_ID CHAR(2).
NUMBER(p,s)NumbersPrecision p (1–38 digits), scale s (digits after the decimal point). NUMBER alone is unconstrained.

3.1 Choose Your Installation Method

You need three things: a running Oracle Database, a client to type SQL into, and the sample schemas (Chapter 4). Oracle AI Database 26ai Free is Oracle’s free, fully featured edition for learning and development. Pick one row of the table; every later chapter works the same on all of them.

MethodBest forNotes
A. Windows installerWindows 10/11 x64 laptopsDownload a ZIP, run setup.exe; the database runs as a Windows service.
B. Linux RPMOracle Linux / RHEL-compatible VMs and serversdnf install the preinstall and database RPMs, then run the configure script.
C. Docker containerApple Silicon Macs (M1–M4), Intel Macs, Linux, Windows with WSL2Oracle publishes images for Arm64 and x86-64. No VM needed. Recommended for every Mac.
D. Prebuilt VMStudents who prefer an isolated, disposable machineA VirtualBox appliance on x86-64 hosts. Not usable on Apple Silicon (VirtualBox there runs only Arm64 guests).

Caution: Mac users: Oracle does not ship macOS installer binaries, and a VirtualBox/VMware image built for x86-64 will not run on an Apple Silicon Mac. Use method C (Docker). Oracle’s Free container image for Apple Silicon runs natively without emulation.

3.2 Method A — Windows

  1. Download the Microsoft Windows x64 ZIP from Oracle’s Oracle AI Database Free page (oracle.com/database/free) and extract it.
  2. Open the extracted folder and double-click setup.exe. Accept the licence, keep the default install folder, and enter an administrative password when asked. It is used for the SYS, SYSTEM and PDBADMIN accounts — write it down.
  3. Wait for the installer to finish. The listener starts on port 1521 and two services are created: FREE (the container) and FREEPDB1 (the pluggable database you will use).
  4. Open a new Command Prompt and continue with “Client Tools” below.
C:\> sc query | findstr /i "OracleService OracleOraDB"      # confirm the Oracle services are runningC:\> lsnrctl status                                          # the listener must show FREEPDB1 as READY
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
C:\> :: Settings > Apps: uninstall "Oracle AI Database Free" (or re-run setup.exe and choose remove)

3.3 Method B — Linux (RPM)

On Oracle Linux, RHEL, Rocky or Alma, as root. Oracle’s download page lists the exact package names for your release; the pattern is:

# 1) Install the preinstall package (kernel settings, oracle OS user) and the database package$ sudo dnf install -y oracle-ai-database-preinstall-26ai$ sudo dnf install -y ./oracle-ai-database-free-26ai-*.rpm# 2) Create and configure the database (asks for the administrative password)$ sudo /etc/init.d/oracle-free-26ai configure# 3) Check the listener and the services$ sudo systemctl status oracle-free-26ai

Note: The configure script creates the container database FREE with one pluggable database FREEPDB1 and a listener on port 1521. Configuration parameters live in /etc/sysconfig/oracle-free-26ai.conf. Package and script names follow Oracle’s download page and installation guide for your release: use the exact names printed there and by the RPM installation.

↩ RESET — undo this exercise
$ sudo /etc/init.d/oracle-free-26ai delete       # removes the database$ sudo dnf remove -y oracle-ai-database-free-26ai   # removes the software

3.4 Method C — Docker (all Macs, Linux, Windows with WSL2)

This is the quickest and the only reliable option for Apple Silicon. Install Docker Desktop (docker.com) first, then give it enough memory: Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → Memory: 4 GB minimum, 6–8 GB recommended.

Wait for the ready message$ docker logs -f oracle-free...#########################DATABASE IS READY TO USE!#########################

A SQL Developer connection (graphical)
  1. Open SQL Developer → New Connection (the green plus).
  2. Name: FreePDB1 - SYSTEM. Username: SYSTEM. Password: your administrative password.
  3. Connection type Basic: Hostname localhost, Port 1521, Service name FREEPDB1 (not SID).
  4. Click Test, then Connect. A worksheet opens: type a statement and press Ctrl+Enter (run one statement) or F5 (run a whole script).

3.8 The Lab Folder and login.sql

Create one folder for all your scripts and start SQLcl from inside it, so that relative paths such as @labs/ch05/05_01.sql work. A file named login.sql in that folder is read automatically at start-up by SQLcl and sets friendly defaults.

$ mkdir -p ~/oracle-labs/labs && cd ~/oracle-labs        # Windows: mkdir C:\oracle-labs\labs$ cat > login.sql <<'EOF'REM login.sql - runs automatically when SQLcl starts in this folderSET SQLPROMPT "_USER> "REM characters per output line, and rows between column headingsSET LINESIZE 160SET PAGESIZE 100REM show messages from PL/SQL, elapsed time and the n rows selected messageSET SERVEROUTPUT ONSET TIMING ONSET FEEDBACK ONEOF$ ln -s ~/oracle-labs/login.sql $ORACLE_HOME/sqlcl/login.sql   #login.sql default source location

Tip: In SQL Developer there is no prompt; type the statement shown after the prompt and ignore the prompt itself. Settings such as SET LINESIZE apply to SQLcl and to script runs (F5) in SQL Developer.

SQLcl in five minutes

  • Recall and edit: press Up and Down to bring back statements you typed before; move with Left and Right to fix a typo and press Enter to run it again. A statement that spans several lines can be edited line by line before you run it.
  • Complete with Tab: type the start of a keyword, table or column name and press Tab, for example SELECT * FROM emp then Tab.
  • History: HISTORY lists the statements of your session; HELP HISTORY shows how to run an earlier one again in your version.
  • Help: HELP lists all commands; HELP command explains one.
  • Inspect a table: INFO employees shows columns, indexes and constraints; DDL employees shows its CREATE statement.
  • Output format: SET SQLFORMAT CSV prints results as CSV; SET SQLFORMAT ANSICONSOLE returns to the normal table layout.
  • Finish: end a statement with ; and press Enter; EXIT leaves SQLcl and commits your work.

3.9 Troubleshooting Connections

SymptomLikely cause and fix
ORA-12541: TNS:no listenerThe database or container is not running, or the port is wrong. Start it (docker start oracle-free, the Windows service, or systemctl start) and check port 1521.
ORA-12514: service FREEPDB1 not known / ORA-12528The database is still starting (wait for “DATABASE IS READY TO USE!”) or you mistyped the service name.
ORA-01017: invalid username/passwordWrong password. For SYSTEM it is the administrative password you chose.
ORA-28000: the account is lockedUnlock it as SYSTEM: ALTER USER hr ACCOUNT UNLOCK;
Connection works but CON_NAME is CDB$ROOTYou used the service FREE. Reconnect with localhost:1521/FREEPDB1.
sql: command not foundSQLcl’s bin folder is not on your PATH, or Java is missing.
Docker: container exits at onceNot enough memory for Docker Desktop (give it 4 GB or more) or a leftover volume from an older release.

4.8 The HR Schema in Detail

Figure 4.1 — The HR schema (1 = parent side, N = child side of each relationship)

Think of a company. Each box in the diagram is one table, and the lines show how the tables connect. The company has regions, each region has countries, each country has locations (offices), and each location has departments. Every employee works in a department and has a job. A "1" on a line means one row on that side, and an "N" means many rows on the other. So one department has many employees, but each employee belongs to only one department. Every table has a PK (primary key), an ID that identifies each row, and an FK (foreign key), a column that holds the ID of a row in another table. That is how the tables link. Two details to remember: the EMPLOYEES table also points to itself through manager_id, because a manager is just another employee. JOB_HISTORY keeps the past jobs of an employee who changed role.

TableRowsHoldsKey columns
REGIONS5Geographic regions (Europe, Americas, Asia, Oceania, Africa)REGION_ID (PK)
COUNTRIES25Countries and their regionCOUNTRY_ID CHAR(2) (PK), REGION_ID (FK)
LOCATIONS23Office/warehouse addressesLOCATION_ID (PK), COUNTRY_ID (FK)
DEPARTMENTS27Departments, each with one location and an optional managerDEPARTMENT_ID (PK), LOCATION_ID, MANAGER_ID (FKs)
JOBS19Job titles with minimum and maximum salaryJOB_ID VARCHAR2(10) (PK)
EMPLOYEES107Employees: name, e-mail, hire date, job, salary, commission, manager, departmentEMPLOYEE_ID (PK); JOB_ID, MANAGER_ID, DEPARTMENT_ID (FKs)
JOB_HISTORY10Past jobs of employees who changed job or department(EMPLOYEE_ID, START_DATE) (PK)
Other HR objectsNotes
Sequences DEPARTMENTS_SEQ, EMPLOYEES_SEQ, LOCATIONS_SEQGenerate new key values (Chapter 19).
View EMP_DETAILS_VIEWA ready-made join of employees, departments, jobs, locations, countries and regions (Chapter 20).
Procedures ADD_JOB_HISTORY, SECURE_DML; triggers SECURE_EMPLOYEES, UPDATE_JOB_HISTORYProgram units. UPDATE_JOB_HISTORY fires when JOB_ID or DEPARTMENT_ID of an employee is updated and inserts a JOB_HISTORY row. SECURE_EMPLOYEES is delivered disabled; if it is enabled, DML outside office hours is refused.

Caution: Because of those triggers, update the real EMPLOYEES table only inside a transaction you roll back. Committed changes belong on a LAB_ copy (a table created with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT does not copy triggers).

A feeling for the HR data
  • Employee 100, Steven King, is the president: his MANAGER_ID is NULL and he works in department 90 (Executive).
  • One employee (Kimberely Grant) has no department: her DEPARTMENT_ID is NULL. Remember her; she makes outer joins interesting.
  • Department 50 (Shipping) has 45 employees and department 80 (Sales) has 34; sixteen departments have no employees at all.
  • Only sales people earn a commission (COMMISSION_PCT): 35 employees have one, 72 do not.

4.9 The CO Schema in Detail

Figure 4.2 — The CO schema

Think of an online and in-store shop. Customers place orders at a store, and each order contains one or more lines in order_items, where each line is a product with its price and quantity. The company also sends goods to customers, which is tracked in shipments, and an order line can point to the shipment that delivers it. Inventory records how many units of each product a store has in stock. As in the HR diagram, a "1" on a line means one row on that side and an "N" means many on the other, so one customer can have many orders but each order belongs to one customer. The PK identifies each row, and an FK is a column that holds the ID of a row in another table, which is how the tables link. One special detail: the products table stores extra information (colour, brand, reviews) as a JSON document in product_details.

TableHoldsNotes
CUSTOMERSOne row per customer: CUSTOMER_ID, EMAIL_ADDRESS, FULL_NAMEE-mail is unique
STORESPhysical and online stores: name, web address, physical address, latitude/longitude, logoAt least one of web or physical address must exist (a CHECK constraint)
PRODUCTSProducts with UNIT_PRICE and PRODUCT_DETAILS, a JSON document stored in a BLOBThe data represents a clothing line (Chapter 28)
ORDERSORDER_ID, ORDER_TMS (TIMESTAMP), CUSTOMER_ID, ORDER_STATUS, STORE_IDStatus values are limited by a CHECK constraint
ORDER_ITEMSThe lines of each order: product, price at purchase time, quantity, shipmentComposite key (ORDER_ID, LINE_ITEM_ID)
SHIPMENTSDelivery address and status for goods sent to customers
INVENTORYQuantity of each product available in each storeOne row per store and product

Note: In CO the primary key columns are generated automatically when you insert NULL or omit them (identity columns), which keeps INSERT statements short in Chapter 15.

4.10 The SH Schema in Detail

Figure 4.3 — The SH star schema (the COSTS fact table has the same dimension keys as SALES)

SH is built like a star. In the middle is the SALES table, which records every sale: which product, which customer, which day, which channel and which promotion, plus how many units were sold and the amount. Around it are the small "who, what, when, how" tables that describe those sales: PRODUCTS (what was sold), CUSTOMERS (who bought, with their COUNTRIES), TIMES (when), CHANNELS (how, for example direct or internet) and PROMOTIONS (which campaign). The big table in the middle is called a fact table and the small ones around it are dimension tables. The lines work as in the other diagrams: a "1" is one row, an "N" is many, so one product appears in many sales. To answer a question such as "sales per quarter per channel", you join SALES to the dimension tables you need. The COSTS table is a second fact table with the same keys, but it holds the unit cost and price instead of sales. It has no lines drawn in this picture, to keep it readable.

SH is a star schema: a large fact table (SALES, COSTS) holds measures such as AMOUNT_SOLD, surrounded by small dimension tables that describe the facts: TIMES, CHANNELS, PROMOTIONS, PRODUCTS, CUSTOMERS and COUNTRIES. Questions like “sales by quarter, product category and channel” simply join the fact table to its dimensions.

TableTypeMeaning
SALESFactOne row per sale: product, customer, date, channel, promotion, QUANTITY_SOLD, AMOUNT_SOLD
COSTSFactUnit cost and unit price by product, date, promotion and channel
TIMESDimensionOne row per day with calendar and fiscal weeks, months, quarters and years
CHANNELSDimensionSales channels (for example direct, partners, internet)
PROMOTIONSDimensionMarketing promotions with category, cost and dates
PRODUCTSDimensionProducts with subcategory, category, list price and status
CUSTOMERSDimensionCustomers with city, state, income level and country
COUNTRIESDimensionCountries with sub-region and region

SH also contains partitioned fact tables, bitmap indexes, dimension objects, materialized views and a PROFITS view, depending on the script release. Chapter 29 shows you how to discover exactly what is present with the data dictionary.

4.11 Resetting a Sample Schema

SituationWhat to do
You changed rows but have not committedROLLBACK;
You created LAB_ objects and want them goneDROP TABLE lab_xxx PURGE; (or the cleanup script of Chapter 21)
You committed changes to an original table, dropped a table or damaged constraintsReinstall the schema: run its *_install.sql as SYSTEM and answer YES to overwrite. Oracle’s manual states that a reinstall simply drops the old user and all its objects first.
You want the schema goneRun the matching *_uninstall.sql as SYSTEM.

Exam focus

  • The data dictionary shows object names in uppercase because unquoted identifiers are stored in uppercase. Remember it when you write WHERE table_name = 'EMPLOYEES' in Chapter 21.

Hint: Use two scalar subqueries against dual, or COUNT(*) ... WHERE department_id IS NULL.

Challenge 4.2 List the three tables of SH that are the largest by number of rows.

Hint: Query USER_TABLES (the NUM_ROWS column holds optimizer statistics) or count the rows of each table.

Chapter 5: SELECT Basics

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 2: Retrieving Data Using the SQL SELECT Statement • Read-only chapter: nothing to reset.

Topics in this chapter

  • 5.1 The SELECT Statement
  • 5.2 Column Aliases
  • 5.3 Arithmetic Expressions
  • 5.4 Concatenation and Literal Strings
  • 5.5 Eliminating Duplicate Rows: DISTINCT
  • 5.6 Expressions Without a Table: DUAL
  • 5.7 Formatting Output in SQLcl
  • 5.8 Writing Readable SQL
  • 5.9 Common Errors in Simple Queries
  • 5.10 Answers to the Lab Challenges

5.1 The SELECT Statement

SELECT retrieves data and never changes it. Its two mandatory parts are the select list (what you want) and the FROM clause (where it lives). In database terms you project columns and select rows.

SELECT  [DISTINCT | UNIQUE]  { * | column [[AS] alias] | expression [[AS] alias] } [, ...]FROM    table_or_view[WHERE  condition]  [GROUP BY ...]  [HAVING ...]  [ORDER BY ... ASC | DESC];

Exercise 5.1 Meet the HR tables with DESCRIBE

DESCRIBE (abbreviated DESC) is a SQLcl command — not a SQL statement — that lists the columns, nullability and data types of a table without reading any rows.

HR> DESC[RIBE] employeesName            Null?    Type--------------- -------- ------------EMPLOYEE_ID     NOT NULL NUMBER(6)FIRST_NAME               VARCHAR2(20)LAST_NAME       NOT NULL VARCHAR2(25)EMAIL           NOT NULL VARCHAR2(25)PHONE_NUMBER             VARCHAR2(20)HIRE_DATE       NOT NULL DATEJOB_ID          NOT NULL VARCHAR2(10)SALARY                   NUMBER(8,2)COMMISSION_PCT           NUMBER(2,2)MANAGER_ID               NUMBER(6)DEPARTMENT_ID            NUMBER(4)-- try the others: regions, countries, locations, jobs, job_historyHR> DESC departments

Exercise 5.2 Select everything, then select what you need

-- * returns every column in the order the table was createdHR> SELECT * FROM departments;DEPARTMENT_ID DEPARTMENT_NAME   MANAGER_ID LOCATION_ID------------- ----------------- ---------- -----------           10 Administration           200        1700           20 Marketing                201        1800           30 Purchasing               114        1700...                                                 (27 rows in all) -- an explicit column list returns only those columns, in the order YOU chooseHR> SELECT department_name, department_id FROM departments;

Tip: In production code, list the columns you need instead of using SELECT *: it is faster, survives table changes and documents intent. SELECT * is fine for exploring.

Exam focus

  • SELECT *, salary*12 FROM employees is invalid (ORA-00923). To mix * with other items qualify it: SELECT employees.*, salary*12 FROM employees.
  • Keywords, table names and column names are not case-sensitive; character data between quotes is.
  • A SQL statement may span several lines and ends with ; in SQLcl or / on its own line.

5.2 Column Aliases

An alias gives a column or expression a different heading in the result. It exists only for that statement and never changes the table. AS is optional. Without double quotes an alias is shown in uppercase and must be one word; double quotes keep case and allow spaces and special characters.

Exercise 5.3 Alias rules

HR> SELECT last_name                  AS surname,        -- AS makes the alias obvious    salary * 12                     annual_salary,     -- AS is optional    commission_pct                  "Commission %"     -- quotes: mixed case and a space    FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 145;SURNAME   ANNUAL_SALARY Commission %--------- ------------- ------------Singh           168000          .4

Exam focus

  • An alias cannot be used in the WHERE clause of the same query (WHERE is evaluated before the select list). It can be used in ORDER BY.
  • A column alias in double quotes keeps its exact case and may contain spaces; unquoted aliases are folded to uppercase.

5.3 Arithmetic Expressions

You may use + - * / on NUMBER and DATE columns and on literals. Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction; operators of the same precedence run left to right; parentheses override everything. Oracle has no integer-division operator: 7/2 is 3.5.

Exercise 5.4 Annual salary and a raise

HR> SELECT last_name, salary,           salary * 12            AS annual,            -- * before +           salary + 100 * 12      AS wrong_raise,       -- 100*12 first, then + salary           (salary + 100) * 12    AS annual_after_raise -- parentheses force the addition first    FROM   employees    WHERE  employee_id = 100;LAST_NAME   SALARY   ANNUAL WRONG_RAISE ANNUAL_AFTER_RAISE----------- ------ -------- ---------- ------------------King         24000   288000      25200             289200
NULL in arithmetic

Any arithmetic that involves NULL gives NULL. Only sales people have a commission, so a calculation that uses COMMISSION_PCT is NULL for everyone else.

HR> SELECT last_name, salary, commission_pct,           salary * commission_pct AS commission_amount    FROM   employees    WHERE  employee_id IN (145, 100);LAST_NAME   SALARY COMMISSION_PCT COMMISSION_AMOUNT----------- ------ -------------- -----------------Singh        14000             .4              5600King         24000-- King’s commission_pct is NULL, so the product is NULL (shown as blank)

Tip: You will fix that NULL problem with NVL and COALESCE in Chapter 9. For now simply recognise it.

5.4 Concatenation and Literal Strings

The concatenation operator || joins strings. A literal is a fixed value written in the statement: character and date literals go in single quotes, numeric literals do not. A single quote inside a literal is written twice (''). The alternative quote operator q'[ ... ]' lets you pick your own delimiter so you do not have to double quotes.

Exercise 5.5 Build sentences from columns

HR> SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name           AS full_name,           last_name || '''s job id is ' || job_id  AS sentence      -- '' = one apostrophe    FROM   employees    WHERE  employee_id = 100;FULL_NAME     SENTENCE------------- ----------------------------Steven King   King's job id is AD_PRES -- the alternative quote operator: any delimiter pair [] {} () <> or !! worksHR> SELECT q'[It's Steven King's record]'            AS note1,           q'{Dept "Sales" - it's big}'              AS note2    FROM   dual;

CONCAT(a, b) joins exactly two strings (nest calls for more). In Oracle, concatenating a NULL is harmless: it behaves like an empty string.

HR> SELECT CONCAT(CONCAT(first_name, ' '), last_name) AS full_name,   -- two nested CONCAT calls           'Commission: ' || commission_pct            AS comm_text       -- NULL becomes nothing    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 145);

Exam focus

  • || treats NULL as an empty string; CONCAT also does; arithmetic + with NULL gives NULL — know the difference.
  • 'It''s' and q'[It's]' produce the same string.
  • A number used with || is converted to text implicitly (see Chapter 9).

5.5 Eliminating Duplicate Rows: DISTINCT

DISTINCT (or its synonym UNIQUE) removes duplicate rows from the result. It applies to the combination of all selected columns, not to one column, and treats two NULLs as the same value. It is written once, immediately after SELECT.

Exercise 5.6 Which departments and jobs are in use?

HR> SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees ORDER BY department_id;...    (11 department numbers and one NULL, which sorts last)HR> SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) AS departments_with_staff FROM employees;11                                  -- COUNT ignores the NULLHR> SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_id FROM employees ORDER BY 1, 2;-- the unique PAIRS: the same department appears several times, once per job it contains
You writeMeaning
SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_idone row per distinct (department, job) pair
SELECT department_id, DISTINCT job_idError: DISTINCT must come directly after SELECT
SELECT UNIQUE job_ididentical to DISTINCT (Oracle synonym)

5.6 Expressions Without a Table: DUAL

A query needs a FROM clause. When you only want to evaluate an expression or a function, use the one-row table DUAL.

HR> SELECT 2 + 3 AS five, 'Oracle' || ' SQL' AS name, SYSDATE AS now FROM dual;HR> SELECT user AS who_am_i FROM dual;                         -- the current user: HR

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: Oracle 23ai and later allow a query without a FROM clause: SELECT 2 + 3;. On the 19c-level exam, FROM dual is still required.

5.7 Formatting Output in SQLcl

COLUMN controls how a column is displayed by the client; it never changes the data. A15 means “text, 15 characters wide”; numeric formats use 9 (digit), 0 (forced zero), , and $.

HR> COLUMN last_name  FORMAT A15HR> COLUMN salary     FORMAT $99,999.00HR> COLUMN last_name  HEADING 'Employee'HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100;Employee            SALARY--------------- ----------King          $24,000.00HR> COLUMN last_name CLEAR      -- remove the setting (CLEAR COLUMNS removes all of them)

5.8 Writing Readable SQL

  • One clause per line; keywords in UPPERCASE, object names in lowercase; indent the select list.
  • Always alias calculated columns and use meaningful aliases.
  • Qualify columns with a table alias as soon as a statement uses more than one table (Chapter 11).
  • Put a comment above anything not obvious: -- text to the end of the line, or /* text */ for several lines.

5.9 Common Errors in Simple Queries

ErrorTypical causeExample
ORA-00923: FROM keyword not found where expectedA missing comma, or * combined with other columns, or a missing FROMSELECT last_name salary FROM employees (no comma: salary becomes an alias, so it works!) versus SELECT *, salary FROM employees (error)
ORA-00904: invalid identifierMisspelled column, or an alias used in WHEREWHERE annual > 1000 where annual is an alias
ORA-00942: table or view does not existMisspelled table, wrong schema, or no privilegeSELECT * FROM employee
ORA-00933: SQL command not properly endedExtra text after the statement, or an unsupported clauseSELECT ... FROM employees LIMIT 5 (LIMIT is not Oracle SQL)
ORA-00936: missing expressionA comma or operator with nothing after itSELECT last_name, FROM employees

Tip: A missing comma between two columns is not always an error: SELECT last_name salary FROM employees silently returns one column named SALARY that actually contains the last names. Always re-read the headings of your result.

Challenge 5.1 Show each employee as one text column named badge: ID 100 | KING | AD_PRES (last name in uppercase).

Hint: Concatenate literals with employee_id, UPPER(last_name) and job_id.

Chapter 6: Restricting and Sorting Data

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 3: Restricting and Sorting Data • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 6.1 The WHERE Clause
  • 6.2 IN, BETWEEN and LIKE in Depth
  • 6.3 Logical Operators and Precedence
  • 6.4 Sorting with ORDER BY
  • 6.5 Limiting the Rows Returned
  • 6.6 Substitution Variables
  • 6.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

6.1 The WHERE Clause

WHERE keeps only the rows for which its condition is TRUE (rows where the condition is FALSE or UNKNOWN are discarded). It follows the FROM clause. Character and date literals go in single quotes; character comparisons are case-sensitive.

OperatorMeaningExample
= <> != ^=Equal / not equal (three spellings of not-equal)WHERE department_id <> 50
< <= > >=Less / greater, with or without equalityWHERE salary >= 10000
BETWEEN a AND bInclusive range; write the lower value firstWHERE salary BETWEEN 5000 AND 6000
IN (list)Equal to any value in the listWHERE department_id IN (10, 20, 30)
LIKE patternPattern match: % any characters, _ exactly oneWHERE last_name LIKE ‘K%’
IS NULL / IS NOT NULLTest for the absence / presence of a valueWHERE commission_pct IS NULL

Exercise 6.1 Filter with comparison operators

HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 90;EMPLOYEE_ID LAST_NAME   SALARY----------- ---------- -------        100 King         24000        101 Yang         17000        102 Garcia       17000 HR> SELECT last_name, job_id FROM employees WHERE job_id = 'IT_PROG';   -- 5 programmersHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE last_name = 'king';            -- no rows: case matters-- 1 row: compare in one caseHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'KING';

Exam focus

  • BETWEEN 6000 AND 5000 returns no rows and no error: the lower limit must come first.
  • Both limits of BETWEEN are included (>= low AND <= high).
  • Comparing with NULL (= NULL, <> NULL) is never TRUE; use IS NULL.

6.2 IN, BETWEEN and LIKE in Depth

Exercise 6.2 Lists, ranges and patterns

HR> SELECT last_name, department_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (10, 20, 40);-- IN is shorthand for OR:  department_id = 10 OR department_id = 20 OR department_id = 40HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 9000 AND 10000;HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE last_name LIKE 'K%';       -- starts with KHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE last_name LIKE '%son';     -- ends with sonHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE last_name LIKE '_a%';      -- second letter is aHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE last_name LIKE '%a%a%';    -- at least two letter a
Searching for a real % or _ : ESCAPE

When the text you search contains % or _, declare an escape character and put it in front of the wildcard you mean literally. HR’s job codes contain underscores (IT_PROG).

HR> SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE job_id LIKE 'IT\_%' ESCAPE '\';-- IT\_%  means: the letters IT, a literal underscore, then anythingJOB_ID----------IT_PROGHR> SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE job_id LIKE 'IT_%';-- without ESCAPE the _ matches any single character: IT_PROG still matches, but so would ITXPROG
Dates in conditions

Never compare a DATE column with an ambiguous string. Use an ANSI date literal (DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD') or TO_DATE with an explicit format (Chapter 9). A DATE also contains a time; a literal date means midnight of that day.

HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date FROM employees    WHERE  hire_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND hire_date < DATE '2018-01-01';   -- all of 2017HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date FROM employees    WHERE  hire_date BETWEEN TO_DATE('01-JAN-2015','DD-MON-YYYY')                         AND TO_DATE('31-DEC-2015','DD-MON-YYYY');

Exam focus

  • LIKE '%' does not match a NULL value.
  • NOT IN (list) with a NULL inside the list returns no rows (Chapter 13).
  • The default date display format is DD-MON-RR unless the session setting NLS_DATE_FORMAT is changed; always use explicit formats in code.

6.3 Logical Operators and Precedence

AND, OR and NOT combine conditions. They have a defined order: Oracle evaluates in this order of precedence (highest first), and parentheses always win.

LevelOperators
1Arithmetic: unary + -, then * /, then + - and the concatenation ||
2Comparison conditions: = < > <= >= <>
3IS [NOT] NULL, [NOT] LIKE, [NOT] BETWEEN, [NOT] IN
4NOT
5AND
6OR (lowest)

Exercise 6.3 The AND/OR trap

-- AND binds tighter than OR. This means:  IT_PROG  OR  (FI_MGR AND salary > 15000)HR> SELECT last_name, job_id, salary FROM employees    WHERE  job_id = 'IT_PROG' OR job_id = 'FI_MGR' AND salary > 15000;5 rows: the five programmers (the only FI_MGR earns 12008, so that branch adds nothing) -- Parentheses change the meaning:  (IT_PROG OR FI_MGR)  AND  salary > 15000HR> SELECT last_name, job_id, salary FROM employees    WHERE  (job_id = 'IT_PROG' OR job_id = 'FI_MGR') AND salary > 15000;no rows selected
NULL tests
-- 72 employees earn no commissionHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE commission_pct IS NULL;HR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE commission_pct IS NOT NULL;   -- 35 doHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NULL;       -- 1 row: GrantHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE commission_pct = NULL;        -- 0 : never TRUE

6.4 Sorting with ORDER BY

ORDER BY sorts the result. It is always the last clause and the only place besides the select list where a column alias is allowed. Default is ascending (ASC). You may sort by columns, expressions, aliases, or the position of an item in the select list.

Exercise 6.4 Sorting options

HR> SELECT last_name, department_id, salary FROM employees    ORDER BY department_id ASC, salary DESC;        -- department first, then highest pay firstHR> SELECT last_name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM employees    ORDER BY annual DESC;                           -- sort by an alias-- by position: salary desc, then nameHR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1;-- you may sort by a column you do not showHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
Where do NULLs go?

In an ascending sort Oracle puts NULLs last; in a descending sort it puts them first (Oracle treats NULL as larger than any value). You can override this with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.

-- NULLs lastHR> SELECT last_name, commission_pct FROM employees ORDER BY commission_pct;-- NULLs firstHR> SELECT last_name, commission_pct FROM employees ORDER BY commission_pct DESC;HR> SELECT last_name, commission_pct FROM employees    -- highest commissions first, the 72 NULLs at the end    ORDER BY commission_pct DESC NULLS LAST;

Exam focus

  • With SELECT DISTINCT, ORDER BY may only use columns that appear in the select list.
  • Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed, even if the rows appear in the same order today.
  • Sorting by position (ORDER BY 2) refers to the select list, not to the table.

6.5 Limiting the Rows Returned

FETCH FIRST ... (12c and later, ANSI style)
HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC    FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY;                 -- top 3: King 24000, Yang    17000, Garcia  17000HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC    FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS WITH TIES;            -- 3 rows: the 17000 tie is kept togetherHR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC    FETCH FIRST 5 PERCENT ROWS ONLY;         -- the top 5% of the 107 rows (rounded up: 6 rows)-- pagination: skip 10 rows, return the next 10  (page 2 of a report)HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees ORDER BY employee_id    OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
ROWNUM (the classic way)

ROWNUM is a pseudocolumn that numbers rows as they are fetched, before ORDER BY is applied. That makes the following common mistake very important to understand.

-- WRONG for "top 3 salaries": Oracle takes any 3 rows FIRST, then sorts only thoseHR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 ORDER BY salary DESC; -- RIGHT: sort first inside an inline view, then number the sorted rowsHR> SELECT last_name, salary    FROM  (SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC)    WHERE ROWNUM <= 3; -- ROWNUM is assigned only to rows that pass; "= 2" can never be true, because row 1 is never producedHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE ROWNUM = 2;      -- no rows selected

Exam focus

  • ROWNUM <= n works; ROWNUM = 2 and ROWNUM > 1 return no rows.
  • FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY and OFFSET are applied after ORDER BY.
  • WITH TIES can return more than n rows; ONLY never does.

6.6 Substitution Variables

A substitution variable is a placeholder processed by the client (SQLcl, SQL Developer) before the statement is sent to the server. &name asks for a value every time; &&name asks once and remembers the value for the session. Character and date values need quotes: write '&name'.

Exercise 6.5 Prompt for values

HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = &dept;Enter value for dept: 90old   1: SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = &deptnew   1: SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 90... (the three Executive employees) HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE job_id = '&job_id';     -- quotes around a text valueHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE department_id = &&dept;   -- asked once ...HR> SELECT department_name FROM departments WHERE department_id = &&dept;  -- ... remembered here
DEFINE, UNDEFINE, ACCEPT and VERIFY
CommandPurpose
DEFINE name = valueCreate a variable without any prompt. DEFINE alone lists all variables; DEFINE name shows one.
UNDEFINE nameDelete a variable (so &&name asks again).
ACCEPT name PROMPT ‘text’Ask the user once, with your own prompt text; add DEFAULT value (before PROMPT) or HIDE if needed.
SET VERIFY OFF / ONHide / show the old and new lines that show the substitution.
SET DEFINE OFFStop the client from treating & as special (needed when a literal contains &, such as ‘AT&T’).
HR> SET VERIFY OFFHR> DEFINE min_sal = 10000HR> ACCEPT dept NUMBER DEFAULT 80 PROMPT 'Department number: 'HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees    WHERE  department_id = &dept AND salary >= &min_sal    ORDER BY salary DESC;HR> DEFINE dept                       -- shows: DEFINE DEPT = 80 (NUMBER)HR> UNDEFINE dept min_sal             -- clean up

Exam focus

  • && defines the variable the first time and reuses it; & prompts again every time it is seen.
  • Variables can hold column names, table names, whole WHERE clauses or ORDER BY clauses — they are plain text replacement.
  • In SQL Developer, & shows a prompt window; use SET DEFINE OFF before running scripts that contain a genuine &.

Chapter 7: Single-Row Functions: Characters and Numbers

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 4: Using Single-Row Functions to Customize Output (character and number functions) • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 7.1 What a Single-Row Function Is
  • 7.2 Case Conversion Functions
  • 7.3 Character Manipulation Functions
  • 7.4 Number Functions
  • 7.5 Functions and Performance in One Paragraph
  • 7.6 Answers to the Lab Challenges

7.1 What a Single-Row Function Is

A single-row function takes values from one row and returns one value per row. (Group functions, Chapter 10, collapse many rows into one.) Single-row functions can appear in the select list, in WHERE, in ORDER BY and inside each other. They are grouped by the type of data they handle:

CategoryExamplesChapter
CharacterUPPER, LOWER, INITCAP, SUBSTR, INSTR, LENGTH, LPAD, TRIM, REPLACE7
NumberROUND, TRUNC, MOD, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, POWER7
DateSYSDATE, MONTHS_BETWEEN, ADD_MONTHS, NEXT_DAY, LAST_DAY8
ConversionTO_CHAR, TO_NUMBER, TO_DATE9
General / NULL handlingNVL, NVL2, NULLIF, COALESCE, CASE, DECODE9

Tip: Practise any function against dual first: SELECT UPPER('oracle') FROM dual;. Because the input is a literal you can predict the answer and check yourself.

7.2 Case Conversion Functions

FunctionResult for the argument ‘hELLO wORLD’
UPPER(x)HELLO WORLD
LOWER(x)hello world
INITCAP(x)Hello World (first letter of each word upper, the rest lower)

Exercise 7.1 Case-insensitive search

HR> SELECT UPPER('Oracle') AS up, LOWER('SQL') AS low, INITCAP('hELLO wORLD') AS init FROM dual;UP      LOW INIT------- --- -----------ORACLE  sql Hello World -- stored names are Mixed case, so compare in ONE case on both sidesHR> SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees WHERE LOWER(last_name) = 'king';100 King

7.3 Character Manipulation Functions

FunctionPurposeExample → result
CONCAT(a, b)Join two stringsCONCAT(‘Hello’, ‘World’) → HelloWorld
SUBSTR(s, start [, len])Extract part of a string. Position 1 is the first character; a negative start counts from the end.SUBSTR(‘HelloWorld’, 1, 5) → Hello; SUBSTR(‘HelloWorld’, -5) → World
LENGTH(s)Number of charactersLENGTH(‘HelloWorld’) → 10
INSTR(s, find [, start [, n]])Position of the first n-th occurrence of find; 0 if not foundINSTR(‘HelloWorld’, ‘o’) → 5; INSTR(‘HelloWorld’, ‘o’, 1, 2) → 7
LPAD(s, n, pad)Pad on the left to total length nLPAD(‘7’, 3, ‘0’) → 007
RPAD(s, n, pad)Pad on the right to total length nRPAD(‘Ab’, 5, ‘*’) → Ab***
TRIM([LEADING|TRAILING|BOTH] c FROM s)Remove a single character (default: space, both ends)TRIM(BOTH ‘0’ FROM ‘00120’) → 12
LTRIM(s [, set]), RTRIM(s [, set])Remove any characters of set from the left / rightLTRIM(‘xxabc’, ‘x’) → abc
REPLACE(s, old [, new])Replace every occurrence; omit new to deleteREPLACE(‘JACK and JUE’, ‘J’, ‘BL’) → BLACK and BLUE
TRANSLATE(s, from, to)Character-by-character substitutionTRANSLATE(‘ABC123’, ‘ABC’, ‘xyz’) → xyz123
ASCII(c) / CHR(n)Character code of the first character / character of a codeASCII(‘A’) → 65; CHR(65) → A

Exercise 7.2 Work with HR text columns

-- a login name: first initial + last name, lowercase        (King -> sking)HR> SELECT employee_id, LOWER(SUBSTR(first_name, 1, 1) || last_name) AS login_name    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 103);100 sking103 ajames -- phone numbers look like 1.515.555.0100 : extract the country code and change the separatorsHR> SELECT phone_number,           -- up to the first dot           SUBSTR(phone_number, 1, INSTR(phone_number, '.') - 1) AS first_part,           REPLACE(phone_number, '.', '-')                       AS dashed    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;1.515.555.0100   1   1-515-555-0100 -- zero-padded ids and fixed-width textHR> SELECT LPAD(employee_id, 6, '0') AS padded_id, RPAD(last_name, 12, '.') AS dotted    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;000100   King........ -- functions in WHERE and ORDER BYHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE LENGTH(last_name) > 9;HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE SUBSTR(job_id, 1, 2) = 'IT';HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees WHERE INSTR(last_name, 'a') > 0 ORDER BY LENGTH(last_name) DESC;

Exam focus

  • SUBSTR(s, 0, n) behaves like start position 1. A start beyond the string length returns NULL.
  • INSTR returns 0 (not NULL, not -1) when the text is not found.
  • TRIM removes only one character; LTRIM/RTRIM accept a set of characters.
  • The functions return NULL when the main argument is NULL, and in Oracle LENGTH('') is NULL because an empty string is NULL.
Nesting functions

Functions can be nested to any depth. Oracle evaluates from the innermost function outward, so read nested calls from the inside.

-- TRIM, then LOWER, then INITCAPHR> SELECT INITCAP(LOWER(TRIM('  jOHN   '))) AS tidy_name FROM dual;JohnHR> SELECT UPPER(SUBSTR(last_name, 1, 3)) || '-' || LPAD(employee_id, 4, '0') AS code    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;KIN-0100

7.4 Number Functions

FunctionPurposeExample → result
ROUND(n [, d])Round to d decimal places (default 0). Half values round away from zero; negative d rounds left of the decimal point.ROUND(45.926, 2) → 45.93; ROUND(45.926) → 46; ROUND(45.926, -1) → 50
TRUNC(n [, d])Cut off without roundingTRUNC(45.926, 2) → 45.92; TRUNC(45.926, -1) → 40
MOD(m, n)Remainder; the result has the sign of mMOD(10, 3) → 1; MOD(-10, 3) → -1
CEIL(n) / FLOOR(n)Smallest integer ≥ n / largest integer ≤ nCEIL(4.1) → 5; FLOOR(-4.1) → -5
ABS(n) / SIGN(n)Absolute value / -1, 0 or 1ABS(-7) → 7; SIGN(-3) → -1
POWER(n, p) / SQRT(n)Power / square rootPOWER(2, 10) → 1024; SQRT(144) → 12
REMAINDER(m, n)IEEE remainder: m minus n times the nearest integer quotientREMAINDER(11, 3) → -1

Exercise 7.3 Numbers in HR

HR> SELECT ROUND(45.926, 2) r2, ROUND(45.926) r0, ROUND(45.926, -1) rm1,           TRUNC(45.926, 2) t2, TRUNC(45.926, -1) tm1,           MOD(10, 3) m1, MOD(-10, 3) m2, CEIL(4.1) c, FLOOR(-4.1) f    FROM   dual;R2    R0   RM1  T2    TM1  M1  M2   C   F----- ---- ---- ----- ---- --- ---- --- ---45.93  46   50  45.92  40   1   -1   5   -5 -- a daily rate, rounded to cents; and salary rounded to the nearest thousandHR> SELECT last_name, salary, ROUND(salary / 22, 2) AS daily_rate, ROUND(salary, -3) AS nearest_k    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;-- every other employee: even or odd employee idsHR> SELECT employee_id, MOD(employee_id, 2) AS odd_flag FROM employees WHERE employee_id < 105;

Exam focus

  • ROUND(-2.5) is -3 and ROUND(2.5) is 3 (half away from zero).
  • TRUNC(n, -1) replaces the units digit with 0; ROUND(n, -1) goes to the nearest ten.
  • MOD(n, 0) returns n (no error).
  • ROUND and TRUNC also work on dates (Chapter 8).

7.5 Functions and Performance in One Paragraph

A function applied to a column in WHERE (for example WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'KING') stops Oracle from using an ordinary index on that column, because the index stores the original values, not the uppercased ones. The remedy is a function-based index (Chapter 19). Applying the function to the literal side (WHERE last_name = INITCAP('KING')) keeps indexes usable.

Chapter 8: Dates and Date Functions

Prompt: HR> • Exam topics 4 and 16: single-row date functions, date arithmetic, current date/time functions • Session settings you change here reset themselves at disconnect.

Topics in this chapter

  • 8.1 How Oracle Stores and Shows Dates
  • 8.2 The Current Date and Time
  • 8.3 Arithmetic with Dates
  • 8.4 Date Functions
  • 8.5 Traps with Dates and Times
  • 8.6 Answers to the Lab Challenges

8.1 How Oracle Stores and Shows Dates

The DATE data type stores century, year, month, day, hour, minute and second (7 bytes) — always both date and time, with a range from 4712 BC to 9999 AD. It has no time zone and no fractions of a second (TIMESTAMP has both, see Chapter 23). What you see is only a text rendering controlled by the session parameter NLS_DATE_FORMAT; the stored value does not change.

Exercise 8.1 See and change the display format

HR> SELECT hire_date FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100;HIRE_DATE---------17-JUN-13                                    -- default display format DD-MON-RR hides the time HR> ALTER SESSION SET NLS_DATE_FORMAT = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS';HR> SELECT hire_date, SYSDATE FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100;HIRE_DATE            SYSDATE-------------------  -------------------2013-06-17 00:00:00  2026-10-04 09:15:42    -- hire dates in HR are all midnight
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
-- the usual default (or simply reconnect)HR> ALTER SESSION SET NLS_DATE_FORMAT = 'DD-MON-RR';
↪ REPLAY — redo it quickly
HR> ALTER SESSION SET NLS_DATE_FORMAT = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS';
The RR year rule

A two-digit year typed with the RR format element is interpreted relative to the current two-digit year, so that dates stay near today:

Two-digit year givenCurrent year 00–49Current year 50–99
00–49Current centuryNext century
50–99Previous centuryCurrent century

YY (the other two-digit element) always uses the current century. Example in 2026: TO_DATE('01-JAN-30','DD-MON-RR') is 2030, TO_DATE('01-JAN-80','DD-MON-RR') is 1980, but TO_DATE('01-JAN-80','DD-MON-YY') is 2080.

8.2 The Current Date and Time

FunctionReturnsTime zone used
SYSDATEDATEThe database server operating system
SYSTIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONEThe database server
CURRENT_DATEDATEThe session time zone
CURRENT_TIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONEThe session time zone
LOCALTIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP (no zone)The session time zone

SYSDATE and CURRENT_DATE differ only when your session time zone differs from the server’s; Chapter 23 explores this fully. None of these functions takes parentheses.

8.3 Arithmetic with Dates

A date behaves like a number of days. The rules are few and examinable:

ExpressionResultMeaning
date + numberDATEAdd that many days (fractions are hours: 1/24 = one hour)
date - numberDATESubtract days
date - dateNUMBERThe difference in days (with a fraction for the time of day)
date + date—Invalid

Exercise 8.2 Tenure and review dates

-- days between two fixed dates and 36 hours laterHR> SELECT DATE '2024-03-15' - DATE '2024-03-01'                   AS days_between,   -- 14           -- 2024-03-02 12:00           TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-01' + 1.5, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')  AS plus_36_hours    FROM   dual; -- how long has each employee been with the company, in days and in whole years?HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date,           ROUND(SYSDATE - hire_date)                       AS days_employed,           TRUNC((SYSDATE - hire_date) / 365.25)            AS years_employed    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 101); -- 90 days after hire (an end-of-probation date)HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date, hire_date + 90 AS probation_end FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100;King  17-JUN-13  15-SEP-13

Exam focus

  • Subtracting two DATE values gives a number of days, not a date and not an interval.
  • SYSDATE - hire_date is fractional because SYSDATE contains the time; wrap in ROUND or TRUNC when you want whole days.
  • You cannot add two dates; you can subtract them.

8.4 Date Functions

FunctionPurposeExample → result
MONTHS_BETWEEN(d1, d2)Months from d2 to d1, as a decimal; negative if d1 is earlier. An integer if both are the same day number or both are month-ends.MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE ‘2024-03-15’, DATE ‘2024-01-15’) → 2
ADD_MONTHS(d, n)Add n months (n may be negative). If d is the last day of its month, the result is the last day of the result month.ADD_MONTHS(DATE ‘2024-01-31’, 1) → 29-FEB-24
NEXT_DAY(d, ‘day’)The first given weekday after d (never d itself); the day name follows the session language.NEXT_DAY(DATE ‘2024-03-15’, ‘FRIDAY’) → 22-MAR-24
LAST_DAY(d)Last day of d’s month (keeps the time of day)LAST_DAY(DATE ‘2024-02-10’) → 29-FEB-24
ROUND(d [, fmt])Round to a unit; default ’DD’ = nearest midnightROUND(DATE ‘2024-03-16’, ‘MONTH’) → 01-APR-24
TRUNC(d [, fmt])Cut down to a unit; default = midnight (removes the time)TRUNC(DATE ‘2024-03-15’, ‘YEAR’) → 01-JAN-24
EXTRACT(part FROM d)YEAR, MONTH or DAY from a DATE (HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND need a TIMESTAMP)EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) → 2013

Exercise 8.3 Try every date function

HR> SELECT MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2024-03-15', DATE '2024-01-15')  AS m1,      -- 2           -- 1 (both month-ends)           MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2024-03-31', DATE '2024-02-29')  AS m2,           MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2024-01-15', DATE '2024-03-15')  AS m3       -- -2    FROM   dual;HR> SELECT ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2024-01-31', 1)  AS a1,       -- 29-FEB-24           ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2023-02-28', 1)  AS a2,       -- 31-MAR-23 (28-FEB-23 is a month-end)           ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2024-05-10', -6) AS a3        -- 10-NOV-23    FROM   dual;-- 22-MAR-24 (15 MAR 2024 is a Friday)HR> SELECT NEXT_DAY(DATE '2024-03-15', 'FRIDAY') AS next_fri,           LAST_DAY(DATE '2024-02-10')           AS month_end,  -- 29-FEB-24           TRUNC(DATE '2024-03-15', 'MONTH')     AS first_of_month,   -- 01-MAR-24           -- 01-APR-24 (16th rounds up)           ROUND(DATE '2024-03-16', 'MONTH')     AS rounded_month,           -- 01-JAN-25 (July rounds up)           ROUND(DATE '2024-07-01', 'YEAR')      AS rounded_year    FROM   dual;
Date format elements for ROUND and TRUNC
FormatUnitTRUNC gives
’YEAR’ or ’YYYY’YearJanuary 1st
’Q’QuarterFirst day of the quarter
’MONTH’, ’MON’, ’MM’MonthFirst day of the month
’DAY’, ’DY’, ’D’WeekThe first day of the week (depends on NLS_TERRITORY: Sunday in AMERICA)
’IW’ISO weekMonday of the ISO week
’DD’ (default)DayMidnight (00:00:00)
’HH’, ’MI’Hour, minuteThe start of the hour or minute

Exercise 8.4 Date functions on the HR data

-- King was hired on Mon 17-JUN-13: 6-month review, month-end, first Monday after hireHR> SELECT hire_date,           ADD_MONTHS(hire_date, 6)        AS review_date,     -- 17-DEC-13           LAST_DAY(hire_date)             AS month_end,       -- 30-JUN-13           NEXT_DAY(hire_date, 'MONDAY')   AS first_monday,    -- 24-JUN-13           TRUNC(hire_date, 'YEAR')        AS start_of_year    -- 01-JAN-13    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100; -- tenure in whole years and in months, as of todayHR> SELECT last_name,           TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(SYSDATE, hire_date) / 12)   AS years,           TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(SYSDATE, hire_date))        AS months    FROM   employees ORDER BY hire_date FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;      -- the five longest-serving -- employees hired in a given year, using EXTRACTHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) = 2015;

Exam focus

  • NEXT_DAY(d, 'FRIDAY') on a Friday returns the following Friday.
  • ADD_MONTHS never produces an invalid date; it clamps to the end of the month.
  • ROUND(date) and TRUNC(date) with no format work on the day (midnight).
  • MONTHS_BETWEEN can return a fraction (a 31-day month is assumed for the fractional part).

8.5 Traps with Dates and Times

TrapWhy it failsDo this instead
WHERE hire_date = SYSDATESYSDATE has a time-of-day; rows are at midnight, so almost nothing equals itWHERE hire_date = TRUNC(SYSDATE)
BETWEEN DATE ‘2024-01-01’ AND DATE ‘2024-01-31’The upper limit is midnight at the start of 31 January, so 31 January 10:00 is excluded>= DATE ‘2024-01-01’ AND < DATE ‘2024-02-01’
WHERE hire_date = ‘17-JUN-13’Relies on the session’s NLS_DATE_FORMAT and language (implicit conversion)WHERE hire_date = DATE ‘2013-06-17’ or TO_DATE with a format
SELECT hire_date + hire_dateAdding two dates is not allowedSubtract dates, add numbers to dates
NEXT_DAY(d, ‘MONDAY’) in a German sessionDay names depend on NLS_DATE_LANGUAGENEXT_DAY(d, ‘MONDAY’) after ALTER SESSION SET NLS_DATE_LANGUAGE = ‘ENGLISH’

Challenge 8.1 List employees hired in the first quarter of 2017 (January to March), using TRUNC, ADD_MONTHS or date literals.

Hint: A half-open range >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND < DATE '2017-04-01' is the safest.

Challenge 8.2 For each employee show the date of their next work anniversary after today.

Hint: Add whole years of tenure plus one to the hire date with ADD_MONTHS(hire_date, 12 * n).

Challenge 8.3 Return the last working day (Friday) of the month of each employee’s hire, assuming weekends are Saturday/Sunday.

Hint: NEXT_DAY(LAST_DAY(hire_date) - 7, 'FRIDAY') finds the last Friday of the month.

Challenge 8.4 How many employees were hired in each calendar year? Show the year and the count (needs Chapter 10, try it as a preview).

Hint: GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date).

Challenge 8.5 Show how many hours and minutes remain until midnight tonight.

Hint: TRUNC(SYSDATE) + 1 is tomorrow at midnight; multiply the day difference by 24 and 1440.

Project milestone — Chapter 8

Add a service-anniversary report for the HR team. Save it as labs/ei_08_anniversaries.sql.
