Chapter 9: Conversion Functions and Conditional Expressions

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 5: Using Conversion Functions and Conditional Expressions • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 9.1 Implicit and Explicit Data Type Conversion
  • 9.2 TO_CHAR with Dates
  • 9.3 TO_CHAR with Numbers
  • 9.4 TO_NUMBER and TO_DATE
  • 9.5 Handling NULL: NVL, NVL2, NULLIF and COALESCE
  • 9.6 Conditional Expressions: CASE and DECODE
  • 9.7 Common Errors in This Chapter
  • 9.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

9.1 Implicit and Explicit Data Type Conversion

Oracle converts between data types in two ways. Implicit (automatic) conversion happens when Oracle needs a different type than the one you supplied. Explicit conversion is what you request with TO_CHAR, TO_NUMBER, TO_DATE or CAST. Professional code uses explicit conversion: implicit conversion depends on session settings, can hide errors and can stop indexes from being used.

FromToImplicit?Example
VARCHAR2 / CHARNUMBERYesWHERE employee_id = ‘100’ works; ‘abc’ raises ORA-01722
VARCHAR2 / CHARDATEYes (uses NLS_DATE_FORMAT)WHERE hire_date = ‘17-JUN-13’ — fragile
NUMBERVARCHAR2Yes‘Id ’ || employee_id
DATEVARCHAR2Yes (uses NLS_DATE_FORMAT)‘Hired ’ || hire_date
NUMBERDATENoSYSDATE + ‘10’ works only because ‘10’ becomes a NUMBER first

Exam focus

  • A date string is implicitly converted only if it matches the session NLS_DATE_FORMAT; otherwise you get ORA-01843/ORA-01858 — always supply the format.
  • Implicit conversion of a column (not a literal) in a WHERE clause can prevent index use.
  • NUMBER and DATE are never converted into each other implicitly.

9.2 TO_CHAR with Dates

TO_CHAR(date, 'format') turns a date into text exactly as the format model says. The format is case-aware: Month gives ‘June’, MONTH gives ‘JUNE’, month gives ‘june’.

ElementMeaningExample (17 June 2013, 14:05:09)
YYYY / YY / YEAR4-digit year / 2-digit / spelled-out year2013 / 13 / TWENTY THIRTEEN
MM / MON / MONTHMonth number / abbreviated / full name06 / JUN / JUNE
DD / DDD / DDay of month / of year / of week17 / 168 / 2 (Monday in AMERICA)
DY / DAYWeekday abbreviated / fullMON / MONDAY
Q / WW / IWQuarter / week of year / ISO week2 / 24 / 25
HH / HH24 / MI / SSHour (12h) / hour (24h) / minute / second02 / 14 / 05 / 09
AM or PMMeridian indicatorPM
th / sp / spthOrdinal / spelled-out / both17th / seventeen / seventeenth
”text”Literal text in double quotesDD ”of” Month
fmFill mode: removes the blank padding and leading zeros that Oracle addsfmMonth → June instead of June (padded)

Exercise 9.1 Format hire dates for people

HR> SELECT TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'DD-MON-YYYY HH24:MI')            AS stamp,           TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'fmMonth DD, YYYY')                 AS long_form,           TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'fmDay, DDth Month YYYY')           AS spoken,           TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'fmDD "of" Month, YYYY')            AS literal_text    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;STAMP              LONG_FORM      SPOKEN                      LITERAL_TEXT-----------------  -------------  --------------------------  ------------------17-JUN-2013 00:00  June 17, 2013  Monday, 17th June 2013      17 of June, 2013 -- group or filter by a part of the dateHR> SELECT TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'YYYY') AS yr, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'YYYY') ORDER BY 1;HR> SELECT last_name, TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'Day') AS weekday FROM employees WHERE employee_id < 103;

9.3 TO_CHAR with Numbers

ElementMeaningExample
9A digit; leading zeros are shown as spacesTO_CHAR(45, ‘999’) → ’ 45’
0A digit; forces a zeroTO_CHAR(45, ‘000’) → ’ 045’
, and .Group separator and decimal point (shown where typed)TO_CHAR(24000, ‘99,999.99’)
$ / LDollar sign / the local currency symbol (NLS_CURRENCY)TO_CHAR(24000, ‘$99,999’)
FMRemove padding spacesTO_CHAR(24000, ‘FM$99,999.00’) → $24,000.00
MI / PR / STrailing minus / negative in angle brackets / leading signTO_CHAR(-5, ‘999PR’) → <5>
EEEEScientific notationTO_CHAR(12345, ‘0.99EEEE’) → 1.23E+04

Exercise 9.2 Currency and percentages

HR> SELECT last_name,           TO_CHAR(salary, 'FM$99,999.00')                    AS salary_text,     -- $24,000.00           TO_CHAR(commission_pct * 100, 'FM990') || '%'      AS commission_text  -- 40%    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 145);King    $24,000.00Singh   $14,000.00   40% -- the format model must be wide enough: if not, Oracle fills the result with #HR> SELECT TO_CHAR(1234567, '9,999') AS too_narrow FROM dual;       -- ########

9.4 TO_NUMBER and TO_DATE

TO_NUMBER(text [, format]) and TO_DATE(text [, format]) do the reverse. The format model must match the text; if it does not, Oracle raises an error rather than guessing.

Exercise 9.3 Convert text to numbers and dates

HR> SELECT TO_NUMBER('1,210.73', '9,999.99')            AS n1,      -- 1210.73           TO_NUMBER('$24,000.00', '$99,999.00')         AS n2,      -- 24000           TO_NUMBER('42')                               AS n3       -- 42    FROM   dual;HR> SELECT TO_DATE('15-02-2024', 'DD-MM-YYYY')                  AS d1,   -- 15-FEB-24           TO_DATE('2024-03-15 14:30', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')    AS d2,   -- with the time of day           TO_DATE('March 5, 2024', 'fmMonth DD, YYYY')         AS d3    -- 05-MAR-24    FROM   dual;-- ANSI literals need no format at all (always YYYY-MM-DD):HR> SELECT DATE '2024-03-15' AS d, TIMESTAMP '2024-03-15 14:30:00' AS ts FROM dual;
ErrorMeaning
ORA-01722: invalid numberThe text cannot be converted to a number (for example ‘abc’ or ‘12,5’ with a mismatched format).
ORA-01843: not a valid monthThe text does not match the month part of the format.
ORA-01861: literal does not match format stringText and format differ in a separator or length (the default is non-strict only for some elements; use FX to force an exact match).
ORA-01830 / ORA-01847The format ended before the text did / the day number is invalid for the month.

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: Since 12.2 you can convert safely: TO_NUMBER('abc' DEFAULT 0 ON CONVERSION ERROR) returns 0 instead of raising ORA-01722, and VALIDATE_CONVERSION(text AS NUMBER) returns 1 or 0 to test input first. The same DEFAULT ... ON CONVERSION ERROR clause works with TO_DATE.

CAST

CAST(expression AS datatype) is the ANSI-standard conversion. It uses the session settings for dates, so prefer TO_DATE with a format.

HR> SELECT CAST('15' AS NUMBER)                AS n,           CAST(24000 AS VARCHAR2(10))         AS t,           CAST(SYSDATE AS TIMESTAMP)          AS ts    FROM   dual;

Exam focus

  • The format model of TO_CHAR is not validated against the data type until it runs: TO_CHAR(salary, 'DD') fails.
  • 'fm' removes blank padding in dates and numbers; without it Month is padded to 9 characters.
  • TO_CHAR(date) without a format uses NLS_DATE_FORMAT.

9.5 Handling NULL: NVL, NVL2, NULLIF and COALESCE

FunctionReturnsExample → result
NVL(e1, e2)e2 if e1 is NULL, otherwise e1NVL(NULL, 0) → 0
NVL2(e1, e2, e3)e2 if e1 is not NULL, otherwise e3NVL2(commission_pct, ‘Y’, ‘N’)
NULLIF(e1, e2)NULL if e1 = e2, otherwise e1NULLIF(5, 5) → NULL; NULLIF(5, 6) → 5
COALESCE(e1, e2, ...)The first argument that is not NULL (any number of arguments)COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 3, 4) → 3

Exercise 9.4 Total pay without NULL surprises

HR> SELECT last_name, salary, commission_pct,           -- NULL for non-sales staff           salary + salary * commission_pct                   AS wrong_total,           salary + salary * NVL(commission_pct, 0)           AS total_pay,           NVL2(commission_pct, 'Commissioned', 'Salary only') AS pay_type    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 145);LAST_NAME  SALARY COMMISSION_PCT WRONG_TOTAL TOTAL_PAY PAY_TYPE---------- ------ -------------- ----------- --------- ------------King        24000                                24000 Salary onlySingh       14000             .4       19600     19600 Commissioned -- NULL when the lengths are equalHR> SELECT NULLIF(LENGTH(first_name), LENGTH(last_name)) AS differs    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;HR> SELECT last_name, COALESCE(phone_number, TO_CHAR(manager_id), 'no contact') AS contact    -- the first non-NULL value    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id = 100;

Exam focus

  • All arguments of NVL/COALESCE must be of the same data type family; NVL(commission_pct, 'none') fails (ORA-01722) because the text cannot be a number.
  • NVL always evaluates both arguments; COALESCE stops at the first non-NULL one (short-circuit).
  • NULLIF(a, b) is equivalent to CASE WHEN a = b THEN NULL ELSE a END; its first argument cannot be the literal NULL.

9.6 Conditional Expressions: CASE and DECODE

A conditional expression implements IF-THEN-ELSE logic inside SQL. CASE is ANSI standard and more powerful; DECODE is the older Oracle function and tests equality only.

-- simple CASE: compares ONE expression with several valuesCASE expr  WHEN value1 THEN result1  [WHEN value2 THEN result2 ...]  [ELSE default]  END-- searched CASE: evaluates independent conditions (ranges, AND/OR, IS NULL ...)CASE  WHEN condition1 THEN result1  [WHEN condition2 THEN result2 ...]  [ELSE default]  ENDDECODE(expr, search1, result1 [, search2, result2 ...] [, default])

Exercise 9.5 Pay bands and raises

HR> SELECT last_name, salary,           CASE WHEN salary < 5000  THEN 'Low'                WHEN salary < 10000 THEN 'Medium'                ELSE                     'High'           END AS pay_band                                   -- searched CASE with ranges    FROM   employees WHERE employee_id IN (100, 107, 103);King  24000  High  /  Nguyen   4200  Low  /  James   9000  Medium -- the classic exam raise: IT_PROG +10%, ST_CLERK +15%, everyone else unchangedHR> SELECT last_name, job_id, salary,           CASE job_id WHEN 'IT_PROG'  THEN salary * 1.10                       WHEN 'ST_CLERK' THEN salary * 1.15                       ELSE salary END                       AS new_salary    -- simple CASE    FROM   employees WHERE job_id IN ('IT_PROG', 'ST_CLERK', 'AD_PRES') AND ROWNUM <= 6; -- the same with DECODE (pairs of search/result, last value = default)HR> SELECT last_name, job_id,           DECODE(job_id, 'IT_PROG', salary * 1.10, 'ST_CLERK', salary * 1.15, salary) AS new_salary    FROM   employees WHERE job_id IN ('IT_PROG', 'ST_CLERK') AND ROWNUM <= 3;
CASE and DECODE rules worth memorising
  • A CASE without ELSE returns NULL when no branch matches.
  • Branches are tested in order and the first TRUE one wins; later branches are not evaluated.
  • All result expressions must have the same data type family (ORA-00932 inconsistent datatypes otherwise).
  • DECODE treats two NULLs as equal: DECODE(commission_pct, NULL, 'none', 'has') works; CASE commission_pct WHEN NULL ... never matches because = NULL is never true. Use CASE WHEN commission_pct IS NULL.
  • CASE can be used anywhere an expression is allowed: select list, WHERE, ORDER BY, and inside other functions.
-- CASE in ORDER BY: put the president first, then everyone by salaryHR> SELECT last_name, job_id, salary FROM employees    ORDER BY CASE job_id WHEN 'AD_PRES' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, salary DESC;-- conditional counting is a favourite reporting trick (Chapter 10 builds on it)HR> SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN commission_pct IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS no_commission,           SUM(CASE WHEN commission_pct IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS with_commission    FROM   employees;                                         -- 72 and 35

9.7 Common Errors in This Chapter

ErrorTypical cause
ORA-01722: invalid numberNVL(number_column, ‘text’), or TO_NUMBER of non-numeric text
ORA-00932: inconsistent datatypes: expected NUMBER got CHARA CASE/DECODE/COALESCE whose results mix numbers and text
ORA-01858: a non-numeric character was found where a numeric was expectedDate text that does not match the format
ORA-01481: invalid number format modelA number format element misspelled or used on the wrong type
ORA-00907 / ORA-00905Missing END in a CASE, or missing parenthesis in DECODE

Project milestone — Chapter 9

Create the payroll sheet for finance: total monthly pay with commission, nicely formatted, with pay band and seniority. Save as labs/ei_09_payroll.sql.

HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name,           TO_CHAR(salary + salary * NVL(commission_pct, 0), 'FM$999,999.00') AS total_monthly_pay,           CASE WHEN salary < 5000 THEN 'Low' WHEN salary < 10000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'High' END AS pay_band,           TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'fmDD Mon YYYY')                                 AS hired    FROM   employees    ORDER  BY salary DESC;

GRP    EMPLOYEES-----  ---------Exec           3IT             5Other         99(DECODE returns Other for the employee whose department is NULL)

Chapter 10: Group Functions and Aggregation

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 6: Reporting Aggregated Data Using Group Functions • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 10.1 What a Group Function Does
  • 10.2 Creating Groups: GROUP BY
  • 10.3 Restricting Groups: HAVING
  • 10.4 Nesting Group Functions and Conditional Aggregation
  • 10.5 DISTINCT inside Aggregates, MEDIAN and Statistics
  • 10.6 LISTAGG: Many Rows into One Text
  • 10.7 Common Errors
  • 10.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

10.1 What a Group Function Does

A group function (aggregate function) works on a set of rows and returns one value per group. Without a GROUP BY clause the whole table is one group, so the query returns a single row.

FunctionReturnsNotes
COUNT(*)Number of rowsCounts every row, including rows full of NULLs
COUNT(expr)Number of rows where expr is not NULL
COUNT(DISTINCT expr)Number of different non-NULL values
SUM(expr) / AVG(expr)Total / arithmetic meanNUMBER only; NULLs are ignored
MIN(expr) / MAX(expr)Smallest / largestWork on NUMBER, DATE and text
STDDEV(expr) / VARIANCE(expr)Standard deviation / varianceNUMBER only
MEDIAN(expr)The middle valueNUMBER or DATE
LISTAGG(expr, sep) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)The values joined into one textChapter section below

Exercise 10.1 Summarise the whole company

HR> SELECT COUNT(*)                AS employees,           -- 107           COUNT(commission_pct)     AS with_commission,     -- 35  (NULLs not counted)           MIN(salary)               AS lowest,              -- 2100           MAX(salary)               AS highest,             -- 24000           SUM(salary)               AS payroll,             -- 691416           ROUND(AVG(salary), 2)     AS average_salary,      -- 6461.83           MIN(hire_date)            AS first_hire,           MAX(hire_date)            AS last_hire    FROM   employees;
NULLs and AVG: a very common exam question

Group functions skip NULLs. AVG(commission_pct) divides by the 35 employees who have a commission, not by 107. To treat missing values as zero, replace them first.

-- about .2229 : 35 values onlyHR> SELECT AVG(commission_pct)              AS avg_of_sales_staff,           -- about .0729 : NULL counted as 0           AVG(NVL(commission_pct, 0))      AS avg_of_everyone,           COUNT(*) - COUNT(commission_pct) AS without_commission     -- 72    FROM   employees;

Exam focus

  • Every group function except COUNT(*) ignores NULLs.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different non-NULL values.
  • SUM/AVG of a column containing only NULLs is NULL, while COUNT of it is 0.
  • MIN/MAX work on dates and text, but SUM/AVG do not.

10.2 Creating Groups: GROUP BY

GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same value(s) of the grouping expression(s); every group function is then calculated once per group. Every item in the select list that is not inside a group function must appear in the GROUP BY clause, otherwise Oracle raises ORA-00979.

Exercise 10.2 Per-department statistics

HR> SELECT department_id,           COUNT(*)                AS headcount,           ROUND(AVG(salary), 2)   AS avg_salary,           SUM(salary)             AS payroll    FROM   employees    GROUP  BY department_id    ORDER  BY department_id;DEPARTMENT_ID HEADCOUNT AVG_SALARY PAYROLL------------- --------- ---------- -------           10         1       4400    4400           20         2       9500   19000           30         6       4150   24900           40         1       6500    6500           50        45    3475.56  156400           60         5       5760   28800           70         1      10000   10000           80        34    8955.88  304500           90         3   19333.33   58000          100         6    8601.33   51608          110         2      10154   20308                     1       7000    7000          -- the employee with no department forms its own group

Note: A NULL grouping value forms one group of its own (all NULLs are considered equal for grouping), so Kimberely Grant appears as the 12th row.

Several grouping columns, and expressions
HR> SELECT department_id, job_id, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS payroll    FROM   employees    GROUP  BY department_id, job_id            -- one row per distinct (department, job) pair    ORDER  BY department_id, job_id;HR> SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS hire_year, COUNT(*) AS hires    FROM   employees    GROUP  BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)    -- group by an EXPRESSION; repeat it exactly    ORDER  BY hire_year;
You may group by a column you do not display
HR> SELECT COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department_id ORDER BY headcount DESC;-- legal, but unreadable: the department id is not shown

Exam focus

  • Aliases cannot be used in GROUP BY (unlike ORDER BY), and you cannot group by column position.
  • A column in the select list that is neither aggregated nor in GROUP BY gives ORA-00979: not a GROUP BY expression.
  • The GROUP BY columns need not appear in the select list.
  • ORDER BY may use group functions even if they are not in the select list: ORDER BY AVG(salary).

10.3 Restricting Groups: HAVING

WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters groups after they are formed, so it is the only place where a group function can be used as a condition.

HR> SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary    FROM   employees    GROUP  BY department_id    HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000                 -- a condition on a group result    ORDER  BY avg_salary DESC;90 3 19333.33 / 110 2 10154 / 70 1 10000 / 20 2 9500 / 80 34 8955.88 / 100 6 8601.33 -- WHERE and HAVING together: first remove rows, then groupsHR> SELECT job_id, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS avg_salary    FROM   employees    WHERE  department_id IS NOT NULL          -- row filter (before grouping)    GROUP  BY job_id    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5                      -- group filter (after grouping)    ORDER  BY n DESC;
ClauseFiltersCan contain a group function?
WHEREIndividual rows, before groupingNo (ORA-00934: group function is not allowed here)
HAVINGGroups, after groupingYes
Logical order of evaluation of a query
StepClauseWhat happens
1FROM (and joins)The source rows are assembled
2WHERERows are filtered
3GROUP BYRows are grouped
4HAVINGGroups are filtered
5SELECTExpressions and aliases are computed; DISTINCT is applied
6ORDER BYThe result is sorted (aliases are visible here)
7OFFSET / FETCHRows are skipped / limited

Exam focus

  • This order explains why aliases work in ORDER BY but not in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING (all evaluated before SELECT).
  • A HAVING clause may be written without GROUP BY: the whole table is then one group.

10.4 Nesting Group Functions and Conditional Aggregation

With a GROUP BY, one group function can be wrapped in another: the inner function is calculated per group and the outer one summarises those results.

HR> SELECT MAX(AVG(salary)) AS best_department_average,       -- 19333.33  (Executive)           MIN(AVG(salary)) AS lowest_department_average       -- 3475.56   (Shipping)    FROM   employees GROUP BY department_id;-- note: the select list may then contain ONLY the nested aggregates (no plain columns)

A group function over a CASE expression is the standard technique to build cross-tabulations in plain SQL, without PIVOT (Chapter 25 shows PIVOT):

HR> SELECT department_id,           SUM(CASE WHEN commission_pct IS NULL     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS no_commission,           SUM(CASE WHEN commission_pct IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS with_commission,           -- COUNT skips the NULLs           COUNT(CASE WHEN salary >= 10000 THEN 1 END)                 AS earning_10k_plus    FROM   employees    WHERE  department_id IN (50, 80, 90)    GROUP  BY department_id;

10.5 DISTINCT inside Aggregates, MEDIAN and Statistics

HR> SELECT COUNT(job_id)             AS jobs_counted,          -- 107 : every employee has a job           COUNT(DISTINCT job_id)    AS different_jobs,        -- 19           COUNT(DISTINCT manager_id) AS different_managers    -- the number of distinct managers    FROM   employees;HR> SELECT department_id, MEDIAN(salary) AS median_salary, ROUND(STDDEV(salary), 2) AS std_dev    FROM   employees WHERE department_id IN (50, 80) GROUP BY department_id;-- duplicates removed firstHR> SELECT SUM(DISTINCT salary) AS sum_of_distinct_salaries FROM employees;

Note: COUNT(job_id) returns 107, not 106: the one employee without a department still has a job. Always check which column you count.

10.6 LISTAGG: Many Rows into One Text

LISTAGG concatenates the values of a group into one string. WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) is required and decides the order.

HR> SELECT department_id,           LISTAGG(last_name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY last_name) AS staff    FROM   employees    WHERE  department_id IN (10, 20, 90)    GROUP  BY department_id;10  Whalen20  Davis, Martinez90  Garcia, King, Yang

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: The result of LISTAGG is limited to 4000 bytes; longer lists raise ORA-01489. From 12.2 you can write LISTAGG(last_name, ', ' ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE '...') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY last_name). APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT gives fast approximate distinct counts on very large tables.

10.7 Common Errors

ErrorCause
ORA-00979: not a GROUP BY expressionA select-list column is not in the GROUP BY clause and not aggregated
ORA-00934: group function is not allowed hereA group function in WHERE or GROUP BY; use HAVING
ORA-00937: not a single-group group functionSELECT department_id, COUNT(*) with no GROUP BY at all
ORA-00935: group function is nested too deeplyThree levels of aggregates, or two without GROUP BY

Chapter 11: Joins I: Inner Joins, Cartesian Products and Non-Equijoins

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 7: Displaying Data from Multiple Tables • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 11.1 Why Joins
  • 11.2 Cartesian Product (CROSS JOIN)
  • 11.3 Inner Joins with ON
  • 11.4 USING and NATURAL JOIN
  • 11.5 Joining Three or More Tables
  • 11.6 More Than Equality: Non-Equijoins and Extra Conditions
  • 11.7 Aliases, Ambiguity and Readability
  • 11.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

11.1 Why Joins

Employees store only a DEPARTMENT_ID; the name lives in DEPARTMENTS. A join combines rows of two or more tables by comparing columns, normally a foreign key with the primary key it references. The comparison is the join condition. Two syntaxes exist: the ANSI/SQL:1999 syntax (JOIN ... ON) recommended for all new code, and Oracle’s traditional syntax (tables separated by commas, join condition in WHERE). The exam tests both.

11.2 Cartesian Product (CROSS JOIN)

If no join condition links two tables, Oracle pairs every row of the first with every row of the second: this is a Cartesian product. It is almost always an accident, and it explodes quickly.

-- 107 x 27 = 2889  rows (no condition: accident!)HR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees, departments;-- the same, but written on purposeHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments;

Caution: A forgotten join condition across three tables of 100, 1,000 and 10,000 rows produces 1,000,000,000 rows. Always sanity-check the row count of a join against what you expect.

Tip: Intentional cross joins are useful: every combination of two small lists, such as all months x all regions to build a report skeleton.

11.3 Inner Joins with ON

An inner join returns only the rows for which the condition is true. Rows without a partner are dropped. Always give tables aliases and qualify every column that exists in more than one table; a column that is ambiguous raises ORA-00918.

Exercise 11.1 Employees with their department names

-- ANSI syntax (recommended)HR> SELECT e.last_name, e.department_id, d.department_name    FROM   employees e    -- INNER is the default join type    JOIN   departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    WHERE  e.job_id = 'IT_PROG';James      60 IT / Miller 60 IT / Williams 60 IT / Jackson   60 IT / Nguyen  60 IT -- the same query in traditional Oracle syntaxHR> SELECT e.last_name, e.department_id, d.department_name    FROM   employees e, departments d    WHERE  e.department_id = d.department_id    AND    e.job_id = 'IT_PROG'; -- how many rows? 107 employees, but one has no department, so the inner join returns 106-- 106HR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
ConceptANSI syntaxTraditional syntax
Join conditionJOIN ... ON a.x = b.xWHERE a.x = b.x
Extra row filterWHERE ... after the joinsAND ... in the same WHERE
Cartesian productCROSS JOINcomma without condition
Outer joinLEFT/RIGHT/FULL [OUTER] JOIN(+) operator (Chapter 12)

Exam focus

  • Once a table has an alias, you must use the alias; the table name is no longer valid: employees.last_name fails with ORA-00904 if you wrote FROM employees e.
  • A column appearing in several tables must be qualified in the select list, WHERE and ORDER BY (ORA-00918: column ambiguously defined).
  • N tables need at least N-1 join conditions.

11.4 USING and NATURAL JOIN

When the join columns have the same name in both tables you can shorten the syntax. USING (col) names the shared column(s). NATURAL JOIN joins on all columns with identical names, so you do not even name them.

HR> SELECT last_name, department_id, department_name    -- department_id has NO qualifier    FROM   employees JOIN departments USING (department_id); HR> SELECT department_name, city    -- the only shared name is location_id    FROM   departments NATURAL JOIN locations;

Caution: employees NATURAL JOIN departments joins on both DEPARTMENT_ID and MANAGER_ID, because both tables have both columns. The result silently shrinks to the employees whose manager is also their department’s manager. NATURAL JOIN is dangerous and a favourite exam trap.

Exam focus

  • With USING or NATURAL JOIN the join column must not be qualified anywhere in the statement (not e.department_id), or you get ORA-25154.
  • A column in USING cannot be mixed with an ON clause for the same join, and NATURAL JOIN cannot have USING or ON.
  • SELECT * with USING/NATURAL shows the common column once, first.

11.5 Joining Three or More Tables

Add one join per extra table. Each JOIN links the next table to anything already in the statement. Follow the foreign keys in the ER diagram (Figure 4.1).

Exercise 11.2 Where does everybody work?

HR> SELECT e.last_name, j.job_title, d.department_name, l.city, c.country_name, r.region_name    FROM   employees   e    JOIN   jobs        j ON e.job_id        = j.job_id    JOIN   departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    JOIN   locations   l ON d.location_id   = l.location_id    JOIN   countries   c ON l.country_id    = c.country_id    JOIN   regions     r ON c.region_id     = r.region_id    WHERE  e.employee_id = 100;King  President  Executive  Seattle  United States of America  Americas -- the same six tables in traditional syntax: five conditions for six tablesHR> SELECT e.last_name, j.job_title, d.department_name, l.city, c.country_name, r.region_name    FROM   employees e, jobs j, departments d, locations l, countries c, regions r    WHERE  e.job_id = j.job_id AND e.department_id = d.department_id AND d.location_id = l.location_id    AND    l.country_id = c.country_id AND c.region_id = r.region_id AND e.employee_id = 100;

Tip: HR already contains this join as the view EMP_DETAILS_VIEW (Chapter 20). Query it with SELECT * FROM emp_details_view WHERE employee_id = 100.

Join + aggregate
HR> SELECT d.department_name, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary    FROM   departments d JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id    GROUP  BY d.department_name    -- Shipping 45, Sales 34, Finance 6, Purchasing 6, IT 5 ...    ORDER  BY headcount DESC;

11.6 More Than Equality: Non-Equijoins and Extra Conditions

A non-equijoin uses an operator other than = in the join condition, most often BETWEEN, < or >. Typical use: matching a value into a range stored in another table. HR’s JOBS table stores a minimum and maximum salary for every job.

Exercise 11.3 Which jobs does each salary fit?

HR> SELECT e.last_name, e.salary, j.job_id AS fitting_job, j.min_salary, j.max_salary    FROM   employees e    JOIN   jobs j ON e.salary BETWEEN j.min_salary AND j.max_salary      -- a range condition    WHERE  e.employee_id = 107;-- Nguyen  earns 4200: she fits several jobs whose salary range contains 4200 HR> SELECT e.last_name, e.job_id, e.salary, j.min_salary, j.max_salary    FROM   employees e JOIN jobs j ON e.job_id = j.job_id               -- equijoin on the key ...    -- ... plus a range test: data quality check    AND    e.salary NOT BETWEEN j.min_salary AND j.max_salary;

Conditions can be added to the ON clause with AND, which is useful with outer joins (Chapter 12), or placed in WHERE. For an inner join the two are equivalent.

HR> SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name    FROM   employees e JOIN departments d           -- extra condition in ON           ON  e.department_id = d.department_id AND d.location_id = 1700    WHERE  e.salary > 10000;

11.7 Aliases, Ambiguity and Readability

  • Choose short, meaningful aliases (e for employees, d for departments). Use the same alias for the same table throughout the labs and in your own code.
  • A table alias is valid only inside its own statement. It may be 1 to 128 characters; do not use reserved words.
  • Put one join per line and indent the ON condition; the query then reads like the ER diagram.
  • In ANSI joins keep join conditions in ON and row filters in WHERE.
ErrorCause
ORA-00918: column ambiguously definedAn unqualified column that exists in two tables of the query
ORA-00904: “E”.“NAME”: invalid identifierWrong alias or column; or using the table name after aliasing it
ORA-25154: column part of USING clause cannot have qualifierQualified a USING or NATURAL JOIN column
ORA-00905 / ORA-00933A missing keyword, usually ON or a stray comma between JOIN clauses

HR> SELECT d.department_name, l.city, c.country_name,           COUNT(*)              AS headcount,           SUM(e.salary)         AS monthly_payroll,           ROUND(AVG(e.salary),2) AS avg_salary    FROM   employees e    JOIN   departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    JOIN   locations   l ON d.location_id   = l.location_id    JOIN   countries   c ON l.country_id    = c.country_id    GROUP  BY d.department_name, l.city, c.country_name    ORDER  BY monthly_payroll DESC;

Chapter 12: Joins II: Outer Joins and Self Joins

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 7: Displaying Data from Multiple Tables (OUTER joins, self-joins) • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 12.1 Why Inner Joins Lose Rows
  • 12.2 LEFT, RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN
  • 12.3 The Oracle (+) Operator
  • 12.4 Self Joins
  • 12.5 Combining Several Join Types
  • 12.6 Join Techniques Compared
  • 12.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

12.1 Why Inner Joins Lose Rows

An inner join returns only matching rows. In HR two kinds of rows have no partner: one employee has no department, and 16 of the 27 departments have no employees. An outer join keeps the rows of one or both tables even when no match exists and fills the missing side with NULLs.

Join typeKeeps unmatched rows ofANSI syntax
Innerneither tablea JOIN b ON ...
Left outerthe left table (the one written first)a LEFT [OUTER] JOIN b ON ...
Right outerthe right tablea RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN b ON ...
Full outerboth tablesa FULL [OUTER] JOIN b ON ...

12.2 LEFT, RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN

Exercise 12.1 Find the missing partners

-- LEFT: every employee, with the department name if there is oneHR> SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name    FROM   employees e LEFT OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    WHERE  e.employee_id IN (100, 178);King   ExecutiveGrant  (null)                              -- kept, department columns are NULL -- RIGHT: every department, with its employees; empty departments appear once with NULLsHR> SELECT d.department_name, e.last_name    FROM   employees e RIGHT OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    WHERE  d.department_id = 120;Treasury  (null) -- FULL: all employees and all departments, matched where possibleHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
QueryRows returned
employees JOIN departments (inner)106
employees LEFT JOIN departments107 (adds Grant)
employees RIGHT JOIN departments122 (106 + the 16 empty departments)
employees FULL JOIN departments123 (106 + Grant + 16 empty departments)
Anti-join: find what has no partner

An outer join followed by a test for NULL on the other table’s key finds rows with no match. This is called an anti-join.

-- departments with no employeesHR> SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name    FROM   departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id    WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL;                -- 16 rows-- employees with no departmentHR> SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    WHERE  d.department_id IS NULL;              -- Grant
ON versus WHERE in an outer join

This is the subtlest point of outer joins. A condition in ON decides which rows match; unmatched rows still survive. A condition in WHERE is applied after the join and can throw the NULL-extended rows away, silently turning an outer join into an inner join.

-- ALL departments, but only employees earning more than 12000 are matchedHR> SELECT d.department_name, e.last_name, e.salary    FROM   departments d LEFT JOIN employees e           -- filter in ON: still 27+ rows           ON e.department_id = d.department_id AND e.salary > 12000; -- same condition in WHERE: the empty departments (NULL salary) are removed againHR> SELECT d.department_name, e.last_name, e.salary    FROM   departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id    -- behaves like an inner join    WHERE  e.salary > 12000;

Exam focus

  • LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are identical; the word OUTER is optional.
  • Filtering the outer table in WHERE cancels the outer join; filter it in ON instead.
  • RIGHT JOIN is a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.

12.3 The Oracle (+) Operator

Before ANSI joins, Oracle used the (+) operator in the WHERE clause. It is placed on the side of the condition that is missing rows (the side that will be filled with NULLs). The exam still tests it.

-- left outer join: employees without a department are kept, so (+) goes on the DEPARTMENTS columnHR> SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name    FROM   employees e, departments d    WHERE  e.department_id = d.department_id (+); -- right outer join: every department is kept, so (+) goes on the EMPLOYEES columnHR> SELECT d.department_name, e.last_name    FROM   employees e, departments d    WHERE  e.department_id (+) = d.department_id;
Rule for (+)Why it matters
Put it on the side that may be missing rowsThe table whose rows are always kept has no (+)
Cannot be on both sides of one conditionA full outer join cannot be written with (+); use ANSI FULL OUTER JOIN or UNION of two outer joins
A condition with (+) cannot use OR or IN with another conditionRaises ORA-01719
A table can be outer-joined to only one other tableRaises ORA-01417
Extra conditions on the (+) table must also carry (+)Otherwise the outer join is cancelled, like a WHERE filter in ANSI syntax
-- keep all employees AND filter the department side correctly: the (+) belongs on the extra condition tooHR> SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name    FROM   employees e, departments d    WHERE  e.department_id = d.department_id (+) AND d.location_id (+) = 1700;

12.4 Self Joins

A self join joins a table to itself. You must give the two uses different aliases, so that Oracle (and you) can tell them apart. In HR the classic case is the manager of an employee: MANAGER_ID is a foreign key to EMPLOYEE_ID of the same table.

Exercise 12.2 Employees and their managers

HR> SELECT w.employee_id, w.last_name AS employee, m.last_name AS manager    FROM   employees w    JOIN   employees m ON w.manager_id = m.employee_id        -- w = the worker, m = the manager    WHERE  w.department_id = 60;103 James   Garcia  / 104 Miller James  / 105 Williams James  / 106 Jackson   James  / 107 Nguyen  James -- King has no manager: only a LEFT join keeps him (106 rows from the inner join, 107 here)HR> SELECT w.last_name AS employee, NVL(m.last_name, '*** top of the company ***') AS manager    FROM   employees w LEFT JOIN employees m ON w.manager_id = m.employee_id    WHERE  w.manager_id IS NULL; -- who earns more than their manager?HR> SELECT w.last_name, w.salary, m.last_name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary    FROM   employees w JOIN employees m ON w.manager_id = m.employee_id    WHERE  w.salary > m.salary;-- every pair of colleagues of department 90, each pair onceHR> SELECT a.last_name AS a, b.last_name AS b, a.department_id    FROM   employees a JOIN employees b ON a.department_id = b.department_id AND a.employee_id < b.employee_id    -- each pair once: (King, Yang), (King, Garcia), ...    WHERE  a.department_id = 90;

Tip: a.employee_id < b.employee_id is the standard trick to list each pair of rows only once and to avoid pairing a row with itself.

12.5 Combining Several Join Types

Outer and inner joins can be mixed. Read the statement from top to bottom: each join links the already-built result to the next table. If you later inner-join to a table that is joined to the NULL side, you may lose the rows you wanted to keep — use LEFT joins all the way.

HR> SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name, m.last_name AS manager, l.city    FROM   employees e    LEFT   JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    LEFT   JOIN employees   m ON e.manager_id    = m.employee_id    LEFT   JOIN locations   l ON d.location_id   = l.location_id    WHERE  e.employee_id IN (100, 178, 103)    ORDER  BY e.employee_id;King  Executive  (no manager)  Seattle  /  James   IT  Garcia   Southlake  /  Grant  (no dept)  Zlotkey  (no city)

Note: Whenever you are not sure which join a report needs, ask: “Do I need rows that have no partner?” If yes, outer join; if you only want matched rows, inner join.

12.6 Join Techniques Compared

You wantUse
Only rows that exist in both tablesInner join
All rows of table A, matched to B when possibleA LEFT JOIN B
Rows of A that have no match in BA LEFT JOIN B ... WHERE B.key IS NULL (or NOT EXISTS, Chapter 13)
Every pair of rowsCROSS JOIN
A row linked to another row of the same tableSelf join (two aliases)
A value matched against rangesNon-equijoin (BETWEEN)

HR> SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name                                  AS employee,           NVL(m.last_name, '- none -')                           AS manager,           NVL(d.department_name, '- no department -')            AS department,           NVL(l.city, '-')                                        AS city    FROM   employees e    LEFT   JOIN employees   m ON e.manager_id    = m.employee_id    LEFT   JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id    LEFT   JOIN locations   l ON d.location_id   = l.location_id    ORDER  BY e.employee_id;

Challenge 12.4 Produce a list of the departments that have no manager assigned and the departments that have a manager who works in a different department.

HR> SELECT d.department_name, 'no manager' AS issue FROM departments d WHERE d.manager_id IS NULL    UNION ALL    SELECT d.department_name, 'manager in other dept' FROM departments d JOIN employees m ON d.manager_id = m.employee_id    WHERE  m.department_id <> d.department_id;

DEPARTMENT_NAME        ISSUE--------------------   ----------Treasury               no managerCorporate Tax          no managerControl And Credit     no manager...(16 rows, all "no manager": the 11 departments that have a manager all employ him or her)

Challenge 12.5 List every region with its countries, keeping regions that have none (the extra join to LOCATIONS repeats a country once per office).

HR> SELECT r.region_name, c.country_name    FROM   regions r LEFT JOIN countries c ON c.region_id = r.region_id    LEFT   JOIN locations l ON l.country_id = c.country_id    ORDER  BY r.region_name, c.country_name;

Chapter 13: Subqueries

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 8: Using Subqueries to Solve Queries (single-row, multiple-row; correlated subqueries are used again to update and delete in Chapter 15) • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 13.1 What a Subquery Is
  • 13.2 Single-Row Subqueries
  • 13.3 Multiple-Row Subqueries: IN, ANY, ALL
  • 13.4 Multiple-Column Subqueries
  • 13.5 Correlated Subqueries and EXISTS
  • 13.6 Subqueries in FROM (Inline Views) and the WITH Clause
  • 13.7 Choosing Between a Join and a Subquery
  • 13.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

13.1 What a Subquery Is

A subquery (inner query) is a SELECT statement nested inside another statement (the outer query). It answers an intermediate question whose result the outer query uses: “Who earns more than James?” is “What does James earn?” followed by “Who earns more than that?”. Subqueries are written in parentheses and may appear in WHERE, HAVING, FROM (inline views), the select list, and in DML (Chapter 15).

KindReturnsOperators allowed
Single-row subqueryExactly one row (one column)= <> < <= > >=
Multiple-row subqueryZero, one or many rows (one column)IN, NOT IN, ANY, SOME, ALL
Multiple-column subquerySeveral columnsCompared as a pair: (a, b) IN (SELECT x, y ...)
Correlated subqueryReferences a column of the outer query; runs once per outer rowEXISTS, NOT EXISTS, or any comparison
Scalar subqueryOne value, used like an expressionIn the SELECT list, WHERE, ORDER BY
Inline viewA subquery in the FROM clauseUsed as a table; needs an alias if you reference its columns

13.2 Single-Row Subqueries

Exercise 13.1 Compare with a calculated value

-- who earns more than James? (the subquery returns ONE value: 9000)HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees    WHERE  salary > (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE last_name = 'James')    ORDER  BY salary; -- employees paid above the company average, and the average as a reference columnHR> SELECT last_name, salary,           -- scalar subquery in the select list           (SELECT ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) FROM employees) AS company_avg    FROM   employees    WHERE  salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)    ORDER  BY salary DESC; -- colleagues of employee 103 who do the same job, excluding 103 himselfHR> SELECT last_name, job_id FROM employees    WHERE  job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 103)    AND    employee_id <> 103; -- subqueries in HAVING: departments whose average salary beats the company averageHR> SELECT department_id, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary FROM employees    GROUP  BY department_id    HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);

Caution: A single-row operator with a subquery that returns more than one row fails with ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row. If the subquery returns no row, the comparison is with NULL and the outer query returns nothing.

HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees    -- ORA-01427: one MIN per department    WHERE  salary = (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id);

13.3 Multiple-Row Subqueries: IN, ANY, ALL

OperatorMeaningSame as
INEqual to any value in the list= ANY
NOT INDifferent from every value in the list<> ALL
> ANY (list)Greater than the smallest value> MIN(list)
< ANY (list)Less than the largest value< MAX(list)
> ALL (list)Greater than the largest value> MAX(list)
< ALL (list)Less than the smallest value< MIN(list)

Exercise 13.2 Lists and comparisons

-- employees who work in a department located in Seattle (location 1700 has several departments)HR> SELECT last_name, department_id FROM employees    WHERE  department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE location_id = 1700); -- earn less than ANY programmer (below the highest programmer salary) but are not programmersHR> SELECT last_name, job_id, salary FROM employees    WHERE  salary < ANY (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE job_id = 'IT_PROG')    AND    job_id <> 'IT_PROG'; -- earn more than ALL programmers (above 9000)HR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees    WHERE  salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE job_id = 'IT_PROG') ORDER BY salary; -- who is a manager? (anybody whose id appears as somebody’s manager_id)HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees    WHERE  employee_id IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL);
The NOT IN and NULL trap

NOT IN means “different from every value”. If the list contains a single NULL, the comparison with that NULL is UNKNOWN, so no row can ever qualify and the query returns nothing.

-- employees who are NOT managers - looks right, returns NO ROWS because manager_id contains a NULL (King)HR> SELECT last_name FROM employees    -- no rows selected    WHERE  employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees); -- fix 1: remove the NULLs from the listHR> SELECT last_name FROM employees    WHERE  employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL);-- fix 2: use NOT EXISTS (next section), which is immune to NULLs

Exam focus

  • x NOT IN (list containing NULL) is never TRUE; x IN (list containing NULL) can still be TRUE when x matches another value.
  • ANY and SOME are synonyms. = ANY equals IN; <> ALL equals NOT IN.
  • > ALL (SELECT ...) over an empty result is TRUE for every row; > ANY over an empty result is FALSE.

13.4 Multiple-Column Subqueries

A subquery can return several columns that are compared in the outer query as a pair (all columns must match together). A pairwise comparison is stricter than two separate single-column comparisons.

-- pairwise: employees who share BOTH the manager AND the department of employees 120 or 145HR> SELECT employee_id, manager_id, department_id FROM employees    WHERE  (manager_id, department_id) IN (SELECT manager_id, department_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id IN (120, 145))    AND    employee_id NOT IN (120, 145); -- non-pairwise (two independent lists): matches ANY manager of the list with ANY department of the listHR> SELECT employee_id, manager_id, department_id FROM employees    WHERE  manager_id    IN (SELECT manager_id    FROM employees WHERE employee_id IN (120, 145))    AND    department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id IN (120, 145))    AND    employee_id NOT IN (120, 145);

13.5 Correlated Subqueries and EXISTS

In a correlated subquery the inner query uses a column of the current outer row. Conceptually it is re-evaluated for every outer row, which makes it ideal for “above the average of their own group” and for existence tests.

Exercise 13.3 Compare each row with its own group

-- earn more than the average of their OWN department (alias o = outer row, i = inner rows)HR> SELECT o.last_name, o.department_id, o.salary    FROM   employees o    WHERE  o.salary > (SELECT AVG(i.salary) FROM employees i WHERE i.department_id = o.department_id)    ORDER  BY o.department_id, o.salary DESC; -- the highest-paid employee of each department (a classic): salary equals the department maximumHR> SELECT o.last_name, o.department_id, o.salary FROM employees o    WHERE  o.salary = (SELECT MAX(i.salary) FROM employees i WHERE i.department_id = o.department_id);
EXISTS and NOT EXISTS

EXISTS (subquery) is TRUE as soon as the subquery returns at least one row; the selected columns do not matter (conventionally SELECT 1). NOT EXISTS is TRUE when it returns no row. Both ignore NULLs, so NOT EXISTS is the safe replacement for NOT IN.

-- managers: employees for whom at least one employee reports to themHR> SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees e    WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.employee_id); -- NOT managers: no row reports to them (correct, 89 rows, no NULL problem)HR> SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees e    WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.employee_id); -- departments that currently have no employees (compare the 16 rows with Chapter 12’s anti-join)HR> SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name FROM departments d    WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id);

Exam focus

  • A correlated subquery cannot be run on its own, because it needs the outer row.
  • EXISTS stops at the first matching row, so it is often faster than IN when the inner table is large.
  • In EXISTS, SELECT 1, SELECT * and SELECT NULL are equivalent.

13.6 Subqueries in FROM (Inline Views) and the WITH Clause

A subquery in the FROM clause is an inline view: it behaves like a temporary table that exists only for this statement. It lets you compute an aggregate first and then join or filter on it.

HR> SELECT d.department_name, s.headcount, s.avg_salary    FROM   (SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary            FROM   employees GROUP BY department_id) s              -- the inline view, alias s    JOIN   departments d ON d.department_id = s.department_id    WHERE  s.headcount > 5    ORDER  BY s.avg_salary DESC; -- top-N per question: the 3 highest paid, the safe pre-12c way and the 12c wayHR> SELECT last_name, salary FROM (SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC) WHERE ROWNUM <= 3;

The WITH clause (subquery factoring) names a query once so you can use it several times and read the statement top to bottom.

HR> WITH dept_stats AS (          SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary          FROM   employees GROUP BY department_id )    SELECT d.department_name, s.headcount, ROUND(s.avg_salary, 2) AS avg_salary    FROM   dept_stats s JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = s.department_id    -- the factored query is reused    WHERE  s.avg_salary > (SELECT AVG(avg_salary) FROM dept_stats)    ORDER  BY avg_salary DESC;

13.7 Choosing Between a Join and a Subquery

SituationPrefer
You need columns from both tables in the resultJoin
You only need rows of A that have (or lack) a partner in BEXISTS / NOT EXISTS (or IN / NOT IN without NULLs)
Compare with one calculated value (average, maximum)Single-row subquery
Compare each row with a value from its own groupCorrelated subquery, or a join to an inline view
Reuse the same intermediate result several timesWITH clause

Tip: Oracle’s optimizer often rewrites a subquery into a join (and vice versa) internally. Choose the form that makes the question clearest; tune only if the plan (Chapter 29) shows a problem.

Chapter 14: Set Operators

Prompt: HR> • Exam topic 9: Using SET Operators • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 14.1 Combining Result Sets
  • 14.2 Rules for the Select Lists
  • 14.3 UNION and UNION ALL
  • 14.4 INTERSECT and MINUS
  • 14.5 ORDER BY, Parentheses and Several Operators
  • 14.6 The Matching Rule in Practice
  • 14.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

14.1 Combining Result Sets

A set operator combines the rows of two or more queries into one result (a join combines columns). The queries are independent; they only need compatible select lists.

OperatorReturnsDuplicatesSorted?
UNIONRows in either queryRemovedYes (as a side effect)
UNION ALLRows in either queryKeptNo — fastest
INTERSECTRows in both queriesRemovedYes
MINUSRows of the first query that are not in the secondRemovedYes

Oracle uses MINUS; the ANSI name is EXCEPT (Oracle 21c and later also accept EXCEPT). Set operators treat two NULLs as equal, which differs from comparisons in WHERE.

14.2 Rules for the Select Lists

  • Every query must return the same number of columns (ORA-01789 otherwise).
  • Corresponding columns must be in the same data type group: numbers with numbers, text with text, dates with dates (ORA-01790).
  • Column names do not matter; the headings come from the first query. Use aliases in the first query.
  • ORDER BY may appear only once, at the very end, and must use column names/aliases of the first query or positions.
  • With more than two queries all set operators have equal precedence and Oracle evaluates them left to right (the SQL standard would run INTERSECT first, Oracle does not). Use parentheses to be explicit.
  • A literal or NULL can fill a missing column: SELECT job_id, NULL FROM ...; use TO_CHAR(NULL) or TO_NUMBER(NULL) to give NULL the right type.

14.3 UNION and UNION ALL

Exercise 14.1 Which jobs have ever existed?

-- jobs in use today, jobs in the past: UNION removes the duplicatesHR> SELECT job_id FROM employees    UNION    SELECT job_id FROM job_history    ORDER  BY job_id;                                  -- ORDER BY once, at the end -- UNION ALL keeps every row: 107 employees + 10 history rows-- 117HR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT job_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT job_id FROM job_history);-- 19 distinct jobsHR> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT job_id FROM employees UNION     SELECT job_id FROM job_history);

Exercise 14.2 Combine unlike sources into one report

-- one list of "people events": hires from EMPLOYEES and job changes from JOB_HISTORYHR> SELECT employee_id, hire_date AS event_date, 'Hired' AS event FROM employees WHERE employee_id < 105    UNION ALL    SELECT employee_id, start_date, 'Started ' || job_id FROM job_history    ORDER  BY employee_id, event_date; -- fill a missing column with NULL of the right typeHR> SELECT department_id, department_name, TO_NUMBER(NULL) AS salary FROM departments WHERE department_id = 10    UNION ALL    SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 200;

Exam focus

  • UNION sorts and removes duplicates; UNION ALL does neither and is faster. Use UNION ALL when you know there are no duplicates.
  • The duplicate removal compares entire rows, so one different column makes two rows distinct.

14.4 INTERSECT and MINUS

-- jobs held today AND in the past (people who returned to a job type they once had)HR> SELECT job_id FROM employees INTERSECT SELECT job_id FROM job_history; -- jobs held today but NEVER in the historyHR> SELECT job_id FROM employees MINUS SELECT job_id FROM job_history; -- departments with no employees, the set way (16 department ids; compare with Chapters 12 and 13)HR> SELECT department_id FROM departments MINUS SELECT department_id FROM employees; -- employees who changed department in the past AND are still in the companyHR> SELECT employee_id FROM job_history INTERSECT SELECT employee_id FROM employees;

Note: MINUS is not symmetrical: A MINUS B and B MINUS A give different results. MINUS removes duplicates and NULLs compare as equal, so departments MINUS employees correctly ignores the employee whose department is NULL.

QuestionSet operatorAlternative
In A or B?UNIONOR, or a join
In both A and B?INTERSECTIN / EXISTS / inner join
In A but not in B?MINUSNOT EXISTS / anti-join

14.5 ORDER BY, Parentheses and Several Operators

-- the column heading and the sort key come from the FIRST queryHR> SELECT employee_id AS id, last_name AS name FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10    UNION    SELECT department_id, department_name FROM departments WHERE department_id = 10    -- ORDER BY 1 or ORDER BY id  (not "employee_id")    ORDER  BY 1; -- parentheses decide the evaluation order of three queriesHR> (SELECT department_id FROM departments     MINUS     SELECT department_id FROM employees)    UNION    SELECT 10 FROM dual; -- INTERSECT first, then MINUS, because of the parenthesesHR> SELECT job_id FROM employees WHERE department_id = 50    MINUS    (SELECT job_id FROM employees WHERE salary > 3000 INTERSECT SELECT job_id FROM job_history);

Exam focus

  • SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM employees UNION SELECT department_id FROM departments fails: ORA-01789 (different number of columns).
  • SELECT job_id FROM employees UNION SELECT salary FROM employees fails: ORA-01790 (text and number).
  • A set operator cannot be used on LONG, BLOB, CLOB columns.

14.6 The Matching Rule in Practice

HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100    UNION    SELECT department_name, NULL FROM departments WHERE department_id = 10;-- ORA-01790? NO: NULL adapts to DATE, last_name/department_name are both text -> works HR> SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100    UNION    SELECT last_name, employee_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 100;-- ORA-01790: expression must have same datatype as corresponding expression (number vs text)

15.1 Set Up Your Practice Tables

From now on you change data. Do it on copies, never on the original sample tables. CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS) copies the rows and the column definitions (including NOT NULL) of a query into a new table; it does not copy primary keys, identity settings or foreign keys.

Exercise 15.1 Create the CO lab copies

$ sql co@localhost:1521/FREEPDB1                            # password Lab_Pass_2026CO> CREATE TABLE lab_customers   AS SELECT customer_id, email_address, full_name FROM customers;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_products    AS SELECT product_id, product_name, unit_price FROM products;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_orders      AS SELECT order_id, order_tms, customer_id, order_status, store_id FROM orders;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_order_items AS SELECT order_id, line_item_id, product_id, unit_price, quantity FROM order_items;-- all four are thereCO> SELECT table_name FROM user_tables WHERE table_name LIKE 'LAB%' ORDER BY 1;CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_orders;                                                    -- 1950
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_order_items PURGE;CO> DROP TABLE lab_orders      PURGE;CO> DROP TABLE lab_products    PURGE;CO> DROP TABLE lab_customers   PURGE;

CO> @labs/ch15/15_00_setup.sql        -- the four CREATE TABLE statements above saved in one file

Note: Because DML is not permanent until you COMMIT (Chapter 16), you can also run every exercise of this chapter, check the result, and finish with ROLLBACK;. SQLcl does not auto-commit by default.

15.2 INSERT

INSERT INTO table [(column [, column ...])]  VALUES (value [, value ...]);INSERT INTO table [(column ...)]  subquery;

Exercise 15.2 Add rows in different ways

-- best practice: always list the columnsCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers (customer_id, email_address, full_name)    VALUES (9001, 'ada.lovelace@example.com', 'Ada Lovelace'); -- omitted columns become NULL (or their DEFAULT); here every column is mandatory, so list all of themCO> INSERT INTO lab_orders (order_id, order_tms, customer_id, order_status, store_id)    VALUES (90001, SYSTIMESTAMP, 9001, 'OPEN', 1);                -- a function as a value -- without a column list the values must match ALL columns, in table order (fragile: avoid)CO> INSERT INTO lab_order_items VALUES (90001, 1, 1, 25.50, 2); -- text and date literals in quotes; an apostrophe is doubledCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9002, 'o.brien@example.com', 'Seán O''Brien'); -- how many rows did we add?CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers;                           -- 394 (392 + 2)
INSERT ... SELECT: copy rows with a query
-- an archive table with the same structure, empty (WHERE 1 = 0 is never true)CO> CREATE TABLE lab_orders_archive AS SELECT * FROM lab_orders WHERE 1 = 0;-- load the cancelled orders into it, with ONE statement (no VALUES clause)CO> INSERT INTO lab_orders_archive SELECT * FROM lab_orders WHERE order_status = 'CANCELLED';CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_orders_archive;
Typical INSERT errors
ErrorCause
ORA-01400: cannot insert NULL into (“CO”.“LAB_CUSTOMERS”.“EMAIL_ADDRESS”)A NOT NULL column was omitted or given NULL
ORA-12899: value too large for columnText longer than the column definition
ORA-00947: not enough values / ORA-00913: too many valuesThe number of values does not match the number of columns
ORA-01722: invalid number / ORA-01858A value cannot be converted to the column data type
ORA-00001: unique constraint violatedA duplicate key on the original tables (the LAB_ copies have no keys yet; Chapter 18 adds them)
ORA-02291: integrity constraint violated - parent key not foundA foreign key value without a parent row (original tables)
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> ROLLBACK;                                  -- if you have not committed yetCO> DELETE FROM lab_customers WHERE customer_id IN (9001, 9002);   -- or remove the rows by hand

15.3 UPDATE

UPDATE table [alias]  SET column = expression [, column = expression ...]  [WHERE condition];UPDATE table SET (col1, col2) = (subquery)  [WHERE condition];

Caution: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause changes every row. Before running an UPDATE or a DELETE, run the same WHERE clause in a SELECT and count the rows.

Exercise 15.3 Change rows

CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_orders WHERE order_status = 'OPEN';        -- count first!CO> UPDATE lab_orders SET order_status = 'CANCELLED' WHERE order_status = 'OPEN' AND order_tms < SYSDATE - 365;12 rows updated.                                                          -- SQLcl always tells you how many -- several columns at once; a calculation based on the current valueCO> UPDATE lab_products SET unit_price = ROUND(unit_price * 1.05, 2), product_name = UPPER(product_name)    WHERE  unit_price < 50; -- the value may come from a (single-row) subqueryCO> UPDATE lab_order_items oi    SET    unit_price = (SELECT p.unit_price FROM lab_products p WHERE p.product_id = oi.product_id)    -- correlated: the inner query uses the outer row (oi)    WHERE  oi.order_id = 1; -- set several columns from ONE multi-column subqueryCO> UPDATE lab_customers c    SET   (email_address, full_name) = (SELECT LOWER(email_address), INITCAP(full_name) FROM lab_customers x WHERE x.customer_id = c.customer_id)    WHERE c.customer_id = 9001;

Exam focus

  • If a subquery in SET returns more than one row you get ORA-01427; if it returns no row the column is set to NULL.
  • The WHERE clause may also contain a subquery: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT ...) or WHERE EXISTS (...).
  • A column can be set to DEFAULT or to NULL explicitly: SET status = DEFAULT.
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
-- or recreate the lab table from the original: DROP TABLE lab_products PURGE; then CREATE ... AS SELECT againCO> ROLLBACK;

15.4 DELETE and TRUNCATE

DELETE [FROM] table [alias]  [WHERE condition];
-- remove one order lineCO> DELETE FROM lab_order_items WHERE order_id = 90001 AND line_item_id = 1;-- remove with a subquery: all items of cancelled ordersCO> DELETE FROM lab_order_items WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM lab_orders WHERE order_status = 'CANCELLED');-- correlated delete: customers who have never orderedCO> DELETE FROM lab_customers c    WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lab_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);-- DELETE without WHERE removes ALL rows (can still be rolled back)CO> DELETE FROM lab_orders_archive;
DELETETRUNCATE TABLE
CategoryDMLDDL
RemovesSelected rows (all if no WHERE)All rows only
RollbackYes, until COMMITNo (implicit commit)
Speed on big tablesSlow: undo and redo for each rowVery fast: resets the segment
Fires DELETE triggersYesNo
Needs a WHERE clauseOptionalNever allowed
CO> TRUNCATE TABLE lab_orders_archive;          -- all rows gone immediately; the table remains

15.5 MERGE: Update or Insert in One Statement

MERGE (an “upsert”) compares a source with a target using a join condition. Rows that match are updated (and optionally deleted); rows that do not match are inserted. It reads each source row once, which makes it ideal for loading a changed data file into a table.

MERGE INTO target [alias]USING  source_table_or_query [alias]ON     (join_condition)WHEN MATCHED THEN      UPDATE SET col = expr [, ...]  [DELETE WHERE condition]WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN  INSERT (columns) VALUES (values)  [WHERE condition];

Exercise 15.4 Load a changed customer list

-- a small staging table with one changed customer (9001) and one new customer (9100)CO> CREATE TABLE lab_customer_stage (customer_id NUMBER, email_address VARCHAR2(255), full_name VARCHAR2(255));CO> INSERT INTO lab_customer_stage VALUES (9001, 'ada@newmail.example.com', 'Ada King-Lovelace');CO> INSERT INTO lab_customer_stage VALUES (9100, 'grace.hopper@example.com', 'Grace Hopper'); CO> MERGE INTO lab_customers t    USING lab_customer_stage s ON (t.customer_id = s.customer_id)    WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.email_address = s.email_address, t.full_name = s.full_name    WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, email_address, full_name)                          VALUES (s.customer_id, s.email_address, s.full_name);2 rows merged.                                  -- 1 updated + 1 inserted

Exam focus

  • You cannot update a column that appears in the ON condition (ORA-38104).
  • If several source rows match the same target row, Oracle raises ORA-30926: unable to get a stable set of rows in the source tables.
  • WHEN MATCHED ... DELETE WHERE condition deletes rows that were just updated and satisfy the condition.
  • Both WHEN clauses are optional individually, but at least one must be present.
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> ROLLBACK;CO> DROP TABLE lab_customer_stage PURGE;

15.6 Multitable INSERT

A multitable insert sends the rows of one query into several tables (or several times into one table) in a single statement. Four forms exist.

FormBehaviour
INSERT ALL INTO ... INTO ... SELECTUnconditional: every source row goes into every listed table
INSERT ALL WHEN cond THEN INTO ...Conditional all: a row goes into every table whose condition is true (it may go to several)
INSERT FIRST WHEN ... THEN INTO ...Conditional first: a row goes into only the first table whose condition is true
... ELSE INTO ...Optional: rows that satisfy no condition
Pivoting insertSeveral INTO clauses pull different columns of the same row, producing several target rows

Exercise 15.5 Route orders into three tables

CO> CREATE TABLE lab_open_orders      AS SELECT * FROM lab_orders WHERE 1 = 0;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_completed_orders AS SELECT * FROM lab_orders WHERE 1 = 0;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_other_orders     AS SELECT * FROM lab_orders WHERE 1 = 0; CO> INSERT FIRST      WHEN order_status = 'OPEN'     THEN INTO lab_open_orders      WHEN order_status = 'COMPLETE' THEN INTO lab_completed_orders      ELSE                                INTO lab_other_orders    SELECT * FROM lab_orders;CO> SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_open_orders) + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_completed_orders)         -- 1950: every row went to exactly ONE table         + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_other_orders) AS total FROM dual; -- INSERT ALL conditional: a big order is copied to a second table as wellCO> CREATE TABLE lab_big_items AS SELECT * FROM lab_order_items WHERE 1 = 0;CO> INSERT ALL      WHEN quantity >= 5 THEN INTO lab_big_items      WHEN unit_price >= 50 THEN INTO lab_big_items            -- a row can match BOTH conditions    SELECT * FROM lab_order_items;

Exam focus

  • With INSERT ALL a row can be inserted several times; with INSERT FIRST at most once.
  • A multitable insert cannot target a view or a remote table, and the SELECT cannot use a sequence.
  • Every INTO clause may have its own column list: INTO t (a, b) VALUES (x, y).
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_big_items PURGE;           CO> DROP TABLE lab_other_orders PURGE;CO> DROP TABLE lab_completed_orders PURGE;   CO> DROP TABLE lab_open_orders PURGE;

15.7 DML and Integrity

DML is checked against every constraint at the moment it runs (or at COMMIT for deferred constraints). Chapter 18 builds the constraints; here is what you will see on the original tables, which have them:

CO> INSERT INTO orders (order_id, order_tms, customer_id, order_status, store_id)    VALUES (99999, SYSTIMESTAMP, 123456, 'OPEN', 1);       -- customer 123456 does not existORA-02291: integrity constraint (CO.ORDERS_CUSTOMER_ID_FK) violated - parent key not foundCO> DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1;           -- customer 1 has ordersORA-02292: integrity constraint (CO.ORDERS_CUSTOMER_ID_FK) violated - child record foundCO> ROLLBACK;

Note: The original tables are safe to experiment with when the statement fails, as above. Never succeed in changing them: commit changes only to LAB_ copies.

Chapter 16: Transactions and Concurrency

Prompts: CO> and a second session CO2> • Exam topic 10: Managing Database Transactions, Controlling Transactions • Some exercises need two terminal windows.

Topics in this chapter

  • 16.1 What a Transaction Is
  • 16.2 COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT
  • 16.3 Read Consistency and Isolation
  • 16.4 Locks and Two Sessions
  • 16.5 Beyond COMMIT: Flashback
  • 16.6 Transaction Control Cheat Sheet
  • 16.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

16.1 What a Transaction Is

A transaction is a sequence of statements that Oracle treats as one unit of work: either all of its changes become permanent, or none do. The classic example is a bank transfer: the debit and the credit must succeed or fail together. Oracle guarantees the ACID properties:

PropertyMeaningHow Oracle provides it
AtomicityAll or nothingUndo data lets a transaction be rolled back
ConsistencyData moves from one valid state to anotherConstraints are checked
IsolationConcurrent transactions do not see each other’s uncommitted workRead consistency (multi-version), row locks
DurabilityCommitted work survives a crashRedo log written at COMMIT
When does a transaction start and end?
A transaction begins withA transaction ends with
The first DML statement (or SET TRANSACTION) after the previous transaction endedCOMMIT or ROLLBACK
A DDL or DCL statement (implicit commit)
A normal exit of the client program (implicit commit), or a crash or disconnect (implicit rollback)

Exam focus

  • There is no BEGIN TRANSACTION in Oracle SQL: the first DML starts the transaction.
  • DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) and DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) commit first: pending DML of the session is made permanent even if the DDL then fails.
  • SQLcl commits automatically when you EXIT normally, but not on an abnormal end.

16.2 COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT

StatementEffect
COMMIT [WORK]Makes all changes of the transaction permanent and visible to other sessions; releases all locks
ROLLBACK [WORK]Undoes all changes since the transaction began; releases locks
SAVEPOINT nameMarks a point inside the transaction
ROLLBACK TO [SAVEPOINT] nameUndoes only the changes made after the savepoint; the transaction continues and earlier changes remain pending

Exercise 16.1 Partial rollback with savepoints

CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers;                         -- 394 or so: start value NCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9301, 'one@example.com',   'Customer One');CO> SAVEPOINT after_one;                                         -- a markerCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9302, 'two@example.com',   'Customer Two');CO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9303, 'three@example.com', 'Customer Three');CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers;                         -- N + 3 CO> ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_one;                            -- undo only rows 9302 and 9303-- N + 1 : row 9301 is still pendingCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers;CO> COMMIT;                                                     -- now row 9301 is permanent-- nothing left to undo: has no effectCO> ROLLBACK;

Exam focus

  • After ROLLBACK TO savepoint the savepoint itself remains, but all savepoints created after it are lost.
  • Reusing a savepoint name moves the savepoint.
  • If one statement fails, Oracle rolls back only that statement (statement-level atomicity); the rest of the transaction is intact.
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DELETE FROM lab_customers WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 9301 AND 9303;CO> COMMIT;
A statement-level rollback in action
-- succeeds, pendingCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9401, 'x@example.com', 'Customer X');CO> UPDATE lab_customers SET email_address = NULL WHERE customer_id = 9401;ORA-01407: cannot update ("CO"."LAB_CUSTOMERS"."EMAIL_ADDRESS") to NULL            -- this statement is undone ...-- 1 : ... but the INSERT is still thereCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers WHERE customer_id = 9401;CO> ROLLBACK;

16.3 Read Consistency and Isolation

Oracle never shows you another session’s uncommitted changes (no dirty reads). It also gives every query a read-consistent snapshot as of the moment the query began, rebuilt from undo data when blocks have since changed. As a result readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

Isolation levelBehaviour in Oracle
READ COMMITTED (default)Each statement sees data committed before it started
SERIALIZABLEThe whole transaction sees data as of its start; conflicting changes raise ORA-08177
READ ONLY (SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY)Whole-transaction snapshot; DML is not allowed. Ends at COMMIT/ROLLBACK
CO> SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY;             -- must be the first statement of the transaction-- the same answer all transaction long, even if others commitCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_orders;CO> COMMIT;                                -- ends the read-only transaction

16.4 Locks and Two Sessions

DML takes row locks: the first session that changes a row owns it until it commits or rolls back. A second session that tries to change the same row waits. Rows that are only read are never locked. Try it with two terminal windows connected as CO.

Exercise 16.2 Two sessions, one row

-- ---- session 1 (CO>) ----CO> UPDATE lab_customers SET full_name = 'Ada A.' WHERE customer_id = 9001;     -- locks the row -- ---- session 2 (CO2>) ------ sees the OLD name: no dirty read, no waitingCO2> SELECT full_name FROM lab_customers WHERE customer_id = 9001;-- WAITS: the row is locked by session 1CO2> UPDATE lab_customers SET full_name = 'Ada B.' WHERE customer_id = 9001; -- ---- session 1 ------ the lock is released ...CO> COMMIT;-- ---- session 2 ---- the waiting UPDATE now completes; COMMIT or ROLLBACK to end itCO2> COMMIT;
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows so that nobody else can change them while you decide what to do. The clause controls what happens if the rows are already locked.

ClauseIf a row is already locked by another session
FOR UPDATEWait indefinitely
FOR UPDATE NOWAITFail at once with ORA-00054: resource busy and acquire with NOWAIT
FOR UPDATE WAIT 5Wait up to 5 seconds, then fail with ORA-30006
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDSilently skip the locked rows (useful for work queues)
FOR UPDATE OF columnLock only the rows of the table that owns that column (in a join)
-- lock the row nowCO> SELECT order_id, order_status FROM lab_orders WHERE order_id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;CO> UPDATE lab_orders SET order_status = 'PAID' WHERE order_id = 1;-- also releases the lockCO> COMMIT;
Deadlock

A deadlock occurs when two sessions each hold a lock the other needs: session 1 holds row A and wants B, session 2 holds B and wants A. Oracle detects it, rolls back one statement of one session with ORA-00060: deadlock detected, and writes a trace file. The fix is in the application: lock rows in the same order and commit promptly.

Exam focus

  • Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers; writers block only other writers of the same row.
  • DDL needs exclusive access to the object; it fails with ORA-00054 if the table has uncommitted DML.
  • COMMIT ends the transaction and releases all locks.

16.5 Beyond COMMIT: Flashback

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: Because undo data keeps old row versions for a while, Oracle can show a table as it was in the past: SELECT * FROM lab_orders AS OF TIMESTAMP SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '5' MINUTE; (flashback query) and can restore a table from a mistaken change with FLASHBACK TABLE lab_orders TO TIMESTAMP ... (row movement must be enabled) or from a DROP with FLASHBACK TABLE lab_orders TO BEFORE DROP (Chapter 17). Flashback is not on the 1Z0-071 exam, but it saves careers.

-- how many customers 10 minutes ago?CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_customers AS OF TIMESTAMP SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '10' MINUTE;

16.6 Transaction Control Cheat Sheet

You didPending DML is...
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGEPending: visible only to you
COMMITPermanent and visible to everyone
ROLLBACKDiscarded
CREATE TABLE ... (any DDL)Committed first, then the DDL runs and commits
GRANT / REVOKECommitted first
EXIT in SQLclCommitted
Closing the window / network failureRolled back
A failed single statementThat statement only is undone

Tip: In SQLcl you can turn on automatic commit after each statement with SET AUTOCOMMIT ON. Do not use it while learning: it removes your safety net.

Challenge 16.1 Insert two rows, create a savepoint between them, insert a third row, roll back to the savepoint and commit. How many of the three rows survive?

Hint: Rows inserted before the savepoint survive.

Challenge 16.2 A script runs DELETE FROM lab_orders_archive; CREATE TABLE lab_x (a NUMBER); ROLLBACK;. Is the DELETE undone?

Hint: The DDL statement commits before it runs.

Challenge 16.3 Show how to read the same unchanged snapshot of lab_orders twice in one transaction while another session commits changes.

Hint: A read-only transaction.

Challenge 16.4 Write the statement that lets a batch job lock up to 10 unprocessed orders and skip any that another job already holds.

Hint: ROWNUM with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (the row-limiting FETCH FIRST clause cannot be combined with FOR UPDATE). ROWNUM is applied before locked rows are skipped, so the job may receive fewer than 10 rows.

Challenge 16.5 Why does a second session wait when it tries to update a row, but never waits when it only reads it?

Hint: Think of locks and undo.
