COMMIT the lab tables you created in Chapter 15 and write a transaction script for a realistic business event: a customer places an order of two items. Save as labs/ei_16_place_order.sql.

CO> INSERT INTO lab_orders (order_id, order_tms, customer_id, order_status, store_id) VALUES (90100, SYSTIMESTAMP, 9001, 'OPEN', 1);CO> SAVEPOINT order_header;CO> INSERT INTO lab_order_items (order_id, line_item_id, product_id, unit_price, quantity) VALUES (90100, 1, 1, 25.50, 2);CO> INSERT INTO lab_order_items (order_id, line_item_id, product_id, unit_price, quantity) VALUES (90100, 2, 2, 12.00, 1);-- the header and both lines become permanent together (use ROLLBACK to cancel the whole order)CO> COMMIT;

16.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

Challenge 16.1 Insert two rows, create a savepoint between them, insert a third row, roll back to the savepoint and commit. How many of the three rows survive?

CO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9501, 'a@e.com', 'A');CO> SAVEPOINT s1;CO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9502, 'b@e.com', 'B');CO> INSERT INTO lab_customers VALUES (9503, 'c@e.com', 'C');CO> ROLLBACK TO s1;  COMMIT;                 -- only 9501 survives

Challenge 16.2 A script runs DELETE FROM lab_orders_archive; CREATE TABLE lab_x (a NUMBER); ROLLBACK;. Is the DELETE undone?

-- No. CREATE TABLE issues an implicit COMMIT first, so the DELETE is already permanent when ROLLBACK runs.

Challenge 16.3 Show how to read the same unchanged snapshot of lab_orders twice in one transaction while another session commits changes.

CO> SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY;CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_orders;   -- run again later: the answer does not changeCO> COMMIT;

Challenge 16.4 Write the statement that lets a batch job lock up to 10 unprocessed orders and skip any that another job already holds.

CO> SELECT order_id FROM lab_orders WHERE order_status = 'OPEN' AND ROWNUM <= 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Challenge 16.5 Why does a second session wait when it tries to update a row, but never waits when it only reads it?

-- UPDATE needs the row lock held by the first session; a query uses undo to rebuild the committed version of the row, so it needs no lock.

Chapter 17: DDL I: Creating and Changing Tables

Prompt: CO> • Exam topic 12: Use DDL to Manage Tables and Their Relationships (tables, columns, data types, UNUSED columns, truncating) • Creates only LAB_ objects.

Topics in this chapter

  • 17.1 DDL Basics
  • 17.2 CREATE TABLE
  • 17.3 Identity and Virtual Columns
  • 17.4 Create a Table from a Query (CTAS)
  • 17.5 ALTER TABLE: Changing Columns
  • 17.6 TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT and DROP
  • 17.7 Table Information from the Dictionary
  • 17.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

17.1 DDL Basics

DDL statements define and change the structure of the database. Each one commits the current transaction before and after it runs, and cannot be rolled back. Every object you create is owned by the connected user (its schema). Remember the lab rule: prefix your objects with LAB_.

StatementPurpose
CREATECreate an object (table, view, sequence, index, user ...)
ALTERChange an existing object
DROPRemove an object
TRUNCATERemove all rows of a table (no rollback)
RENAMERename a table, view, sequence or synonym
COMMENTAttach a description to a table or column

17.2 CREATE TABLE

CREATE TABLE [schema.]table_name (    column  datatype  [DEFAULT expression]  [column_constraint ...],    ...    [table_constraint, ...]) [TABLESPACE ts];

Exercise 17.1 Create a table with several data types

CO> CREATE TABLE lab_promotions (      promo_id     NUMBER(6)       NOT NULL,                 -- up to 6 digits, mandatory      promo_name   VARCHAR2(60)    NOT NULL,                 -- variable-length text, max 60 bytes      discount_pct NUMBER(5,2)     DEFAULT 0,                -- 3 digits before the point, 2 after      -- the default is evaluated at INSERT time      starts_on    DATE            DEFAULT SYSDATE,      ends_on      DATE,      created_at   TIMESTAMP       DEFAULT SYSTIMESTAMP,     -- fractional seconds      notes        VARCHAR2(200 CHAR)                        -- 200 CHARACTERS, not bytes    );CO> DESC lab_promotions-- other columns take their DEFAULTsCO> INSERT INTO lab_promotions (promo_id, promo_name) VALUES (1, 'Autumn Sale');CO> SELECT promo_id, discount_pct, starts_on, created_at FROM lab_promotions;
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_promotions PURGE;
↪ REPLAY — redo it quickly
CO> @labs/ch17/17_02_lab_promotions.sql      -- the CREATE TABLE above saved as a script
Choosing data types
StoreUseAvoid
Whole numbers and moneyNUMBER(p) and NUMBER(p,2)Text columns holding numbers
Names, codes, descriptionsVARCHAR2(n); CHAR(n) only for truly fixed-length codesCHAR for variable text (blank-padding surprises)
Calendar datesDATEText such as ‘20240315’
Event times with sub-second precisionTIMESTAMP; TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE for global dataDATE when seconds fractions or zones matter
Large text / filesCLOB / BLOBLONG (obsolete)
Yes/no flagsCHAR(1) with a CHECK (‘Y’/‘N’)

Exam focus

  • A DEFAULT is used only when the column is omitted from the INSERT or DEFAULT is written explicitly; an explicit NULL stays NULL.
  • Table and column names: start with a letter, up to 128 bytes, letters/digits/_ $ #, not a reserved word, unique within the schema.
  • NUMBER(7,2) holds up to 99999.99; NUMBER(3) rejects 1000 with ORA-01438; a scale rounds extra decimals silently.

17.3 Identity and Virtual Columns

The CO schema generates its keys with identity columns (12c and later). GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY attaches an internal sequence to the column. A virtual column stores no data; its value is computed from other columns each time it is read.

CO> CREATE TABLE lab_coupons (      -- the CO style: a NULL is replaced      coupon_id   NUMBER GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,      code        VARCHAR2(20) NOT NULL,      amount      NUMBER(8,2)  NOT NULL,      tax_pct     NUMBER(4,2)  DEFAULT 20,      -- computed, never stored      gross       NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS (ROUND(amount * (1 + tax_pct / 100), 2)) VIRTUAL    );-- coupon_id is generated: 1CO> INSERT INTO lab_coupons (code, amount) VALUES ('WELCOME', 10);CO> INSERT INTO lab_coupons (code, amount) VALUES ('AUTUMN', 25.50);CO> SELECT coupon_id, code, amount, gross FROM lab_coupons;1 WELCOME 10   122 AUTUMN  25.5 30.6
Identity clauseBehaviour
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITYOracle always supplies the value; supplying your own raises ORA-32795
GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITYOracle supplies a value only if you omit the column
GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL AS IDENTITYAlso when you pass NULL explicitly (used by every CO table)
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_coupons PURGE;

17.4 Create a Table from a Query (CTAS)

You already used CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT in Chapter 15. It builds the columns from the select list (names, data types, NOT NULL) and loads the rows. Rename columns by aliasing or by listing names. WHERE 1 = 0 copies the structure only.

-- column names listed hereCO> CREATE TABLE lab_big_customers (cust_id, cust_name, orders_placed) AS      SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, COUNT(o.order_id)      FROM   customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id      GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.full_name      HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) >= 10;CO> SELECT * FROM lab_big_customers FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;-- structure only, no rowsCO> CREATE TABLE lab_orders_shape AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE 1 = 0;

Exam focus

  • CTAS copies NOT NULL constraints but not primary/foreign keys, CHECK constraints, defaults (except as columns), indexes, triggers or grants.
  • A CTAS is DDL: it commits, and it is not part of any transaction you can roll back.

17.5 ALTER TABLE: Changing Columns

TaskSyntax
Add a columnALTER TABLE t ADD (col datatype [DEFAULT x] [NOT NULL]); — new column is NULL (or the default) in existing rows
Change data type or sizeALTER TABLE t MODIFY (col datatype); — widening is always allowed; narrowing needs data that fits
Change/add DEFAULTALTER TABLE t MODIFY (col DEFAULT x); — affects only future rows
Make mandatory / optionalMODIFY (col NOT NULL) needs a value in every row; MODIFY (col NULL) removes it
Rename a columnALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN old TO new;
Drop a columnALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN col; or DROP (col1, col2)
Mark a column unusedALTER TABLE t SET UNUSED (col);
Remove unused columnsALTER TABLE t DROP UNUSED COLUMNS;
Rename the tableALTER TABLE t RENAME TO new; or RENAME t TO new;
Read-only / read-writeALTER TABLE t READ ONLY; / READ WRITE;

Exercise 17.2 Evolve a table

CO> CREATE TABLE lab_stores AS SELECT store_id, store_name, web_address FROM stores;-- existing rows get the defaultCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores ADD (region VARCHAR2(30) DEFAULT 'UNASSIGNED');-- existing rows get NULLCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores ADD (opened_on DATE);-- widen: always worksCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores MODIFY (store_name VARCHAR2(300));CO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores RENAME COLUMN web_address TO url;CO> DESC lab_stores-- narrow: fails if any value is longerCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores MODIFY (store_name VARCHAR2(5));ORA-01441: cannot decrease column length because some value is too big-- fails: existing rows contain NULLCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores MODIFY (opened_on NOT NULL);ORA-02296: cannot enable (CO.) - null values found
Dropping columns and the UNUSED option

DROP COLUMN physically removes the column data from every row, which can take a long time and many resources on a big table. SET UNUSED is instant: the column becomes invisible and unusable immediately; the storage is reclaimed later, at a quiet time, with DROP UNUSED COLUMNS.

-- instant; the column is gone for every userCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores SET UNUSED (opened_on);CO> SELECT * FROM lab_stores FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;        -- opened_on no longer appears-- the table is listed with 1 unused columnCO> SELECT table_name, count FROM user_unused_col_tabs;CO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores DROP UNUSED COLUMNS;              -- reclaim the space, laterCO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores DROP COLUMN region;               -- direct drop of a visible column-- several at once (a table must keep at least one column)CO> ALTER TABLE lab_stores DROP (store_name, url);

Exam focus

  • A column set UNUSED cannot be restored; a new column with the same name may be added afterwards.
  • You cannot drop all columns of a table (ORA-12983).
  • A column that is part of a primary key or referenced by a foreign key cannot be dropped unless you add CASCADE CONSTRAINTS.
  • ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY to a different data type works only if the column is empty (NULL in all rows).

17.6 TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT and DROP

-- all rows gone, structure and constraints stay; no rollbackCO> TRUNCATE TABLE lab_stores;CO> RENAME lab_stores TO lab_shops;                             -- or ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TOCO> COMMENT ON TABLE  lab_shops IS 'Practice copy of the CO stores';CO> COMMENT ON COLUMN lab_shops.store_id IS 'Identifier copied from STORES.STORE_ID';-- comments live in the dictionaryCO> SELECT comments FROM user_tab_comments WHERE table_name = 'LAB_SHOPS';-- goes to the RECYCLE BIN: it can be restoredCO> DROP TABLE lab_shops;-- (or: SHOW RECYCLEBIN)CO> SELECT object_name, original_name, droptime FROM user_recyclebin;CO> FLASHBACK TABLE lab_shops TO BEFORE DROP;                   -- restored, with its dataCO> DROP TABLE lab_shops PURGE;                                 -- gone for good: no recycle bin
StatementEffect on the tableRollback?
DELETE FROM tRemoves rowsYes
TRUNCATE TABLE tRemoves all rows, keeps the tableNo
DROP TABLE tRemoves the table (to the recycle bin since 10g)No, but FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP
DROP TABLE t PURGERemoves the table completelyNo
DROP TABLE t CASCADE CONSTRAINTSAlso drops foreign keys of other tables that point to itNo

Exam focus

  • Dropping a table also drops its indexes, triggers and privileges but not views, synonyms or procedures that use it (they become INVALID).
  • DROP TABLE parent fails with ORA-02449 while foreign keys reference it, unless CASCADE CONSTRAINTS is used.
  • FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP works only if the table is still in the recycle bin.

17.7 Table Information from the Dictionary

CO> SELECT table_name, num_rows, tablespace_name FROM user_tables WHERE table_name LIKE 'LAB%' ORDER BY 1;CO> SELECT column_id, column_name, data_type, data_length, data_precision, data_scale, nullable, data_default    -- what DESC shows, and more    FROM   user_tab_columns WHERE table_name = 'LAB_PROMOTIONS' ORDER BY column_id;

Tip: Chapter 21 covers the dictionary in depth. For now DESC table is enough.

Chapter 18: DDL II: Constraints, Temporary and External Tables

Prompts: CO> and SYSTEM> • Exam topic 12: Managing constraints; creating and using temporary tables and external tables • Creates only LAB_ objects.

Topics in this chapter

  • 18.1 Why Constraints
  • 18.2 Defining Constraints
  • 18.3 Seeing Constraints Work
  • 18.4 Adding, Dropping, Enabling and Disabling
  • 18.5 Constraints in the Original CO Schema
  • 18.6 Global Temporary Tables
  • 18.7 External Tables
  • 18.8 Answers to the Lab Challenges

18.1 Why Constraints

A constraint is a rule that the database itself enforces, whatever program or person changes the data. Constraints keep data correct even when an application has a bug. Oracle supports five types:

TypeCode in the dictionaryRuleNULL allowed?
NOT NULLCThe column must have a valueNo
UNIQUEUNo two rows may have the same value(s)Yes (a NULL does not count as a duplicate; in a composite key, rows with all-NULL are exempt)
PRIMARY KEYPUnique and not null; one per table; identifies the rowNo
FOREIGN KEYRThe value must exist in the referenced parent key (or be NULL)Yes
CHECKCA condition on the row must not be FALSEYes (UNKNOWN passes)

Exam focus

  • A constraint you do not name gets a system name such as SYS_C0012345. Always name constraints: CONSTRAINT lab_cust_pk PRIMARY KEY (customer_id).
  • Oracle creates a unique index automatically to enforce a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint.
  • A CHECK constraint cannot use SYSDATE, subqueries or other rows.

18.2 Defining Constraints

A constraint can be written inline (on the column) or out of line (after all columns). Only out-of-line syntax can cover several columns, and NOT NULL is always inline.

Exercise 18.1 Create related tables with every constraint type

CO> CREATE TABLE lab_customer (      -- inline      customer_id  NUMBER        CONSTRAINT lab_customer_pk PRIMARY KEY,      email        VARCHAR2(255) CONSTRAINT lab_customer_email_nn NOT NULL                                 CONSTRAINT lab_customer_email_uk UNIQUE,      full_name    VARCHAR2(255) NOT NULL,      tier         VARCHAR2(10)  DEFAULT 'STANDARD'                                 CONSTRAINT lab_customer_tier_ck CHECK (tier IN ('STANDARD','GOLD','PLATINUM')) ); CO> CREATE TABLE lab_purchase (      purchase_id  NUMBER        GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL AS IDENTITY,      customer_id  NUMBER        NOT NULL,      purchased_on DATE          DEFAULT SYSDATE NOT NULL,      amount       NUMBER(10,2)  NOT NULL,      status       VARCHAR2(10)  DEFAULT 'OPEN' NOT NULL,      -- out of line      CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_pk       PRIMARY KEY (purchase_id),      CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_cust_fk  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES lab_customer (customer_id),      CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_amount_ck CHECK (amount > 0),      CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_status_ck CHECK (status IN ('OPEN','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED')) ); -- a composite primary key: two columns, so out of lineCO> CREATE TABLE lab_purchase_item (      purchase_id  NUMBER, line_no NUMBER, product_id NUMBER NOT NULL, quantity NUMBER(4) NOT NULL,      CONSTRAINT lab_pitem_pk PRIMARY KEY (purchase_id, line_no),      CONSTRAINT lab_pitem_purch_fk FOREIGN KEY (purchase_id) REFERENCES lab_purchase (purchase_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,      CONSTRAINT lab_pitem_qty_ck CHECK (quantity BETWEEN 1 AND 999) );
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_purchase_item PURGE;   CO> DROP TABLE lab_purchase PURGE;   CO> DROP TABLE lab_customer PURGE;-- children first! (or DROP TABLE lab_customer CASCADE CONSTRAINTS PURGE;)
↪ REPLAY — redo it quickly
CO> @labs/ch18/18_02_constraints.sql
Foreign key actions when the parent row is deleted
ClauseEffect of DELETE FROM parent
(nothing)Refused with ORA-02292 if child rows exist
ON DELETE CASCADEThe child rows are deleted too
ON DELETE SET NULLThe foreign key column of the children is set to NULL

18.3 Seeing Constraints Work

Exercise 18.2 Break every rule once

CO> INSERT INTO lab_customer (customer_id, email, full_name) VALUES (1, 'ada@example.com', 'Ada Lovelace');CO> INSERT INTO lab_customer (customer_id, email, full_name) VALUES (1, 'bob@example.com', 'Bob');ORA-00001: unique constraint (CO.LAB_CUSTOMER_PK) violated                   -- duplicate primary keyCO> INSERT INTO lab_customer (customer_id, email, full_name) VALUES (2, 'ada@example.com', 'Ada 2');ORA-00001: unique constraint (CO.LAB_CUSTOMER_EMAIL_UK) violated             -- duplicate e-mailCO> INSERT INTO lab_customer (customer_id, email, full_name) VALUES (3, NULL, 'No Mail');ORA-01400: cannot insert NULL into ("CO"."LAB_CUSTOMER"."EMAIL")             -- NOT NULLCO> INSERT INTO lab_customer (customer_id, email, full_name, tier) VALUES (4, 'x@example.com', 'X', 'BRONZE');ORA-02290: check constraint (CO.LAB_CUSTOMER_TIER_CK) violated               -- CHECKCO> INSERT INTO lab_purchase (customer_id, amount) VALUES (99, 10);ORA-02291: integrity constraint (CO.LAB_PURCHASE_CUST_FK) violated - parent key not found-- ok; purchase_id generatedCO> INSERT INTO lab_purchase (customer_id, amount) VALUES (1, 10);CO> DELETE FROM lab_customer WHERE customer_id = 1;ORA-02292: integrity constraint (CO.LAB_PURCHASE_CUST_FK) violated - child record foundCO> ROLLBACK;
ErrorConstraint broken
ORA-00001PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE
ORA-01400 / ORA-01407NOT NULL (insert / update)
ORA-02290CHECK
ORA-02291FOREIGN KEY: parent key not found
ORA-02292FOREIGN KEY: child record found (parent delete or key change)

18.4 Adding, Dropping, Enabling and Disabling

CO> ALTER TABLE lab_customer ADD CONSTRAINT lab_customer_name_ck CHECK (full_name = TRIM(full_name));   -- add (checks existing rows)-- NOT NULL is added with MODIFYCO> ALTER TABLE lab_purchase MODIFY (amount NOT NULL);CO> ALTER TABLE lab_customer DROP CONSTRAINT lab_customer_name_ck;-- stop enforcing (for a bulk load)CO> ALTER TABLE lab_purchase DISABLE CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_cust_fk;-- check ALL rows again; fails on violationsCO> ALTER TABLE lab_purchase ENABLE  CONSTRAINT lab_purchase_cust_fk;-- drops the PK and the foreign keys that use itCO> ALTER TABLE lab_customer DROP PRIMARY KEY CASCADE;CO> ALTER TABLE lab_customer RENAME CONSTRAINT lab_customer_pk TO lab_cust_pk;
OptionMeaning
ENABLE VALIDATE (default)Enforce for new changes and check existing rows
ENABLE NOVALIDATEEnforce for new changes only; existing rows are not checked
DISABLENot enforced (a disabled PK/UNIQUE drops its index unless you keep it)
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERREDChecked at COMMIT instead of at each statement (useful for circular references and bulk loads)

Exam focus

  • DROP TABLE parent CASCADE CONSTRAINTS removes the foreign keys of the children but keeps the child tables.
  • When you disable a primary key that is referenced, you must disable (or CASCADE) the foreign keys first.
  • You cannot create a foreign key to a column that is not a primary or unique key (ORA-02270).

18.5 Constraints in the Original CO Schema

The CO tables enforce their business rules with constraints. Look them up in the dictionary (Chapter 21 explains these views):

-- search_condition_vc: the CHECK text (12.2 and later)CO> SELECT table_name, constraint_name, constraint_type, search_condition_vc    FROM   user_constraints    WHERE  table_name IN ('ORDERS','STORES','SHIPMENTS','PRODUCTS') AND constraint_type IN ('C','R','U','P')    ORDER  BY table_name, constraint_type;CO> SELECT cc.table_name, cc.column_name, c.constraint_name    FROM   user_cons_columns cc JOIN user_constraints c ON c.constraint_name = cc.constraint_name    -- every foreign key column in CO    WHERE  c.constraint_type = 'R' ORDER BY cc.table_name;

Note: Use SEARCH_CONDITION on 19c; it is a LONG column that SQLcl can display. The allowed values of ORDER_STATUS and SHIPMENT_STATUS are in these CHECK constraints: use them rather than guessing.

18.6 Global Temporary Tables

A global temporary table has a permanent definition that every session sees, but its rows are private to each session and disappear automatically. Use it for intermediate results in a multi-step report. ON COMMIT controls the lifetime of the rows.

Exercise 18.3 Per-session scratch data

CO> CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE lab_gtt_basket (      product_id NUMBER, quantity NUMBER )    -- rows vanish at COMMIT (or use PRESERVE ROWS: until the session ends)    ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS;CO> INSERT INTO lab_gtt_basket VALUES (1, 2);CO> INSERT INTO lab_gtt_basket VALUES (2, 1);CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_gtt_basket;        -- 2 : visible to me onlyCO> COMMIT;CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_gtt_basket;        -- 0 : ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS emptied it-- Y, SYS$TRANSACTIONCO> SELECT table_name, temporary, duration FROM user_tables WHERE table_name = 'LAB_GTT_BASKET';
Global temporary tableOrdinary table
DefinitionPermanent, sharedPermanent, shared
RowsPrivate to each session; deleted at COMMIT or session endShared and permanent after COMMIT
Redo / undo costLow (little redo)Full
Locks between sessionsNone on the rowsRow locks
Indexes, constraintsAllowed; no foreign keys to/from other tablesAllowed

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: Oracle 18c adds private temporary tables (CREATE PRIVATE TEMPORARY TABLE ora$ptt_basket ...) whose definition also disappears at the end of the transaction or session. The exam still asks about global temporary tables.

↩ RESET — undo this exercise
-- ORA-14452 if another session still uses it: have that session COMMIT or TRUNCATECO> DROP TABLE lab_gtt_basket PURGE;

18.7 External Tables

An external table lets you query a file outside the database (a CSV, for example) with ordinary SELECT statements, without loading it. Oracle stores only the definition; the data stays in the file. The file lives in an operating-system folder that the database accesses through a DIRECTORY object.

Exercise 18.4 Query a CSV file

First an administrator creates the directory object and the file. The path is on the database server (inside the container, if you use Docker).

# 1) Create the folder and the file on the database server (Docker example; use any folder on Linux or Windows)$ docker exec -u root oracle-free mkdir -p /opt/oracle/lab_files$ docker exec -u root oracle-free bash -c "printf 'id,name,city\n1,Ada,London\n2,Grace,New York\n3,Linus,Helsinki\n' > /opt/oracle/lab_files/new_customers.csv"$ docker exec -u root oracle-free chmod -R a+rx /opt/oracle/lab_files -- the object points to the folderSYSTEM> CREATE OR REPLACE DIRECTORY lab_dir AS '/opt/oracle/lab_files';-- object privilege on the directorySYSTEM> GRANT READ, WRITE ON DIRECTORY lab_dir TO co;-- only needed if CO should create directories itselfSYSTEM> GRANT CREATE ANY DIRECTORY TO co;
CO> CREATE TABLE lab_ext_customers (      id NUMBER, name VARCHAR2(50), city VARCHAR2(50) )    ORGANIZATION EXTERNAL (      -- the access driver for text files (ORACLE_DATAPUMP for dump files)      TYPE ORACLE_LOADER      DEFAULT DIRECTORY lab_dir      ACCESS PARAMETERS (        RECORDS DELIMITED BY NEWLINE        SKIP 1                                             -- ignore the header line        FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','                           -- comma-separated        MISSING FIELD VALUES ARE NULL )      LOCATION ('new_customers.csv') )    -- tolerate bad rows (they are written to a .bad file)    REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED;CO> SELECT * FROM lab_ext_customers ORDER BY id;           -- reads the file every time1 Ada   London / 2 Grace New York / 3 Linus Helsinki-- load it into a real tableCO> INSERT INTO lab_customers (customer_id, email_address, full_name)    SELECT id + 9600, LOWER(name) || '@example.com', name FROM lab_ext_customers;
External table facts
AllowedSELECT, joins, views on it, CTAS and INSERT ... SELECT from it, indexes not allowed
Not allowedINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, constraints, indexes (an external table is read-only)
RowsAlways reflect the current content of the file; no statistics until gathered
NeedsA DIRECTORY object, READ privilege on it, and the file readable by the Oracle operating-system user

Exam focus

  • Data in an external table is read-only; DML fails with ORA-30657.
  • ORACLE_LOADER reads text files; ORACLE_DATAPUMP can also write a table out to a binary file (CTAS) that other databases can read.
  • REJECT LIMIT decides how many bad rows are tolerated before the query fails (ORA-30653).
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_ext_customers PURGE;SYSTEM> DROP DIRECTORY lab_dir;CO> DELETE FROM lab_customers WHERE customer_id > 9600;   CO> COMMIT;

Tip: No DBA access or no file system? SQLcl’s LOAD command loads a CSV straight into a table (LOAD lab_customers new_customers.csv) and is how the SH schema is installed.

Chapter 19: Indexes, Sequences and Synonyms

Prompt: CO> (HR> for the HR sequences) • Exam topic 11: Managing Indexes, Synonyms and Sequences • Creates only LAB_ objects.

Topics in this chapter

  • 19.1 Indexes
  • 19.2 Sequences
  • 19.3 Synonyms
  • 19.4 Answers to the Lab Challenges

19.1 Indexes

An index is a separate structure that lets Oracle find rows by the value of one or more columns without reading the whole table, like the index of a book. Indexes speed up queries that filter, join or sort on the indexed columns but add work to every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and use storage. You never name an index in a query: the optimizer decides to use it.

Index typeCreated byBest for
B-tree (default)CREATE INDEXHigh-cardinality columns (many different values); equality and range searches
UniqueCREATE UNIQUE INDEX, or a PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE constraintEnforcing uniqueness
Composite (concatenated)CREATE INDEX ... ON t (a, b)Queries that filter on a, or on a and b (a leading column rule applies)
Function-basedCREATE INDEX ... ON t (UPPER(col))Queries that apply that exact expression: WHERE UPPER(col) = ...
BitmapCREATE BITMAP INDEXLow-cardinality columns in data warehouses (SH uses them); poor for heavy DML
InvisibleCREATE INDEX ... INVISIBLETesting an index without affecting plans

Exercise 19.1 Create, check and use indexes

-- a copy with NO indexesCO> CREATE TABLE lab_big_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders;CO> SELECT index_name FROM user_indexes WHERE table_name = 'LAB_BIG_ORDERS';   -- none -- single columnCO> CREATE INDEX lab_big_orders_cust_ix ON lab_big_orders (customer_id);-- compositeCO> CREATE INDEX lab_big_orders_status_dt_ix ON lab_big_orders (order_status, order_tms);-- uniqueCO> CREATE UNIQUE INDEX lab_big_orders_id_ux ON lab_big_orders (order_id);-- function-basedCO> CREATE INDEX lab_cust_upper_ix ON lab_customers (UPPER(full_name));-- can now use the indexCO> SELECT full_name FROM lab_customers WHERE UPPER(full_name) = 'ADA LOVELACE'; CO> SELECT index_name, uniqueness, index_type FROM user_indexes WHERE table_name = 'LAB_BIG_ORDERS';CO> SELECT index_name, column_position, column_name FROM user_ind_columns    -- which columns, in which order    WHERE  table_name = 'LAB_BIG_ORDERS' ORDER BY index_name, column_position;
Rules of thumb for choosing indexes
  • Index the columns used in WHERE, JOIN conditions and ORDER BY of frequent, selective queries. Index foreign key columns so that deleting a parent row does not scan the whole child table.
  • A composite index on (a, b) helps filters on a and on a AND b, but usually not on b alone (leading-column rule).
  • Do not index tiny tables or columns with very few distinct values (except bitmaps in a warehouse).
  • A function applied to an indexed column (WHERE TRUNC(order_tms) = ..., WHERE UPPER(name) = ...) prevents a plain index; create a function-based index with the same expression, or rewrite the condition as a range.
  • Implicit conversion (a number column compared to a text literal) can also stop the index being used.

Exam focus

  • PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints create their unique indexes automatically; dropping the constraint normally drops the index.
  • You cannot alter an index’s columns: drop and recreate it (ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD only rebuilds).
  • A bitmap index is for low cardinality; a B-tree for high cardinality.
  • DROP TABLE drops its indexes; DROP INDEX never touches the table’s data.
  • A query may be slower with an index if it returns a large part of the table: a full table scan is then cheaper.
CO> ALTER INDEX lab_big_orders_cust_ix RENAME TO lab_big_orders_cust_ix2;-- the optimizer ignores it; DML still maintains itCO> ALTER INDEX lab_big_orders_cust_ix2 INVISIBLE;CO> ALTER INDEX lab_big_orders_cust_ix2 VISIBLE;CO> DROP INDEX lab_big_orders_cust_ix2;
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP TABLE lab_big_orders PURGE;         -- drops its indexes tooCO> DROP INDEX lab_cust_upper_ix;
Does the database use my index? (a first look)
CO> EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM lab_big_orders WHERE customer_id = 10;-- look for INDEX RANGE SCAN (index used) or TABLE ACCESS FULLCO> SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);-- Chapter 29 explains how to read plans

19.2 Sequences

A sequence is a schema object that generates unique numbers, typically for primary keys. It is independent of any table, safe for many sessions at once, and fast because values are cached in memory.

CREATE SEQUENCE name   [START WITH n] [INCREMENT BY n]   [MAXVALUE n | NOMAXVALUE] [MINVALUE n | NOMINVALUE]   [CYCLE | NOCYCLE] [CACHE n | NOCACHE] [ORDER | NOORDER];
OptionDefaultMeaning
START WITH1 (or MINVALUE)The first number generated
INCREMENT BY1Step between numbers; negative = descending
MAXVALUE / MINVALUENOMAXVALUE (10^28) / 1Limits
CYCLE / NOCYCLENOCYCLERestart at MINVALUE after the max (CYCLE) or raise an error (NOCYCLE)
CACHE n / NOCACHECACHE 20Number of values kept in memory; unused cached values are lost on restart (gaps)

Exercise 19.2 Generate and use numbers

CO> CREATE SEQUENCE lab_invoice_seq START WITH 1000 INCREMENT BY 5 MAXVALUE 1020 NOCYCLE NOCACHE;CO> SELECT lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual;     -- 1000 : NEXTVAL generates the next numberCO> SELECT lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual;     -- 1005-- 1005 : CURRVAL repeats the last value THIS session gotCO> SELECT lab_invoice_seq.CURRVAL FROM dual; CO> CREATE TABLE lab_invoice (invoice_no NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(10,2));CO> INSERT INTO lab_invoice VALUES (lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL, 1, 99.90);       -- 1010CO> INSERT INTO lab_invoice VALUES (lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL, 2, 15.00);       -- 1015-- the rows are undone, the sequence is NOT: numbers 1010 and 1015 are lost (a gap)CO> ROLLBACK;CO> SELECT lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual;     -- 1020 : the last allowed valueCO> SELECT lab_invoice_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual;ORA-08004: sequence LAB_INVOICE_SEQ.NEXTVAL exceeds MAXVALUE and cannot be instantiated
-- change most options (but NOT START WITH)CO> ALTER SEQUENCE lab_invoice_seq MAXVALUE 99999 INCREMENT BY 1;CO> SELECT sequence_name, last_number, increment_by, cache_size, cycle_flag FROM user_sequences;CO> DROP SEQUENCE lab_invoice_seq;
Using a sequence as a default (12c and later)
CO> CREATE SEQUENCE lab_ticket_seq;CO> CREATE TABLE lab_ticket (ticket_no NUMBER DEFAULT lab_ticket_seq.NEXTVAL PRIMARY KEY, subject VARCHAR2(100));-- ticket_no is filled from the sequenceCO> INSERT INTO lab_ticket (subject) VALUES ('first');-- an identity column (Chapter 17) does the same job with a hidden sequence

Exam focus

  • NEXTVAL must be called in a session before CURRVAL is allowed (ORA-08002).
  • NEXTVAL and CURRVAL can be used in a SELECT list, INSERT ... VALUES, UPDATE ... SET; not in a WHERE clause, a subquery, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, ORDER BY or a view’s query.
  • Sequences are not gap-free: a rollback, an error or a cache loss leaves gaps; they are not transaction safe.
  • ALTER SEQUENCE cannot change START WITH; recreate the sequence instead.
  • If you INSERT ... SELECT with seq.NEXTVAL, every row gets a new number.

Tip: HR has three sequences (DEPARTMENTS_SEQ, EMPLOYEES_SEQ, LOCATIONS_SEQ). Look at them with SELECT sequence_name, last_number, increment_by FROM user_sequences; as HR: the numbers are used by the HR triggers and by the exam’s favourite INSERT statements.

↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP SEQUENCE lab_ticket_seq;       CO> DROP TABLE lab_ticket PURGE;CO> DROP TABLE lab_invoice PURGE;

19.3 Synonyms

A synonym is an alias for another object (table, view, sequence, procedure ...). It hides the owner and the name, shortens long names and lets applications keep working when the real object is moved or renamed. A synonym stores no data.

KindCreated byVisible to
Private synonymCREATE SYNONYM s FOR owner.objectOnly its owner (the schema that created it)
Public synonymCREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM s FOR owner.object (needs the CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM privilege)Every user; but each user also needs privileges on the object

Exercise 19.3 Alias an object across schemas

-- private synonym in my own schemaCO> CREATE SYNONYM lab_cust FOR customers;-- same as SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customersCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_cust; -- as an administrator: let CO read HR, then give CO a short name for it-- the synonym does NOT grant access by itselfSYSTEM> GRANT SELECT ON hr.employees TO co;CO> CREATE SYNONYM hr_emp FOR hr.employees;CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hr_emp;                                  -- 107 CO> SELECT synonym_name, table_owner, table_name FROM user_synonyms;CO> DROP SYNONYM lab_cust;CO> DROP SYNONYM hr_emp;

Exam focus

  • A synonym does not give any privilege: the user still needs a privilege on the underlying object.
  • Dropping the object leaves the synonym in place but INVALID.
  • Dropping a synonym never affects the object.
  • A private synonym takes precedence over a public one with the same name.
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
SYSTEM> REVOKE SELECT ON hr.employees FROM co;

Chapter 20: Views

Prompts: CO> and HR> • Exam topic 13: Managing Views • Creates only LAB_ objects (views named LAB_..._V).

Topics in this chapter

  • 20.1 What a View Is
  • 20.2 Simple and Complex Views
  • 20.3 DML Through Views
  • 20.4 Views as a Security Layer
  • 20.5 Inline Views, FORCE and Replacing
  • 20.6 Answers to the Lab Challenges

20.1 What a View Is

A view is a stored query with a name. It contains no data of its own: each time you query a view, Oracle runs the stored SELECT against the base tables. Views simplify complex joins, restrict access to certain columns or rows, present business names, and give you a stable interface when tables change.

CREATE [OR REPLACE] [FORCE | NOFORCE] VIEW view_name [(alias [, alias ...])]AS  subquery[WITH CHECK OPTION [CONSTRAINT name]][WITH READ ONLY [CONSTRAINT name]];
ClauseMeaning
OR REPLACERedefine the view if it exists (keeps grants)
FORCECreate it even if the base tables do not exist yet (the view is INVALID until they do)
(alias, ...)Names for the view’s columns instead of those of the subquery
WITH CHECK OPTIONDML through the view must produce rows that the view can see
WITH READ ONLYNo DML at all through the view

20.2 Simple and Complex Views

Simple viewComplex view
TablesOneOne or more
Functions / expressionsNoYes
GROUP BY / DISTINCT / aggregatesNoYes
DML through the viewUsually possibleNot always (see below)

Exercise 20.1 Hide, rename and summarise

CO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_open_orders_v AS      SELECT order_id, order_tms, customer_id, store_id      FROM   lab_orders      -- a row filter: the view hides every other status      WHERE  order_status = 'OPEN';CO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_open_orders_v;CO> DESC lab_open_orders_v -- column aliases in the view definition: readable names for end usersCO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_customer_names_v (id, name, mail) AS      SELECT customer_id, full_name, email_address FROM lab_customers; -- a complex view: join + aggregation, ready for reportsCO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_customer_revenue_v AS      SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name,             COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)            AS orders_placed,             SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)      AS revenue      FROM   lab_customers c      JOIN   lab_orders o        ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id      JOIN   lab_order_items oi  ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id      GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.full_name;-- the top five customersCO> SELECT * FROM lab_customer_revenue_v ORDER BY revenue DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
A view of the HR schema you already have
-- the six-table join of Chapter 11, written by OracleHR> SELECT * FROM emp_details_view WHERE employee_id = 100;-- the stored query (a LONG column)HR> SELECT text FROM user_views WHERE view_name = 'EMP_DETAILS_VIEW';

Exam focus

  • ORDER BY is allowed in a view definition, but the order of rows is guaranteed only by the ORDER BY of the query that selects from the view.
  • If the subquery uses expressions, you must give them aliases (or list column names in the view).
  • DROP VIEW never touches the base data.
↩ RESET — undo this exercise
CO> DROP VIEW lab_open_orders_v;   CO> DROP VIEW lab_customer_names_v;   CO> DROP VIEW lab_customer_revenue_v;

20.3 DML Through Views

You can INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE through a view when Oracle can map each view row to exactly one row of one base table. The rules:

If the view definition contains ...DELETEUPDATEINSERT
A simple SELECT of one tableYesYesYes (mandatory columns must be in the view or have defaults)
GROUP BY, aggregate functions, DISTINCT, ROWNUM, set operatorsNoNoNo
An expression or pseudocolumn in a columnYesNot that columnNot that column
A joinOnly if the table is key-preservedColumns of the key-preserved tableOnly that table’s columns
WITH READ ONLYNoNoNo

A table in a join view is key-preserved when each of its rows appears at most once in the view result (its key is also unique in the join). You can update only columns of the key-preserved table.

Exercise 20.2 WITH CHECK OPTION and WITH READ ONLY

CO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_open_orders_v AS      SELECT order_id, order_tms, customer_id, store_id, order_status      FROM   lab_orders WHERE order_status = 'OPEN'      WITH CHECK OPTION CONSTRAINT lab_open_orders_ck; -- fine: the row stays visibleCO> UPDATE lab_open_orders_v SET store_id = 2 WHERE order_id = 90001;CO> UPDATE lab_open_orders_v SET order_status = 'PAID' WHERE order_id = 90001;ORA-01402: view WITH CHECK OPTION where-clause violation                 -- the row would leave the view: refusedCO> INSERT INTO lab_open_orders_v (order_id, order_tms, customer_id, store_id, order_status)    -- also refused: a PAID row would be invisible    VALUES (90201, SYSTIMESTAMP, 1, 1, 'PAID');CO> ROLLBACK; CO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_orders_ro_v AS SELECT order_id, order_status FROM lab_orders WITH READ ONLY;CO> DELETE FROM lab_orders_ro_v WHERE order_id = 90001;ORA-42399: cannot perform a DML operation on a read-only view

Exam focus

  • Without WITH CHECK OPTION you can change a row through a view so that it vanishes from the view.
  • DELETE through a view is not allowed when the view contains DISTINCT, aggregates, GROUP BY, ROWNUM, or a set operator.
  • INSERT through a view fails when a NOT NULL column of the base table is not in the view and has no default (ORA-01400).

Beyond the exam — newer Oracle releases: Complex views can be made updatable with an INSTEAD OF trigger (PL/SQL). Materialized views store the result and refresh it; Chapter 29 shows when they matter for SH.

20.4 Views as a Security Layer

Views let you give a user some columns and some rows of a table without giving the table. The user needs privileges on the view only (Chapter 22 shows the grant).

CO> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_customer_public_v AS      -- only the first name      SELECT customer_id, SUBSTR(full_name, 1, INSTR(full_name || ' ', ' ') - 1) AS first_name      -- no e-mail address at all      FROM   lab_customers;-- (later, Chapter 22) the user sees the view, not the tableCO> GRANT SELECT ON lab_customer_public_v TO hr;

20.5 Inline Views, FORCE and Replacing

A subquery in the FROM clause (Chapter 13) is an inline view: a view that exists only for one statement. A top-N query is the classic use. A view that depends on a table that is later changed or dropped becomes INVALID; Oracle recompiles it automatically on next use if it can.

-- allowed, but with compilation errorsCO> CREATE FORCE VIEW lab_future_v AS SELECT * FROM lab_not_yet_created;CO> SELECT object_name, status FROM user_objects WHERE object_name = 'LAB_FUTURE_V';    -- INVALIDCO> CREATE TABLE lab_not_yet_created (n NUMBER);-- recompiles itself and worksCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_future_v;-- or recompile by handCO> ALTER VIEW lab_future_v COMPILE;CO> DROP VIEW lab_future_v;   CO> DROP TABLE lab_not_yet_created PURGE;
View facts
Where views are listedUSER_VIEWS (name and defining text), USER_OBJECTS (status), USER_TAB_COLUMNS (columns)
RenameRENAME old TO new;
Change the definitionCREATE OR REPLACE VIEW (grants survive), not ALTER VIEW
RemoveDROP VIEW name;

20.6 Answers to the Lab Challenges

Challenge 20.5 Write a view over HR that shows every department with its manager name and headcount, readable by a reporting user.

HR> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lab_dept_summary_v AS      SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, m.last_name AS manager, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS headcount      FROM   departments d LEFT JOIN employees m ON d.manager_id = m.employee_id                           LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id      GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.department_name, m.last_name;

Chapter 21: Data Dictionary Views

Prompts: CO>, HR> and SYSTEM> • Exam topic 15: Managing Objects with Data Dictionary Views • Read-only queries, plus cleanup of your LAB_ objects.

Topics in this chapter

  • 21.1 The Data Dictionary
  • 21.2 The Views You Will Use Every Day
  • 21.3 Generating DDL and Documentation from the Dictionary
  • 21.4 Comments and Dependencies
  • 21.5 Answers to the Lab Challenges

21.1 The Data Dictionary

Oracle describes itself in tables: the data dictionary stores the definition of every object, user, privilege, constraint and storage structure. It is owned by SYS, maintained automatically, and read-only for you. You query it through views with SELECT, like any data. It is the first place to look when you do not know the database.

PrefixShowsWho can query it
USER_Objects you own (no OWNER column)Everyone
ALL_Objects you own plus objects you have been granted access to (has an OWNER column)Everyone
DBA_Every object in the databaseUsers with DBA-level privileges (e.g. SYSTEM)
V$ / GV$Dynamic performance views: the live state of the instance (sessions, memory, waits)Users with SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE or DBA
CDB_DBA_ information across all containersCommon administrators in the root

Exam focus

  • Object names are stored in UPPERCASE (unless created with double quotes): WHERE table_name = 'EMPLOYEES'.
  • USER_ views have no OWNER column; ALL_ and DBA_ do.
  • The dictionary is read-only: Oracle updates it when you run DDL; you never INSERT into it.

Exercise 21.1 Start with the dictionary of the dictionary

-- DICTIONARY (or DICT) lists all dictionary viewsCO> SELECT table_name, comments FROM dictionary WHERE table_name LIKE 'USER_T%' ORDER BY 1;-- what each column of a view meansCO> SELECT column_name, comments FROM dict_columns WHERE table_name = 'USER_TABLES';-- hundreds of viewsCO> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dictionary;

21.2 The Views You Will Use Every Day

ViewAnswers the question
USER_OBJECTSWhat objects do I own, of which type, and are they VALID? (OBJECT_NAME, OBJECT_TYPE, STATUS, CREATED, LAST_DDL_TIME)
USER_TABLESWhich tables do I have? (TABLE_NAME, NUM_ROWS, TEMPORARY, TABLESPACE_NAME)
USER_TAB_COLUMNSWhat are the columns, data types, lengths, nullability and defaults of my tables and views?
USER_CONSTRAINTSWhich constraints exist? (CONSTRAINT_TYPE P, U, R, C; STATUS; R_CONSTRAINT_NAME; DELETE_RULE; SEARCH_CONDITION)
USER_CONS_COLUMNSWhich columns belong to each constraint, in which POSITION?
USER_INDEXES / USER_IND_COLUMNSWhich indexes exist, are they unique, and on which columns?
USER_VIEWSWhich views exist and what is their query (TEXT)?
USER_SEQUENCESWhich sequences exist (LAST_NUMBER, INCREMENT_BY, CACHE_SIZE)?
USER_SYNONYMSWhich synonyms exist and what do they point to?
USER_TAB_PRIVS / USER_SYS_PRIVS / USER_ROLE_PRIVSWhich privileges and roles do I hold or have I granted?
USER_TAB_COMMENTS / USER_COL_COMMENTSWhat do the comments on my tables and columns say?
USER_UNUSED_COL_TABS, USER_RECYCLEBINWhich tables have unused columns / dropped tables in the recycle bin?
USER_DEPENDENCIESWhich object uses which other object?

Exercise 21.2 Explore an unfamiliar schema

-- a census of the schemaCO> SELECT object_type, COUNT(*) AS n FROM user_objects GROUP BY object_type ORDER BY n DESC;-- anything broken?CO> SELECT object_name, status, last_ddl_time FROM user_objects WHERE status <> 'VALID';CO> SELECT table_name, num_rows FROM user_tables WHERE table_name NOT LIKE 'LAB%' ORDER BY table_name;CO> SELECT column_id, column_name, data_type, data_length, nullable    -- the same as DESC orders    FROM   user_tab_columns WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS' ORDER BY column_id; -- constraints of a table, with their type spelled outCO> SELECT constraint_name,           DECODE(constraint_type, 'P','Primary key', 'U','Unique', 'R','Foreign key', 'C','Check / Not null') AS kind,           status    FROM   user_constraints WHERE table_name = 'ORDER_ITEMS' ORDER BY constraint_type; -- which columns form the primary key of ORDER_ITEMS?CO> SELECT cc.column_name, cc.position    FROM   user_constraints c JOIN user_cons_columns cc ON cc.constraint_name = c.constraint_name    WHERE  c.table_name = 'ORDER_ITEMS' AND c.constraint_type = 'P' ORDER BY cc.position;
Foreign keys: child column to parent table
CO> SELECT c.table_name  AS child_table,  cc.column_name AS child_column,           p.table_name  AS parent_table, c.delete_rule    FROM   user_constraints c    JOIN   user_cons_columns cc ON cc.constraint_name = c.constraint_name    -- the referenced primary/unique key    JOIN   user_constraints  p  ON p.constraint_name  = c.r_constraint_name    WHERE  c.constraint_type = 'R' AND c.table_name NOT LIKE 'LAB%'    -- every relationship of the CO diagram    ORDER  BY c.table_name;
ALL_ and DBA_ views
-- only what I may seeHR>     SELECT owner, table_name FROM all_tables WHERE owner IN ('HR','CO','SH') ORDER BY 1, 2;SYSTEM> SELECT owner, COUNT(*) AS tables FROM dba_tables WHERE owner IN ('HR','CO','SH') GROUP BY owner;   -- everythingSYSTEM> SELECT username, account_status, created FROM dba_users WHERE username IN ('HR','CO','SH');

21.3 Generating DDL and Documentation from the Dictionary

Because the dictionary is data, you can generate statements from it. This is how DBAs clean up and how analysts document a schema.

-- the DROP statements for all my LAB_ tables (run the output after reading it!)CO> SELECT 'DROP TABLE ' || table_name || ' CASCADE CONSTRAINTS PURGE;' AS cleanup_statement    FROM   user_tables WHERE table_name LIKE 'LAB%' ORDER BY table_name;CO> SELECT 'DROP VIEW ' || view_name || ';' FROM user_views WHERE view_name LIKE 'LAB%';CO> SELECT 'DROP SEQUENCE ' || sequence_name || ';' FROM user_sequences WHERE sequence_name LIKE 'LAB%'; -- the full CREATE statement of an object, rebuilt by OracleCO> SET LONG 20000CO> SELECT DBMS_METADATA.GET_DDL('TABLE', 'ORDERS') FROM dual; -- a one-line-per-column data dictionary of the schema (names, types, comments)CO> SELECT t.table_name, t.column_name, t.data_type || '(' || t.data_length || ')' AS data_type, c.comments    FROM   user_tab_columns t LEFT JOIN user_col_comments c ON c.table_name = t.table_name AND c.column_name = t.column_name    WHERE  t.table_name IN ('PRODUCTS','ORDERS') ORDER BY t.table_name, t.column_id;

Tip: In SQLcl, INFO orders prints columns, indexes, constraints and statistics of a table in one step, and DDL orders prints its CREATE statement. They are shortcuts over exactly the views of this chapter.

Note: Run the generated DROP statements only for the objects you really want gone. Always read the generated script first.

21.4 Comments and Dependencies

CO> COMMENT ON TABLE lab_orders IS 'Practice copy of ORDERS used by the Enterprise Insight Project';CO> COMMENT ON COLUMN lab_orders.order_status IS 'OPEN, PAID, SHIPPED, COMPLETE, CANCELLED or REFUNDED';CO> SELECT table_name, comments FROM user_tab_comments WHERE table_name LIKE 'LAB_ORD%';CO> SELECT name, type, referenced_name, referenced_type FROM user_dependencies WHERE name = 'LAB_ORDER_TOTALS_V';   -- what does my view rely on?

Exam focus

  • COMMENT ON ... IS '' (empty text) removes a comment.
  • A view that selects from a dropped table is INVALID in USER_OBJECTS; USER_DEPENDENCIES shows what it uses.
  • The columns of a view are in USER_TAB_COLUMNS; its defining query is in USER_VIEWS.TEXT.

HR> SELECT object_type, COUNT(*) FROM user_objects GROUP BY object_type;HR> SELECT object_name, object_type FROM user_objects WHERE object_type IN ('SEQUENCE','TRIGGER') ORDER BY 2, 1;

  • 22.6 What Do I Have? Privileges in the Dictionary
  • 22.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

22.1 Users, Authentication and Authorization

A user is an account in the database; it owns a schema. Authentication proves who you are (a password); authorization decides what you may do. In Oracle authorization is built from privileges, and privileges are collected into roles.

ConceptMeaning
System privilegeThe right to perform a kind of action in the database, for example CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE ANY TABLE, CREATE USER
Object privilegeThe right to perform an action on one specific object, for example SELECT ON hr.employees, UPDATE (salary) ON hr.employees, EXECUTE ON proc
RoleA named group of privileges (system and object) that you grant to users or other roles
SchemaThe objects a user owns. The owner has all privileges on them and can grant them to others

22.2 Creating Users

Exercise 22.1 Create the project analyst account

SYSTEM> CREATE USER insight IDENTIFIED BY "Lab_Insight_2026"          -- the password                   DEFAULT TABLESPACE users                          -- where its tables go                   -- how much space it may use there                   QUOTA 100M ON users;-- without this the user cannot even log inSYSTEM> GRANT CREATE SESSION TO insight;SYSTEM> SELECT username, account_status, default_tablespace FROM dba_users WHERE username = 'INSIGHT'; $ sql insight/Lab_Insight_2026@localhost:1521/FREEPDB1INSIGHT> SELECT USER FROM dual;                                      -- INSIGHTINSIGHT> CREATE TABLE t (n NUMBER);ORA-01031: insufficient privileges                                 -- logging in is allowed, creating tables is not
ALTER USER ...Effect
IDENTIFIED BY "new"Change the password
PASSWORD EXPIREThe user must choose a new password at next login
ACCOUNT LOCK / ACCOUNT UNLOCKBlock / allow logins
QUOTA n ON tablespaceSpace allowance (UNLIMITED allowed)
DEFAULT TABLESPACE, TEMPORARY TABLESPACEWhere objects and sorts are stored
DROP USER u CASCADERemove the user and every object it owns (without CASCADE it fails if objects exist)

Exam focus

  • A new user has no privileges, not even CREATE SESSION.
  • A user needs a quota on a tablespace to create objects that store data (ORA-01950: no privileges on tablespace).
  • Passwords are case-sensitive in current releases.

22.3 System Privileges

PrivilegeAllows
CREATE SESSIONConnect to the database
CREATE TABLECreate tables in your own schema; also lets you create indexes and constraints on them
CREATE VIEW, CREATE SEQUENCE, CREATE SYNONYMThe same for those objects (CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM is separate)
CREATE ANY TABLE, DROP ANY TABLE, SELECT ANY TABLEThe action in any schema: extremely powerful
CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USERManage accounts
UNLIMITED TABLESPACENo quota limit anywhere
SYSTEM> GRANT CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE SEQUENCE, CREATE SYNONYM TO insight;-- WITH ADMIN OPTION: INSIGHT may grant it to othersSYSTEM> GRANT CREATE ANY TABLE TO insight WITH ADMIN OPTION;-- (for a system privilege, revoking does NOT cascade)SYSTEM> REVOKE CREATE ANY TABLE FROM insight;-- the privileges active in this sessionINSIGHT> SELECT * FROM session_privs ORDER BY privilege;

22.4 Object Privileges

PrivilegeOnAllows
SELECTTable, view, sequenceRead rows (for a sequence: use NEXTVAL / CURRVAL)
INSERTTable, viewAdd rows (can be limited to columns)
UPDATETable, viewChange rows (can be limited to columns: UPDATE (salary))
DELETETable, viewRemove rows
ALTERTable, sequenceChange the object
INDEX, REFERENCESTableCreate an index / a foreign key that points to it
EXECUTEProcedure, function, packageRun it
ALL [PRIVILEGES]AnyEvery privilege you hold on the object
GRANT privilege [(column, ...)] [, ...]  ON  [schema.]object  TO  user | role | PUBLIC  [WITH GRANT OPTION];REVOKE privilege [, ...]                  ON  [schema.]object  FROM user | role | PUBLIC;

Exercise 22.2 Let INSIGHT read the three divisions

-- the OWNER (or an administrator) grants object privilegesHR> GRANT SELECT ON employees   TO insight;HR> GRANT SELECT ON departments TO insight;HR> GRANT SELECT ON jobs        TO insight;-- the view of Chapter 20, not the base tablesCO> GRANT SELECT ON lab_order_totals_v TO insight;SH> GRANT SELECT ON sales     TO insight;SH> GRANT SELECT ON products  TO insight;SH> GRANT SELECT ON times     TO insight;SH> GRANT SELECT ON channels  TO insight; -- 107 : the owner’s name qualifies the tableINSIGHT> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hr.employees;INSIGHT> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;ORA-00942: table or view does not exist                           -- not in INSIGHT’s own schema: use hr.employees or a synonym-- needs CREATE SYNONYM (granted above)INSIGHT> CREATE SYNONYM employees FOR hr.employees;INSIGHT> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;                            -- 107INSIGHT> DELETE FROM hr.employees;ORA-01031: insufficient privileges                                -- SELECT only: the table is safe
Column-level privileges
-- may change ONLY these two columnsHR>      GRANT UPDATE (salary, commission_pct) ON employees TO insight;-- allowed (but needs SELECT too for the WHERE)INSIGHT> UPDATE hr.employees SET salary = salary WHERE employee_id = 100;INSIGHT> UPDATE hr.employees SET last_name = 'X' WHERE employee_id = 100;ORA-01031: insufficient privilegesINSIGHT> ROLLBACK;-- column privileges are revoked at table levelHR>      REVOKE UPDATE ON employees FROM insight;
WITH GRANT OPTION and cascading revoke
System privilegeObject privilege
Allow the grantee to pass it onWITH ADMIN OPTIONWITH GRANT OPTION
Revoking from the first granteeDoes not revoke from the users they granted it toCascades: those users lose it too
Can be limited to columnsNoYes (INSERT, UPDATE, REFERENCES)

Exam focus

  • WITH GRANT OPTION is for object privileges; WITH ADMIN OPTION for system privileges and roles.
  • GRANT ... TO PUBLIC gives the privilege to every user, present and future.
  • A user always has all privileges on objects of his own schema.
  • Revoking an object privilege that was passed on with GRANT OPTION also removes it from everyone who received it through that user.

22.5 Roles

Granting dozens of privileges to every user is error-prone. A role bundles privileges: create it, grant privileges to the role, then grant the role to users. Change the role once and every holder changes with it.

Exercise 22.3 A reporting role

SYSTEM> CREATE ROLE ei_analyst;                                   -- a role starts empty-- object privileges go to the roleHR>     GRANT SELECT ON employees   TO ei_analyst;HR>     GRANT SELECT ON departments TO ei_analyst;SH>     GRANT SELECT ON customers   TO ei_analyst;SYSTEM> GRANT CREATE SESSION, CREATE VIEW TO ei_analyst;          -- system privileges too-- the user receives everything at onceSYSTEM> GRANT ei_analyst TO insight;INSIGHT> SELECT role FROM session_roles;                          -- EI_ANALYST -- remove the whole bundle from one userSYSTEM> REVOKE ei_analyst FROM insight;-- delete the role: every holder loses itSYSTEM> DROP ROLE ei_analyst;
Predefined rolesTypical content
CONNECTHistorically only CREATE SESSION (in current releases it is just that)
RESOURCECreate tables, sequences, procedures, triggers in your schema
DB_DEVELOPER_ROLEThe modern bundle of privileges for developers (recommended)
DBANearly all system privileges: never give it to learners
SELECT_CATALOG_ROLERead access to the DBA_/V$ dictionary views

Note: Privileges received through a role do not work inside stored procedures; they need direct grants. This is an advanced point that the exam rarely asks.

Privileges versus roles: which to use
Privilege granted directlyPrivilege granted through a role
AdministrationOne GRANT per user and per privilegeOne GRANT of the role per user; change the role once
Revoking everythingMany REVOKEsOne REVOKE of the role
Good forA one-off exception; stored-procedure accessGroups of people with the same job

22.6 What Do I Have? Privileges in the Dictionary

INSIGHT> SELECT * FROM user_sys_privs;             -- system privileges granted to me directlyINSIGHT> SELECT * FROM user_role_privs;            -- roles granted to me-- object privileges I RECEIVEDINSIGHT> SELECT owner, table_name, privilege, grantor, grantable FROM user_tab_privs_recd;-- object privileges I GRANTEDHR>      SELECT grantee, table_name, privilege, grantable FROM user_tab_privs_made;SYSTEM>  SELECT grantee, privilege, admin_option FROM dba_sys_privs WHERE grantee = 'INSIGHT';SYSTEM>  SELECT grantee, owner, table_name, privilege FROM dba_tab_privs WHERE grantee = 'INSIGHT';

Chapter 23: Time Zones and Intervals

Prompts: SH>, CO> and INSIGHT> • Exam topic 16: Managing Data in Different Time Zones (CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIMESTAMP, INTERVAL data types) • Session settings reset when you disconnect.

Topics in this chapter

  • 23.1 Date and Time Data Types
  • 23.2 The Two Time Zones and the Current Time
  • 23.3 Time Zone Values and Conversion
  • 23.4 INTERVAL Data Types
  • 23.5 Daylight Saving Time and Practical Advice
  • 23.6 Answers to the Lab Challenges

23.1 Date and Time Data Types

TypeStoresTime zone
DATEDate and time to the secondNone
TIMESTAMP(p)Date and time with fractional seconds (p = 0–9 digits, default 6)None
TIMESTAMP(p) WITH TIME ZONEA timestamp plus a stored time zone (an offset such as +02:00 or a region such as Europe/Paris)Stored with the value
TIMESTAMP(p) WITH LOCAL TIME ZONEA timestamp normalised to the database time zone when stored, and shown in the session time zone when readConverted automatically
INTERVAL YEAR(p) TO MONTHA span of years and months—
INTERVAL DAY(p) TO SECOND(s)A span of days, hours, minutes, seconds—

23.2 The Two Time Zones and the Current Time

Two time zones matter. The database time zone (DBTIMEZONE) is a property of the database. The session time zone (SESSIONTIMEZONE) belongs to your connection; by default it is that of your client operating system. The functions for “now” differ in the zone they use:

FunctionReturnsZone
SYSDATEDATEDatabase server operating system
SYSTIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONEDatabase server
CURRENT_DATEDATESession time zone
CURRENT_TIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONESession time zone
LOCALTIMESTAMPTIMESTAMP (without zone)Session time zone

Exercise 23.1 Move the session around the world

-- region names handle daylight saving timeSH> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = 'America/New_York';SH> SELECT SESSIONTIMEZONE, DBTIMEZONE FROM dual;America/New_York   +00:00                                    -- the database zone stays what it is-- they now differ by the zone difference (the NY clock is behind)SH> SELECT SYSDATE, CURRENT_DATE FROM dual;SH> SELECT SYSTIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIMESTAMP FROM dual;04-OCT-26 13.15.42.123456 +00:00 | 04-OCT-26 09.15.42.123456 -04:00 | 04-OCT-26 09.15.42.123456--  server zone with offset      | session zone with offset        | session zone, NO zone shown SH> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = 'Asia/Tokyo';SH> SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_DATE FROM dual;          -- +09:00-- back to the client’s own zone (or '+02:00', or DBTIMEZONE)SH> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = LOCAL;

Exam focus

  • SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP use the database server clock; CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and LOCALTIMESTAMP use the session time zone.
  • ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE accepts a region name, an offset such as '-05:00', LOCAL or DBTIMEZONE, and affects only your session.
  • LOCALTIMESTAMP returns a TIMESTAMP without a zone; CURRENT_TIMESTAMP returns one with a zone.
  • CURRENT_DATE and SYSDATE are both DATE values (no zone, no fractions).

23.3 Time Zone Values and Conversion

A time zone can be written as an offset ('+05:30') or as a region name ('Asia/Kolkata', 'Europe/Paris'). Region names know daylight saving time rules; offsets do not. The valid names are in V$TIMEZONE_NAMES.

SH> SELECT tzname FROM v$timezone_names WHERE tzname LIKE 'Europe/%' ORDER BY tzname FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;   -- needs access to V$ viewsSH> SELECT TZ_OFFSET('Asia/Kolkata') AS kolkata, TZ_OFFSET('America/New_York') AS new_york, TZ_OFFSET(SESSIONTIMEZONE) AS mine FROM dual;+05:30   -04:00 or -05:00 (depends on the date)   ...
Function / clausePurpose
TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ(text, fmt)Text to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (use format elements TZH:TZM or TZR)
FROM_TZ(timestamp, ‘zone’)Attach a zone to a plain TIMESTAMP
expr AT TIME ZONE ‘zone’Convert a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE to another zone; the moment is the same, the clock reading changes
expr AT LOCALConvert to the session time zone
CAST(expr AS TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE)Normalise to a local-zone timestamp
EXTRACT(TIMEZONE_HOUR FROM ts), TIMEZONE_MINUTE, TIMEZONE_REGIONPick out the zone parts
NEW_TIME(date, zone1, zone2)Old function for a few US zone abbreviations (AST, EST, PST ...) on DATE values

Exercise 23.2 A meeting for four offices

-- one instant, shown in four local clocksSH> SELECT TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ('2026-11-10 09:00:00 America/New_York', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS TZR') AS new_york FROM dual;SH> SELECT TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ('2026-11-10 09:00:00 America/New_York', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS TZR') AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London'   AS london,           TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ('2026-11-10 09:00:00 America/New_York', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS TZR') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Singapore'  AS singapore,           TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ('2026-11-10 09:00:00 America/New_York', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS TZR') AT TIME ZONE '+05:30'          AS india    FROM   dual;09:00 in New York = 14:00 in London = 22:00 in Singapore = 19:30 in India -- attach a zone to a plain TIMESTAMP, then convert it: the CO order times are plain TIMESTAMPs (assume they were stored in UTC)CO> SELECT order_id, order_tms,           FROM_TZ(order_tms, 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'America/Los_Angeles' AS order_in_la    FROM   orders WHERE order_id <= 3; -- pieces of a zoned timestampSH> SELECT EXTRACT(TIMEZONE_HOUR FROM CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS tz_hour,           EXTRACT(YEAR FROM SYSTIMESTAMP) AS yr, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM SYSTIMESTAMP) AS hr FROM dual;
TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE in action
CO> CREATE TABLE lab_zone_demo (id NUMBER, plain TIMESTAMP, with_tz TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, local_tz TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE);CO> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = 'UTC';CO> INSERT INTO lab_zone_demo VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP '2026-11-10 12:00:00', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-10 12:00:00 +00:00', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-10 12:00:00 +00:00');-- all three read 12:00 (UTC)CO> SELECT plain, with_tz, local_tz FROM lab_zone_demo;CO> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = 'Asia/Tokyo';CO> SELECT plain, with_tz, local_tz FROM lab_zone_demo;plain        12:00             -- unchanged: no zonewith_tz      12:00 +00:00      -- unchanged: it keeps its own zonelocal_tz     21:00             -- re-expressed in the NEW session zone (UTC+9)CO> DROP TABLE lab_zone_demo PURGE;CO> ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE = LOCAL;

Exam focus

  • TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE keeps the zone you gave it; TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE does not store the zone and always shows the session zone.
  • AT TIME ZONE changes how the same instant is displayed; it does not change the instant.
  • Subtracting two TIMESTAMPs gives an INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND; subtracting two DATEs gives a NUMBER of days.

23.4 INTERVAL Data Types

An interval is a length of time, not a point in time. There are two kinds because months and years are not a fixed number of days:

TypeLiteralRange of fields
INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTHINTERVAL ‘2-6’ YEAR TO MONTH (2 years 6 months); INTERVAL ‘18’ MONTHYears and months
INTERVAL DAY TO SECONDINTERVAL ‘3 04:30:00’ DAY TO SECOND; INTERVAL ‘90’ DAY; INTERVAL ‘36’ HOURDays, hours, minutes, seconds (and fractions)

Exercise 23.3 Arithmetic with intervals

-- ORA-01839: 31 Feb does not exist (use ADD_MONTHS instead)SH> SELECT DATE '2026-01-31' + INTERVAL '1' MONTH       AS month_later_fails,           ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2026-01-31', 1)             AS month_later_ok       -- 28-FEB-26    FROM   dual;-- 2 days 3h30 laterSH> SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-03-15 10:00:00' + INTERVAL '2 03:30:00' DAY TO SECOND AS later,           DATE '2026-03-15' + INTERVAL '90' DAY                  AS in_90_days,           DATE '2026-03-15' - INTERVAL '1' YEAR                  AS year_earlier,           INTERVAL '2-6' YEAR TO MONTH + INTERVAL '10' MONTH     AS combined_months     -- +03-04    FROM   dual; -- the difference of two timestamps is an INTERVAL DAY TO SECONDSH> SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-06-15 18:00:00' - TIMESTAMP '2026-06-10 09:30:00' AS elapsed FROM dual;+000000005 08:30:00.000000                                   -- 5 days 8 hours 30 minutes -- build intervals from numbers and from textSH> SELECT NUMTODSINTERVAL(90, 'MINUTE')  AS ninety_minutes,   -- +00 01:30:00           NUMTOYMINTERVAL(18, 'MONTH')   AS eighteen_months,  -- +01-06           TO_DSINTERVAL('2 12:00:00')    AS two_and_a_half_days,           TO_YMINTERVAL('1-3')           AS fifteen_months    FROM   dual;-- pull fields out of an intervalSH> SELECT EXTRACT(DAY FROM (SYSTIMESTAMP - TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00 +00:00')) AS days_since_new_year FROM dual;
ExpressionResult type
date + intervalDATE
timestamp + intervalTIMESTAMP
timestamp - timestampINTERVAL DAY TO SECOND
date - dateNUMBER (days)
interval + interval (same kind)The same interval kind
interval * numberThe same interval kind
DATE - TIMESTAMPConverts the DATE to a TIMESTAMP, giving an INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND

Exam focus

  • INTERVAL '90' DAY and INTERVAL '3' MONTH use different interval types and cannot be added together.
  • TO_CHAR(date) and TO_DATE never apply the session time zone; only the TIMESTAMP-with-zone types do.
  • Use ADD_MONTHS (not + INTERVAL MONTH) when the day of the month may not exist in the target month.

23.5 Daylight Saving Time and Practical Advice

  • Store event times in TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (or TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE, or UTC in a plain TIMESTAMP) and display them in the user’s zone with AT TIME ZONE.
  • Use region names, not fixed offsets, for people and places: 'America/New_York' knows when the clocks change.
  • On the night of a change, one local hour does not exist (spring) or happens twice (autumn). Arithmetic with INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND counts real elapsed time; adding INTERVAL '1' DAY to a zoned timestamp keeps the wall-clock time.
  • Never compare timestamps from different zones by their text; compare the values.
-- the clocks in New York go forward on 8 March 2026 at 02:00: 24 hours later is 25 hours of wall clock the next daySH> SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-03-08 00:00:00 America/New_York' + INTERVAL '1' DAY                  AS plus_one_day,           TIMESTAMP '2026-03-08 00:00:00 America/New_York' + NUMTODSINTERVAL(24, 'HOUR')       AS plus_24_hours    FROM   dual;

Chapter 24: Analytic (Window) Functions

Prompts: SH> and HR> • Beyond the 1Z0-071 exam, essential for analysts • Read-only chapter.

Topics in this chapter

  • 24.1 Aggregates That Keep Every Row
  • 24.2 Aggregates as Analytic Functions
  • 24.3 Ranking Functions
  • 24.4 LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE
  • 24.5 Percentiles and Statistics
  • 24.6 Choosing Between GROUP BY and Analytic Functions
  • 24.7 Answers to the Lab Challenges

24.1 Aggregates That Keep Every Row

A group function with GROUP BY collapses rows: you lose the detail. An analytic function (window function) computes the same kinds of values without collapsing: every input row is returned, together with a value calculated over a window of related rows. It answers “how does this row compare with its group?” in a single pass.

function_name ( arguments )  OVER  (        [ PARTITION BY expr [, ...] ]          -- the groups (omit for one big group)        [ ORDER BY expr [ASC|DESC] [, ...] ]   -- the order inside each group        -- which rows around the current one        [ ROWS | RANGE BETWEEN frame_start AND frame_end ] )
PartMeaning
PARTITION BYSplits the rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY, but rows stay)
ORDER BY (inside OVER)Orders the rows within each partition; required for ranking, LAG/LEAD, running totals
Window frameThe set of rows around the current row that the function sees. Default with ORDER BY: from the first row up to the current row

Exam focus

  • Analytic functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and before the final ORDER BY, so they may appear only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY, never in WHERE or HAVING.
  • To filter on an analytic result, wrap the query in an inline view and filter the outer query.

24.2 Aggregates as Analytic Functions

Exercise 24.1 Each employee next to the department figures

HR> SELECT department_id, last_name, salary,           SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id)                    AS dept_payroll,           ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id), 2)          AS dept_avg,           ROUND(100 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id), 1) AS pct_of_dept,           salary - ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id))    AS vs_avg    FROM   employees WHERE department_id IN (60, 90)    ORDER  BY department_id, salary DESC;60 James    9000 28800 5760  31.3  324060 Miller   6000 28800 5760  20.8   240...90 King    24000 58000 19333.33 41.4 466790 Yang    17000 58000 19333.33 29.3 -2333 ...        -- every employee is still a row
Running totals and moving averages

With ORDER BY inside OVER, aggregates become cumulative. A frame narrows the window to a number of neighbouring rows.

HR> SELECT employee_id, hire_date, salary,           SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date, employee_id)                                                   AS running_payroll,           ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date, employee_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)) AS moving_avg_3    -- the order is unstable with ROWNUM: shown for the shape only    FROM   employees WHERE department_id = 50 AND ROWNUM <= 8;
FrameMeaning
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROWFrom the partition start to the current row (the default frame with ORDER BY and ROWS/RANGE unspecified: RANGE)
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROWThe current row and the two before it
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWINGThe row, its predecessor and its successor
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWINGThe whole partition
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL ’7’ DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROWA value-based window (rows within 7 days)

Exam focus

  • ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE treats rows with the same ORDER BY value as one position (ties are included together).
  • Without a frame clause, SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY y) uses RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, so tied rows share the same running total.

24.3 Ranking Functions

FunctionBehaviour on tiesSequence for salaries 24000, 17000, 17000, 14000
ROW_NUMBER()Never ties: arbitrary but unique numbers1, 2, 3, 4
RANK()Equal values share a rank; gaps follow1, 2, 2, 4
DENSE_RANK()Equal values share a rank; no gaps1, 2, 2, 3
NTILE(n)Splits the ordered rows into n buckets of nearly equal sizewith n = 2: 1, 1, 2, 2
PERCENT_RANK() / CUME_DIST()Relative position between 0 and 1 / cumulative distribution

Exercise 24.2 Ranking the HR salaries

HR> SELECT last_name, salary,           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_no,           RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rnk    FROM   employees ORDER BY salary DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;King     24000  1 1 1Yang     17000  2 2 2Garcia   17000  3 2 2          -- the tie: RANK repeats 2, ROW_NUMBER keeps countingSingh    14000  4 4 3          -- RANK skips 3, DENSE_RANK does notPartners  13500  5 5 4 -- the highest paid person IN EACH DEPARTMENT (top-N per group): rank, then filter in an outer queryHR> SELECT department_id, last_name, salary    FROM  (SELECT department_id, last_name, salary,                  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk           FROM   employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL)    -- ties would return more than one person per department    WHERE  rnk = 1 ORDER BY department_id; -- split employees into four pay quartilesHR> SELECT last_name, salary, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS quartile FROM employees;

24.4 LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE

FunctionReturns
LAG(expr [, n [, default]]) OVER (...)The value of the row n rows before (default 1); NULL (or default) if there is none
LEAD(expr [, n [, default]]) OVER (...)The value of the row n rows after
FIRST_VALUE(expr) OVER (...)The first value of the window
LAST_VALUE(expr) OVER (...)The last value of the window — remember the frame: add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or you get the current row
NTH_VALUE(expr, n) OVER (...)The n-th value of the window
RATIO_TO_REPORT(expr) OVER (...)The row’s share of the partition total (0 to 1)

Exercise 24.3 Month-over-month sales in SH

SH> SELECT t.calendar_month_desc AS month,           SUM(s.amount_sold)                                                              AS sales,           LAG(SUM(s.amount_sold)) OVER (ORDER BY t.calendar_month_desc)                   AS previous_month,           SUM(s.amount_sold) - LAG(SUM(s.amount_sold)) OVER (ORDER BY t.calendar_month_desc) AS change,           ROUND(100 * RATIO_TO_REPORT(SUM(s.amount_sold)) OVER (), 2)                     AS pct_of_period   -- share of all months shown    FROM   sales s JOIN times t ON t.time_id = s.time_id    WHERE  t.calendar_year = 2000    GROUP  BY t.calendar_month_desc ORDER BY t.calendar_month_desc;-- an analytic function may wrap an aggregate: SUM(...) is computed per month first, then LAG looks at the previous month
HR> SELECT last_name, hire_date, salary,           LAG(salary)  OVER (ORDER BY hire_date, employee_id) AS salary_of_previous_hire,           LEAD(last_name) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date, employee_id) AS next_hire,           FIRST_VALUE(last_name) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC                                        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS best_paid_in_dept    FROM   employees WHERE department_id IN (60, 90);
KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST | LAST): an aggregate that picks a row
-- "the name of the best-paid employee of each department" without a ranking subqueryHR> SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS top_salary,           -- ties would pick the MAX name           MAX(last_name) KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY salary DESC) AS top_earner    FROM   employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY department_id;

24.5 Percentiles and Statistics

HR> SELECT MEDIAN(salary)                                              AS median,           PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)           AS p90_interpolated,           PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)           AS p90_actual_value    FROM   employees;HR> SELECT department_id,           ROUND(STDDEV(salary), 2) AS std_dev, ROUND(VARIANCE(salary), 2) AS var    FROM   employees GROUP BY department_id;

24.6 Choosing Between GROUP BY and Analytic Functions

You wantUse
One row per groupGROUP BY with aggregates
Detail rows and group figures side by sideAnalytic aggregate: SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)
Rank within a group; top-N per groupRANK / DENSE_RANK / ROW_NUMBER + inline view
Compare with the previous or next rowLAG / LEAD
Running totals, moving averagesAggregate with ORDER BY and a frame
